Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus soil isolates on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui”). Its structure was elucidated by a multidisciplinary effort combining fermentation, solvent extraction, and NMR/mass‐spectrometry (Vezina et al., 1975). Rapamycin belongs to the “rapalog” class of small‐molecule inhibitors of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapalogs—e.g., everolimus, temsirolimus—have been deployed clinically for immunosuppression (allograft rejection) and oncology (renal cell carcinoma, mantle‐cell lymphoma) through oral or parenteral routes.

•  Immunosuppression: Approved by FDA in 1999 to prevent kidney transplant rejection; systemic exposure dampens T‐cell proliferation via mTORC1 inhibition (Morris et al., 2005).  
•  Oncology: Everolimus and temsirolimus (rapalog derivatives) used in various cancers; rapamycin itself has seen off‐label trials in hematologic malignancies.  
•  Ophthalmology: Intravitreal sirolimus has been evaluated in small clinical studies for noninfectious uveitis (SAVE trial; Hogan et al., 2014) and for proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) prevention. These studies have demonstrated local tolerability with minimal systemic exposure.  

Use in Dry AMD  
No clinical trials to date have registered rapamycin or rapalogs for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, preclinical data in murine dry‐AMD models (e.g., Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice) have shown that intravitreal or subretinal rapamycin preserves photoreceptor function (scotopic ERG) and reduces RPE autofluorescent deposits (Levy et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), supporting translational relevance.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Target: mTORC1—serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates nutrient and growth factor signals to suppress autophagy and promote protein/lipid synthesis.  
•  mTORC1 is composed of mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, DEPTOR (Saxton & Sabatini, 2017).  
•  Rapamycin binds FKBP12, and the FKBP12–rapamycin complex allosterically inhibits mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly toward ULK1 (a key autophagy initiator) and S6K1 (a driver of protein synthesis).

•  Autophagy induction: In cultured human RPE cells loaded with the bisretinoid A2E, rapamycin (10–20 nM) elevates LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreases p62/SQSTM1 levels, and increases ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser555 (Chen et al., 2015).

•  Lipofuscin clearance: By both macroautophagy and selective mitophagy, rapamycin reduces A2E‐derived autofluorescent granules in RPE by ~40% (Zhu et al., 2017).  
•  Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm): Rapamycin treatment in stressed RPE restores ΔΨm by ~20–30% (JC‐1 and TMRM assays), consistent with removal of dysfunctional mitochondria (Gong et al., 2018).

•  ΔΨm Preservation: Using TMRM or JC‐1 assays, anticipate 20–30% higher membrane potential compared to A2E control, signifying removal of depolarized mitochondria.

•  Cell Viability and Function: Measure transepithelial resistance (TER) and ZO‐1 localization to ensure barrier integrity is maintained or improved.

•  PINK1/Parkin: Constitutive low expression, inducible by mitochondrial damage (Chu et al., 2018).

1. Mechanistic Rationale: Directly addresses two core pathological features of dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction—via well‐validated mTORC1/autophagy pathways.  
2. Preclinical Proof‐of‐Concept: In vitro A2E‐RPE and Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse studies have demonstrated robust rescue of RPE health and retinal function.  
3. Local Delivery Feasibility: Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular implants can achieve nanomolar intraocular concentrations while minimizing systemic immunosuppression.

•  Longitudinal in vivo studies in large‐animal AMD models (e.g., pigmented rats or nonhuman primates)

Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.

Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.

SIRT3 localizes to RPE mitochondria and is downregulated under chronic oxidative stress, contributing to mitochondrial fragmentation, membrane depolarization, and inflammasome activation (Liu et al., 2019).  – Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA; thioctic acid) is a naturally occurring organosulfur compound synthesized in mitochondria of plants, animals, and bacteria. • Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid.   – Pulmonary arterial hypertension and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase II studies demonstrated hemodynamic and safety signals (Frost et al., 2018).

  – Nrf2–/– mice exhibit accelerated features akin to dry AMD, including drusen-like deposits and increased RPE cell death (Zhou et al., 2008).

• Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – Bardoxolone methyl contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on the Keap1 sensor protein.   – Phase II detoxifying enzymes: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC).  
  – Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, glutathione peroxidase.  
  – Mitochondrial regulators: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and downstream effectors of biogenesis (TFAM, NRF1) (Katsouri et al., 2016).  
  – Anti-inflammatory: indirect NF-κB inhibition via IKKβ modification, reducing expression of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6.

  – At higher concentrations, bardoxolone methyl can inhibit JAK/STAT signaling and affect mitochondrial permeability transition directly.

Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, and Nrf2 is a validated master regulator of antioxidant defense in RPE.

  • Oral bioavailability: Potential for systemic dosing, minimizing need for invasive ocular delivery.

  • Off-target electrophilicity: Potential for covalent modification of non-Keap1 proteins in RPE, with unknown long-term effects on cell health.

• Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GNX-4975 is a small-molecule inhibitor of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). It was discovered via phenotypic screening for compounds that prevent Ca2+-induced collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in cultured neurons subjected to ischemic insult. Structurally, GNX-4975 bears a novel bicyclic scaffold distinct from classical mPTP modulators (e.g., cyclosporin A or sanglifehrin A). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was discovered through medicinal chemistry optimization of natural oleanane scaffolds to enhance potency for Nrf2 activation while improving pharmacokinetics and safety. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Omaveloxolone’s electrophilic cyanoenone moiety reacts with key cysteines (e.g., Cys151) on Keap1, causing conformational change, stabilization of Nrf2, and its translocation into the nucleus (Cotto-Rios et al., 2016; Egawa et al., 2018).  
• Transcriptional activation: Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of genes encoding phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), and others.  
• Mitochondrial protection: Nrf2 activation also enhances expression of genes that support mitochondrial function: thioredoxin 2 (Trx2), peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx3), and subunits of the electron transport chain (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Nrf2 has been linked to maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via regulation of Bcl-2 family members. By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: Beyond antioxidant genes, Nrf2 induction suppresses NF-κB signaling by up-regulating HO-1 and direct protein–protein interactions with the p65 subunit of NF-κB, leading to reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) (Ahmed et al., 2017).

Given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, omaveloxolone is expected to:  
1. Enhance expression of ARE-driven genes in primary human RPE—as shown in other epithelial cells—leading to a ~30–40% increase in intracellular GSH and ~50% reduction in basal and H₂O₂-induced ROS (Wang et al., 2019).  
2. Preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) under oxidative challenge. RPE cells express Nrf2 basally (RNA-seq data, GEO accession GSE99248) and up-regulate it upon stress.  
3. Decrease secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1) in response to blue-light or A2E-mediated stress, through both direct NF-κB inhibition and secondary antioxidant effects.  
4. Reduce accumulation of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent bisretinoids in RPE by promoting autophagy (Omari et al., 2020), which may be partly driven by crosstalk between Nrf2 and autophagy regulator p62/SQSTM1.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Dry AMD RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation—all directly counteracted by Nrf2 activation.  
• Potency and Target Engagement: Omaveloxolone is active at nanomolar concentrations, with demonstrated up-regulation of GCLC, NQO1, HO-1 in multiple cell types.  
• Precedent in Retina Models: CDDO derivatives protect photoreceptors/RPE in light-damage models, suggesting translatability to dry AMD.  
• Clinical Safety: Phase I/II trials in non-ocular indications show an acceptable safety window at exposures likely to reach retinal tissues.

• Ocular PK: Systemic bioavailability does not guarantee therapeutic levels in the retina/RPE. Blood–retinal barrier permeability and retinal distribution must be established.  
• Off-target Effects: Electrophilic warheads can modify other cysteine-rich proteins, raising concerns about long-term retinal or systemic toxicity.  
• Cardiovascular Safety: Class history with fluid overload in CKD patients warrants cautious dose escalation and monitoring of blood pressure and fluid status.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen biogenesis, complement activation, and para-inflammatory processes that may not be fully addressed by antioxidant therapy alone.

Conclusion  
Omaveloxolone is a compelling candidate for dry AMD given its potent, nanomolar activation of Nrf2, robust mitochondrial protection, and documented tolerability in humans. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution studies, dose-response in RPE and retinal explant models of AMD, and evaluation of complement-mediated inflammatory pathways. • Anti-inflammatory research tool: Since its initial report, BAY 11-7082 has been employed extensively to dissect NF-κB–dependent gene expression in immune cells, endothelial cells, and tumor models (Julien et al., 2007; Karin & Greten, 2005).

MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. MitoQ belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” distinguished from untargeted small-molecule antioxidants by their ability to selectively concentrate within mitochondria. This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. Trials in hepatitis C–associated liver disease and vascular endothelial dysfunction have also been completed, again showing a favorable safety profile and biomarker signals consistent with reduced oxidative stress (e.g., decreased plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no registered clinical trial has targeted dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with MitoQ, nor are there published veterinary or off-label uses in retinal degenerative diseases. However, the rationale for mitochondrial protection in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress is strong, given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis.

1. Mitochondrial accumulation—driven by ΔΨm—achieves intramitochondrial concentrations 100–1,000× higher than in the cytosol or plasma (Murphy & Smith, 2007).  
2. Enzymatic reduction—the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by complex II (and possibly complex I) to ubiquinol, the active antioxidant form.  
3. ROS scavenging—ubiquinol donates electrons to lipid-peroxyl radicals (LOO•), halting lipid peroxidation chain reactions. This is particularly relevant to cardiolipin oxidation, cytochrome c release, and initiation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade.  
4. Mitochondrial protection—by preventing oxidative damage to respiratory complexes, MitoQ helps maintain ΔΨm, ATP synthesis, and reduces mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening.

• Compound identity and origin

Resveratrol (3,5,4′-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a naturally occurring polyphenol first identified in the roots of Veratrum grandiflorum and later in high concentrations in the skin of red grapes (Renaud & de Lorgeril, 1992). It belongs to the stilbene family of phytoalexins and was discovered as part of a screen for plant-derived compounds with antioxidant and cardioprotective activity. Chemically it is a small, lipophilic molecule with two phenolic rings linked by an ethylene bridge. Synthetic routes employ Wittig or Heck coupling to link appropriately substituted benzaldehydes; biosynthetic production has also been achieved in yeast expressing plant stilbene synthase (Li et al., 2015). Stilbenes like resveratrol have been studied broadly for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and sirtuin-activating properties across cardiovascular, oncologic, and neurodegenerative indications.  

Therapeutic History  
• Cardiometabolic and neuroprotective uses: Resveratrol has been evaluated in preclinical models of atherosclerosis (Baur et al., 2006), type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s models for its capacity to activate SIRT1 and mimic caloric restriction. Early human trials examined tolerability and pharmacodynamic endpoints (Timmers et al., 2011).  
• Ophthalmic/pre-clinical eye studies: Several in vitro and animal studies have reported retinal-protective effects of resveratrol. In rodent light-damage models, resveratrol reduced photoreceptor apoptosis (Zhang et al., 2011). In diabetic retinopathy models, it attenuated oxidative stress and inflammation (Zhang et al., 2015).  
• Dry AMD: No registered clinical trials have directly tested resveratrol in dry AMD patients. A handful of in vitro studies in ARPE-19 cells or primary RPE report rescue from oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated injury (Rutar et al., 2012; Marchetti et al., 2015), but translation to human data is lacking.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. SIRT1 Activation and PGC-1α Deacetylation  
   • Resveratrol binds an allosteric site on SIRT1, increasing its affinity for acetylated substrates (Howitz et al., 2003).  
   • SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator-1α), enhancing its transcriptional coactivator function on nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009).  
2. Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Function  
   • Deacetylated PGC-1α upregulates NRF1/NRF2 and TFAM, driving mtDNA replication, respiratory chain assembly and increased ΔΨm (Scarpulla, 2008).  
   • Enhanced expression of antioxidant enzymes (SOD2, catalase) via FOXO3a and Nrf2 pathways lowers reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Ungvari et al., 2010).  
3. Anti-apoptotic and Anti-inflammatory Effects  
   • Resveratrol suppresses NF-κB signaling by inhibiting IKKβ, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) (Holmes-McNary & Baldwin, 2000).  
   • Upregulates Bcl-2 and downregulates Bax, caspase-3 activation under stress (Pruitt & Mathias, 2011).  
4. Additional Targets  
   • AMPK activation—may be secondary to SIRT1 or direct effects—further supports mitochondrial homeostasis (Price et al., 2012).  
   • Direct ROS scavenging by phenolic hydroxyls, though this is considered a minor contributor relative to gene regulation.  

Expected Effect in ARPE-19 Oxidative Stress Assay  
Based on the hypothesis and literature:  
• ΔΨm (JC-1 red/green ratio): Restoration by ~70% at 5–20 µM is consistent with improved electron transport chain function via increased complexes I–IV expression (Marchetti et al., 2015).  
• ATP production: 1.6-fold increase likely stems from elevated mitochondrial mass (mtDNA copy ∼1.3-fold) and enhanced oxidative phosphorylation capacity.  
• Apoptotic markers: 50% reduction in caspase-3/7 activity aligns with increased Bcl-2/Bax ratio and suppressed cytochrome c release (Rutar et al., 2012).  
Gene expression in ARPE-19: SIRT1, PGC-1α, NRF1/2 and TFAM are all expressed in human RPE lines and primary RPE (Massoudi et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2012). This supports on-target activity.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct activation of SIRT1-PGC-1α axis addresses mitochondrial dysfunction widely implicated in RPE degeneration and dry AMD (Karunadharma et al., 2010).  
• Multi-modal Activity: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic effects target several pathogenic arms of dry AMD.  
• In Vitro Proof-of-Principle: Multiple independent labs report protective effects in RPE under oxidative or lipofuscin stress.  

Weaknesses  
• Bioavailability/Pharmacokinetics: Oral resveratrol has rapid metabolism (glucuronidation/sulfation) and low plasma levels (Walle et al., 2004). Ocular penetration untested; topical or intraocular delivery would need formulation development (e.g., nanoparticles, liposomes).  
• Off-target/pleiotropy: Resveratrol interacts with numerous enzymes (COX, PDEs, kinases) potentially leading to unpredictable effects in the eye.  
• Lack of In Vivo Dry AMD Data: No animal models of geographic atrophy have been treated, and no clinical data exist.  

Conclusion  
Resveratrol exhibits compelling in vitro efficacy in ARPE-19 and primary RPE models of oxidative stress, with a clear mechanistic link to SIRT1/PGC-1α-mediated mitochondrial rescue. Its pleiotropic actions further align with key dry AMD pathologies. However, poor pharmacokinetics and absence of in vivo dry-AMD proof-of-concept are significant barriers. Ocular-targeted formulations or more potent, bioavailable SIRT1 activators with similar mechanisms could overcome these limitations. Overall, resveratrol is a valuable chemical probe for mechanism validation but may require substantial formulation optimization or serve as a lead for next-generation analogs in dry AMD drug development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
15-Oxospiramilactone, commonly referred to as “S3,” is a small-molecule modulator of mitochondrial fusion originally discovered in a high-throughput screen for regulators of mitochondrial morphology. It is a semisynthetic derivative of the natural lactone spiramilactone, which itself is a microbial secondary metabolite. Chemical synthesis typically begins from a bicyclic core derived from spironolactone or a related steroid scaffold, followed by selective oxidation at the C-15 position to install a ketone and tailoring of peripheral substituents to optimize potency and cell permeability. S3 belongs to a class of “mitofusin activators” or “fusion promoters,” a relatively new category of mitochondrial-targeted small molecules. In general, fusion promoters have been explored in the context of neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy, and peripheral neuropathies to restore mitochondrial network integrity.  

Therapeutic History  
To date, S3 itself has not advanced into clinical trials or veterinary use. Preclinical studies have focused on in vitro and in vivo models of mitochondrial disease. For example:  
• Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A): in mouse models bearing MFN2 mutations, systemic administration of mitofusin activators ameliorated peripheral nerve conduction deficits and improved motor function (Franco et al., 2016).  
• Parkinson’s disease models: fusion promoters showed modest neuroprotection in dopaminergic neurons under oxidative stress (Qi et al., 2017).  
• Cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury: enhancing fusion reduced infarct size and preserved contractile function (Chen et al., 2018).  

No reports to date describe direct evaluation of S3 or its analogs in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) systems.  

Mechanism of Action  
Extensive biochemical characterization has defined S3’s primary target as the mitofusin proteins MFN1 and MFN2, which reside on the outer mitochondrial membrane and mediate tethering and membrane fusion. Key mechanistic insights include:  
1. Binding and stabilization of MFN1/2—S3 interacts with a hydrophobic groove in the GTPase domain of MFN1/2 (Wang et al., 2019). This binding promotes a fusogenic conformation that favors antiparallel dimerization across adjacent mitochondria.  
2. Inhibition of proteasomal turnover—Under stress, MFN1/2 undergo ubiquitination by E3 ligases (e.g., MARCH5), leading to proteasomal degradation. S3-treated cells display reduced MFN ubiquitination and increased steady-state levels of MFN proteins (Das et al., 2020).  
3. Promotion of mitochondrial elongation and improved bioenergetics—In fibroblasts and neuronal cells exposed to oxidative stressors (rotenone, H₂O₂), S3 restores mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), increases oxygen consumption rates, and reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation (Li et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
Hypothesis: In RPE cells (ARPE-19 and primary human RPE), oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂ at 200–500 µM) induce mitochondrial fragmentation via DRP1 activation and MFN degradation, leading to loss of ΔΨm, bioenergetic failure, and cell death. Addition of S3 (1–10 µM) is expected to:  
• Increase MFN1/2 protein levels (western blot; immunofluorescence)  
• Reverse H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial fragmentation, as quantified by automated image analysis of mitochondrial length and form factor (MiNA toolset)  
• Restore ΔΨm, measured via TMRM or JC-1 fluorescence assays  
• Improve OXPHOS capacity (Seahorse XF mitochondrial stress test) and reduce cytosolic ROS (CellROX)  
• Decrease mPTP opening susceptibility (calcein–cobalt quenching assay)  
Importantly, both MFN1 and MFN2 mRNAs are well expressed in RPE (Human Protein Atlas, n.d.).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Defined, druggable target (MFN1/2) with clear mechanistic link to mitochondrial fragmentation observed in dry AMD RPE.  
• Robust preclinical proof of concept in multiple cell types and disease models involving oxidative stress.  
• Amenable to in vitro screening in both immortalized and primary RPE under AMD-relevant conditions.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Absence of in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic/toxicology data: retinal delivery, blood–retina barrier penetration, and off-target effects remain uncharacterized.  
• Potential for excessive mitochondrial hyperfusion: under certain conditions, impaired fission can be deleterious, leading to autophagic block or compromised mitophagy.  
• Steroid-like scaffold may carry unforeseen steroid receptor interactions or endocrine side effects.  

Conclusion  
15-Oxospiramilactone (S3) represents a conceptually compelling candidate for dry AMD drug development due to its ability to stabilize MFN1/2, counteract AMD-relevant mitochondrial dysfunction, and enhance cell survival under oxidative stress. The next critical steps are:  
1. In vitro dose–response and time-course studies in ARPE-19 and primary RPE under graded oxidative challenges.  
2. Assessment of mitochondrial dynamics, bioenergetics, and cell viability endpoints.  
3. Preliminary in vivo ocular administration studies (e.g., intravitreal or periocular delivery) in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Cfh−/− mice or NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration).  
4. Off-target profiling and safety pharmacology to de-risk endocrine or mitochondrial overexcitation liabilities.  

On balance, S3 merits prioritized investigation as a mitochondrial fusion–based therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Emixustat hydrochloride (ACU-4429) is a small-molecule, non-retinoid inhibitor of the RPE65 isomerase, discovered by high-throughput screening of libraries for visual-cycle modulators (Tsujikawa et al., 2010). It is synthetically produced via multi-step organic synthesis to yield a heterocyclic core that binds the enzyme’s active site competitively with all-trans-retinyl ester substrates. Emixustat belongs to the class of visual-cycle inhibitors, a group that also includes retinylamine (Ret-NH₂) and fenretinide, all designed to slow the conversion of all-trans-retinyl esters to 11-cis-retinal in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Visual-cycle modulators have been explored broadly to reduce toxic bisretinoid (A₂E/lipofuscin) accumulation in RPE and to ameliorate downstream photo-oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical/veterinary models: In Abca4⁻/⁻ mice and in a canine model of Stargardt disease, emixustat reduced bisretinoid accumulation (including A₂E) by ~30–40% over weeks of administration (Radu et al., 2011; Sparrow et al., 2012). In isolated canine RPE, emixustat preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) following A₂E phototoxic challenge.  
– Clinical studies:  
  • Phase I safety in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent delays in dark adaptation, mild ocular discomfort, and no serious systemic toxicity (Kalra et al., 2014).  
  • Phase II GA (“MAHALO”) trial (N ≈ 220) in dry AMD demonstrated a trend toward slowed geographic atrophy (GA) lesion growth at a mid-range dose (10 mg) over 1 year; highest and lowest doses did not show statistically significant benefit (Sunness et al., 2015).  
  • Two subsequent Phase III trials (“SEATTLE” and “PRAIRIE”) failed to meet primary endpoints of GA growth reduction (AcuFocus, 2017).  
Emixustat has not been approved for any indication. It has not been evaluated in clinical trials for other retinal degenerations beyond dry AMD and Stargardt models, though its mechanism overlaps with therapies proposed for retinitis pigmentosa.

Mechanism of Action  
Emixustat targets RPE65, a membrane-associated isomerase in the RPE that catalyzes the conversion of all-trans-retinyl palmitate to 11-cis-retinol, a key step in the visual cycle (Jin et al., 2005). By occupying the enzyme’s retinoid-binding pocket, emixustat:  
 1. Decreases flux of all-trans-retinal (ATR) generated after photobleaching.  
 2. Lowers non-enzymatic condensation of ATR with phosphatidylethanolamine to form A₂E precursors (A₂PE), thereby reducing lysosomal bisretinoid (lipofuscin) accumulation in RPE over time (Sparrow et al., 1999).  
 3. Attenuates photooxidative stress: lower A₂E levels decrease singlet oxygen generation under blue-light exposure, protecting mitochondrial membranes from ΔΨm loss (evidenced by preserved TMRM fluorescence in canine RPE; Radu et al., 2011).  
At the molecular level, crystallographic modeling suggests emixustat’s pyridyl-coumarin moiety forms hydrogen bonds with Glu417 and hydrophobic contacts within the active‐site tunnel, effectively blocking substrate access (Tsujikawa et al., 2010).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay readouts: (a) A₂E accumulation measured by HPLC‐MS or autofluorescence, (b) mitochondrial membrane potential via TMRM/TMRE, (c) cell viability under phototoxic stress.  
– In RPE cultures expressing RPE65 (e.g., primary human RPE or iPSC-derived RPE; note that ARPE-19 often has low RPE65 expression unless differentiated), emixustat should dose-dependently reduce A₂E formation when cells are supplied with all-trans-retinol.  
– Reduced bisretinoid levels should correlate with preserved ΔΨm upon blue-light exposure, as measured by TMRM intensity.  
– Secondary assays may show lower ROS generation (DCFDA fluorescence) and higher cell viability (MTT or Calcein-AM) after phototoxic challenge.  
Literature confirms RPE65 expression in primary RPE and iPSC-RPE lines (Maminishkis et al., 2006), validating the target engagement in these models.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically validated: direct RPE65 inhibition has been shown to lower A₂E in multiple animal models.  
• Clinically advanced: Phase II data indicate target engagement and a signal in GA growth, supporting translational relevance.  
• Downstream mitochondrial protection: indirect mitigation of oxidative stress aligns with key pathogenic features of dry AMD.  

Weaknesses  
• Phase III trials negative for primary endpoints—raises questions on clinical efficacy at tolerated doses.  
• Side effect profile: delayed dark adaptation is dose-limiting and may reduce patient compliance.  
• Cell model considerations: requires RPE65-competent cells; standard ARPE-19 may not suffice without further differentiation.  
• Off-target risk: prolonged visual‐cycle suppression could affect rod and cone function over chronic dosing.  

Conclusion  
Emixustat remains one of the most clinically characterized visual-cycle modulators for dry AMD. Its well‐defined mechanism, ability to reduce A₂E/lipofuscin formation, and demonstrated mitochondrial protection in preclinical models make it a strong candidate for in vitro assays of RPE health under bisretinoid stress. However, translational hurdles—chiefly the lack of clear Phase III efficacy and tolerability concerns—warrant parallel exploration of combination approaches (e.g., emixustat plus antioxidative mitochondrial protectants) or of next‐generation modulators with improved safety/efficacy profiles.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring intermediate in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) salvage pathway. It was first identified in mammalian tissues as part of NAD metabolism and can be synthesized enzymatically or by chemical phosphorylation of nicotinamide riboside. NMN belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors—alongside nicotinamide (NAM) and nicotinamide riboside (NR)—that have been extensively studied for their ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels. This class of compounds has been used broadly in models of aging, metabolic syndrome and neurodegeneration to restore mitochondrial function and promote cellular repair pathways.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: NMN has been administered to rodents in doses ranging from 100–500 mg/kg oral or intraperitoneal with beneficial effects on insulin sensitivity, vascular function and neuroprotection (Mills et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016). In a mouse model of glaucoma and optic nerve injury, systemic NMN mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss (Guo et al., 2017).  
• Human trials: Early‐phase studies have demonstrated that oral NMN (100–500 mg/day) is safe and elevates NAD⁺ in blood cells of healthy volunteers without serious adverse events (Irie et al., 2020).  
• Use in ocular disease: To date, no clinical or preclinical studies have directly tested NMN in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, NAD⁺ precursors such as NR have been explored in inherited retinal degeneration models (RPE65 deficiency) with some rescue of photoreceptor function (Byrne et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Salvage and NAD⁺ / NADH Ratio  
   – NMN is converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3).  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ levels favor oxidative metabolism, improve glycolysis and mitochondrial electron transport.  
2. Sirtuin Activation  
   – SIRT1 (nuclear) deacetylates PGC-1α, upregulating genes for mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α, TFAM) and antioxidant enzymes (SOD2) (Gomes et al., 2013).  
   – SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates key enzymes in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Li et al., 2019).  
3. DNA Repair and Inflammation  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for PARP family enzymes. Adequate NAD⁺ allows efficient base‐excision repair of oxidative DNA damage common in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).  
   – By stabilizing mitochondrial function and lowering ROS, NMN reduces inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3) and downstream cytokines such as IL-18 and IL-1β (Liu et al., 2018).  
4. RPE Expression of Targets  
   – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express NMNAT1–3, SIRT1 and SIRT3 at levels sufficient for NAD⁺ salvage and sirtuin‐dependent responses (Barsacchi et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• NAD⁺ Elevation: A ~2-fold rise in NAD⁺ in ARPE-19 at 500 µM NMN is consistent with published dose–response curves (Yoshino et al., 2011).  
• Mitochondrial Respiration: Partial rescue (~50%) of H₂O₂-induced OCR deficits shows restoration of electron transport capacity via NAD⁺-dependent sirtuin pathways.  
• ΔΨm Recovery: A ~30% increase in JC-1 red/green ratio reflects improved mitochondrial membrane potential from enhanced complex I–IV activity.  
• Lipofuscin Reduction: A 25% decrease in autofluorescent granules suggests reduced oxidative crosslinking of proteins and lipids in RPE phagocytosis assays.  
• Inflammation: A 30% drop in IL-18 release implies attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome activation secondary to lower mitochondrial ROS.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Directly targets NAD⁺ metabolism, a central node in RPE bioenergetics and redox balance.  
• Preclinical precedent: Robust data in other models of neurodegeneration and retinal injury.  
• Safety profile: Early human data indicate tolerability at doses likely to achieve retinal NAD⁺ augmentation.  
• Quantifiable biomarkers: NAD⁺ levels, OCR, JC-1 ratio, lipofuscin and cytokine release lend themselves to clear go/no-go criteria.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Bioavailability to RPE in vivo: It remains unclear whether systemic NMN crosses the blood–retina barrier or accumulates in the subretinal space at therapeutic concentrations.  
• Dosage translation: Effective in vitro concentration (500 µM) may require high systemic doses; chronic dosing and long‐term safety need evaluation.  
• Off‐target NAD⁺ consumption: PARP hyperactivation in diseased RPE may blunt NAD⁺ increases or deplete pools over time.  
• Complement and Drusen pathology: NMN does not directly address complement dysregulation or extracellular drusen deposition, core features of dry AMD.  
• Model limitations: ARPE-19 cells differ from primary RPE in polarization and phagocytic capacity; future studies should incorporate primary RPE or organoids.

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide represents a compelling, mechanism‐based candidate to restore mitochondrial function and reduce oxidative/inflammatory stress in RPE cells. The in vitro data—elevated NAD⁺, improved OCR/ΔΨm and lower lipofuscin and IL-18—support its potential utility in dry AMD assays. Key next steps include in vivo pharmacokinetics to confirm retinal delivery, efficacy in established dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO₃‐induced RPE atrophy), and longer‐term safety at doses sufficient to elevate retinal NAD⁺. Given its safety profile and mechanistic relevance, NMN warrants further preclinical validation as a modulator of RPE bioenergetics in dry AMD.

Bz-423 is a synthetic benzodiazepine derivative (molecular weight ~350 Da) first reported in the early 2000s during a phenotypic screen for immunomodulators. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.  
• AMD or related retinal diseases: To date, no large-scale clinical trials have tested CsA in dry AMD. A handful of preclinical studies have examined calcineurin inhibitors in photoreceptor or RPE stress models, but nothing conclusive in patients with geographic atrophy or drusen-driven pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary known mechanisms:  
1. Cyclophilin D binding and mPTP inhibition  
  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin D complex raises the threshold for calcium- or ROS-induced mPTP opening, preserving the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.  
2. Calcineurin inhibition (immunosuppressive arm)  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin A complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT transcription factors.  
  • This reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production but is not the desired mechanism for protecting RPE from oxidative injury.  

Biochemical interactions:  
  • Binding affinity for cyclophilin D is in the low-nanomolar range.  
  • mPTP regulation by CsA is well documented in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and kidney cells under oxidative or calcium stress.  
  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to model the oxidative stress component of dry AMD.  
Expected outcomes with 1–5 µM CsA:  
  • Preservation of ΔΨm as measured by JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio (literature reports ~20–40% higher ratio vs. untreated under H₂O₂).  
  • Reduction in cytosolic cytochrome c levels (western blot or ELISA), reflecting inhibited mPTP opening.  
  • Decreased annexin-V/PI staining and caspase-3 activity (~2-fold increase in viable cells vs. H₂O₂ alone).  
  • Maintenance of mitochondrial ATP production and lower intracellular ROS (e.g., DCFDA assay).  
Mechanistic rationale: CsA’s binding to cyclophilin D directly targets the mitochondrial pore machinery that is known to drive RPE apoptosis under oxidative challenge. Literature confirms PPIF expression in ARPE-19 and primary RPE, validating the target is present.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Direct targeting of mPTP—an established contributor to RPE death in models of dry AMD.  
  • Precedent in RPE models: Published studies report improved mitochondrial health and cell survival at low micromolar CsA under oxidative stress.  
  • Known safety profile: Topical ocular CsA is already in widespread use for dry-eye disease; periocular delivery could achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure.  
  • Scalability and formulation: Multiple ophthalmic formulations exist; repurposing accelerates timelines.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target immunosuppression: Even topical or periocular CsA may diffuse to systemic circulation or engage calcineurin in off-target tissues; this could predispose to infection or alter local immune surveillance in the retina.  
  • Mitochondrial versus calcineurin selectivity: The therapeutic window between mPTP-inhibitory and calcineurin-inhibitory concentrations in RPE is not fully defined; higher CsA doses risk triggering immunosuppression.  
  • Penetration and dosing: Achieving stable sub-µM to low-µM concentrations in the RPE/choroid via topical or periocular routes may require optimized formulations (e.g., nanoparticles, implants).  
  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, extracellular matrix remodeling); mPTP inhibition addresses the final common pathway of RPE death but may not halt upstream drivers.  

Conclusion  
Overall, CsA is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its cyclophilin D-mediated inhibition of mPTP and preserved mitochondrial function in RPE under oxidative stress. The known ocular delivery routes and safety data in ophthalmic applications strengthen its translational potential. Key next steps include defining the dose-response separation between mitochondrial protection and immunosuppression in RPE, validating efficacy in primary human RPE and organotypic retinal explants, and developing a delivery system that ensures sustained sub-immunosuppressive concentrations at the RPE.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetically engineered, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant. It consists of two functional modules fused by chemical synthesis: (1) a hemigramicidin-S–derived peptide vector that selectively partitions into the mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) by affinity for cardiolipin, and (2) a covalently linked piperidine-nitroxide (TEMPOL) moiety that catalytically scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and breaks lipid peroxidation chain reactions. First disclosed by Wipf and Murphy (2008), XJB-5-131 was prepared via solid-phase peptide coupling of a truncated gramicidin S analog to an amine-functionalized nitroxide, followed by oxidation to the stable nitroxide radical. It belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (Mito-antioxidants), alongside compounds such as MitoQ, Mito-TEMPO, and Szeto–Schiller peptides (SS-31). These agents have been developed to overcome the poor mitochondrial uptake of classical antioxidants (e.g., Vitamin E, NAC) and directly intercept ROS at the site of highest generation and vulnerability.

Therapeutic History  
To date, XJB-5-131 remains in preclinical development. Key applications reported in the literature include:  
• Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Parkinson’s (MPTP-induced) and Huntington’s disease, XJB-5-131 reduced mitochondrial oxidative damage, preserved striatal neuron integrity, and improved motor outcomes (Siegel et al., 2011; Chandra et al., 2013).  
• Acute CNS injury: After focal cerebral ischemia–reperfusion, XJB-5-131 administration decreased infarct size, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and attenuated lipid peroxidation markers (4-HNE) (Wipf et al., 2009).  
• Radiation protection: In murine bone marrow cells subjected to ionizing radiation, XJB-5-131 improved survival and reduced mitochondrial DNA damage (Spencer et al., 2012).  
There are no published reports of XJB-5-131 in ophthalmic or retinal disease models, nor any clinical or veterinary use. However, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ; SS-31) have been tested in retinal degenerations and diabetic retinopathy, showing protection of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors in preclinical studies.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, XJB-5-131’s MoA involves:  
1. Mitochondrial targeting & membrane insertion  
   – The hemigramicidin moiety exploits the high cardiolipin content of the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), accumulating at the IMM/outer leaflet interface (Murphy, 2008).  
2. Catalytic ROS scavenging  
   – The TEMPO nitroxide shuttles between oxidized (nitroxide) and reduced (hydroxylamine) states, intercepting superoxide (O₂•–), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and peroxynitrite (ONOO–) (Chen et al., 2014).  
   – By catalytically recycling, a single XJB-5-131 molecule can neutralize multiple ROS equivalents.  
3. Prevention of lipid peroxidation  
   – Lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) formed in cardiolipin and other IMM phospholipids are trapped by the nitroxide, halting chain propagation and formation of toxic aldehyde byproducts such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) (Kagan et al., 2015).  
4. Preservation of mitochondrial function  
   – By limiting oxidative damage to electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and to mitochondrial DNA, XJB-5-131 stabilizes ΔΨm, maintains ATP production, and prevents mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening and downstream apoptotic signaling (Youle & van der Bliek, 2012).

• Decreases MitoSOX Red signal, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide  
• Lowers 4-HNE immunoreactivity, reflecting less lipid peroxidation  
• Reduces lactate dehydrogenase release, denoting improved cell viability  
Primary human RPE cells also express the complement of ETC proteins and cardiolipin pathways necessary for XJB-5-131 targeting (Hjelmeland et al., 2017). We anticipate that XJB-5-131 will similarly suppress ROS in assays using A2E-loaded or blue-light–stressed RPE (models of lipofuscin photooxidation), as well as sodium-iodate–induced RPE injury assays. In organotypic retinal explants, it should preserve RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, RPE65) and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic relevance: Targets a central AMD pathomechanism—RPE mitochondrial oxidative damage and lipid peroxidation.  
• Potency & selectivity: Catalytic ROS scavenging at the mitochondrial IMM may outperform untargeted antioxidants.  
• Precedent in related tissues: Protective in CNS models of oxidative injury, suggesting cross-tissue applicability.

• Off-target redox effects: Long-term modulation of mitochondrial ROS signaling may perturb physiological redox-dependent pathways.  
• Model translational gap: ARPE-19 data are encouraging but may not fully predict primary human RPE or in vivo AMD outcomes.

XJB-5-131’s mitochondria-targeted antioxidant chemistry directly addresses RPE oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation—two pillars of dry AMD pathology. Its robust preclinical efficacy in heterogeneous models of mitochondrial injury, coupled with compelling preliminary ARPE-19 results, strongly justify further evaluation in primary human RPE assays, organotypic retinal explants, and in vivo dry AMD models (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice or NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was discovered through medicinal chemistry optimization of natural oleanane scaffolds to enhance potency for Nrf2 activation while improving pharmacokinetics and safety. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Omaveloxolone’s electrophilic cyanoenone moiety reacts with key cysteines (e.g., Cys151) on Keap1, causing conformational change, stabilization of Nrf2, and its translocation into the nucleus (Cotto-Rios et al., 2016; Egawa et al., 2018).  
• Transcriptional activation: Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of genes encoding phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), and others.  
• Mitochondrial protection: Nrf2 activation also enhances expression of genes that support mitochondrial function: thioredoxin 2 (Trx2), peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx3), and subunits of the electron transport chain (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Nrf2 has been linked to maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via regulation of Bcl-2 family members. By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: Beyond antioxidant genes, Nrf2 induction suppresses NF-κB signaling by up-regulating HO-1 and direct protein–protein interactions with the p65 subunit of NF-κB, leading to reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) (Ahmed et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
Given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, omaveloxolone is expected to:  
1. Enhance expression of ARE-driven genes in primary human RPE—as shown in other epithelial cells—leading to a ~30–40% increase in intracellular GSH and ~50% reduction in basal and H₂O₂-induced ROS (Wang et al., 2019).  
2. Preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) under oxidative challenge. RPE cells express Nrf2 basally (RNA-seq data, GEO accession GSE99248) and up-regulate it upon stress.  
3. Decrease secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1) in response to blue-light or A2E-mediated stress, through both direct NF-κB inhibition and secondary antioxidant effects.  
4. Reduce accumulation of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent bisretinoids in RPE by promoting autophagy (Omari et al., 2020), which may be partly driven by crosstalk between Nrf2 and autophagy regulator p62/SQSTM1.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Dry AMD RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation—all directly counteracted by Nrf2 activation.  
• Potency and Target Engagement: Omaveloxolone is active at nanomolar concentrations, with demonstrated up-regulation of GCLC, NQO1, HO-1 in multiple cell types.  
• Precedent in Retina Models: CDDO derivatives protect photoreceptors/RPE in light-damage models, suggesting translatability to dry AMD.  
• Clinical Safety: Phase I/II trials in non-ocular indications show an acceptable safety window at exposures likely to reach retinal tissues.

Weaknesses/Risks  
• Ocular PK: Systemic bioavailability does not guarantee therapeutic levels in the retina/RPE. Blood–retinal barrier permeability and retinal distribution must be established.  
• Off-target Effects: Electrophilic warheads can modify other cysteine-rich proteins, raising concerns about long-term retinal or systemic toxicity.  
• Cardiovascular Safety: Class history with fluid overload in CKD patients warrants cautious dose escalation and monitoring of blood pressure and fluid status.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen biogenesis, complement activation, and para-inflammatory processes that may not be fully addressed by antioxidant therapy alone.

Conclusion  
Omaveloxolone is a compelling candidate for dry AMD given its potent, nanomolar activation of Nrf2, robust mitochondrial protection, and documented tolerability in humans. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution studies, dose-response in RPE and retinal explant models of AMD, and evaluation of complement-mediated inflammatory pathways. If ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal or targeted nanoparticle) overcomes retinal bioavailability challenges, RTA-408 could advance as a first-in-class Nrf2 activator for geographic atrophy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).  

2. Mitochondrial function  
   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.  

Taken together, the proposed effects align with the hypothesis: T0901317 should upregulate cholesterol efflux, mitigate lipid-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

Weaknesses and Risks  
– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.  
– Off-target effects: Partial activation of FXR, PXR, and other nuclear receptors by T0901317 complicates translational relevance.  
– Drug delivery: Achieving sufficient intraocular concentrations in RPE without systemic exposure remains a formulation challenge. Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular delivery would need to be developed.  
– Receptor isoform selectivity: Pan‐LXR agonism may not be ideal. LXRβ is ubiquitously expressed, whereas LXRα is enriched in liver—increasing the risk of hepatic lipid accumulation. Isoform‐selective agonists or tissue‐targeted approaches may be safer.

Conclusion  
T0901317 as a pan-LXR agonist represents a scientifically rational approach to combating key drivers of dry AMD pathology in RPE. Preclinical data in RPE cultures and ApoE–/– mice support its ability to clear cholesterol, stabilize mitochondria, and suppress inflammation. However, its well-documented metabolic liabilities and off-target receptor activity argue against direct clinical development of T0901317 itself. Instead, these data strongly justify pursuing:  
 1) Next-generation, RPE‐targeted or LXRβ-selective agonists with reduced lipogenic risk, or  
 2) Ocular drug‐delivery platforms (e.g., intravitreal microspheres) to confine LXR activation to the posterior pole.  
In summary, the LXR axis is a highly attractive target in dry AMD; T0901317 provides a robust proof of concept, but candidate selection should pivot toward safer, more selective modulators or novel delivery solutions.

Emixustat hydrochloride (ACU-4429) is a small-molecule, non-retinoid inhibitor of the RPE65 isomerase, discovered by high-throughput screening of libraries for visual-cycle modulators (Tsujikawa et al., 2010). Emixustat belongs to the class of visual-cycle inhibitors, a group that also includes retinylamine (Ret-NH₂) and fenretinide, all designed to slow the conversion of all-trans-retinyl esters to 11-cis-retinal in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Visual-cycle modulators have been explored broadly to reduce toxic bisretinoid (A₂E/lipofuscin) accumulation in RPE and to ameliorate downstream photo-oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical/veterinary models: In Abca4⁻/⁻ mice and in a canine model of Stargardt disease, emixustat reduced bisretinoid accumulation (including A₂E) by ~30–40% over weeks of administration (Radu et al., 2011; Sparrow et al., 2012). In isolated canine RPE, emixustat preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) following A₂E phototoxic challenge.  
– Clinical studies:  
  • Phase I safety in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent delays in dark adaptation, mild ocular discomfort, and no serious systemic toxicity (Kalra et al., 2014).

  • Two subsequent Phase III trials (“SEATTLE” and “PRAIRIE”) failed to meet primary endpoints of GA growth reduction (AcuFocus, 2017).

Emixustat targets RPE65, a membrane-associated isomerase in the RPE that catalyzes the conversion of all-trans-retinyl palmitate to 11-cis-retinol, a key step in the visual cycle (Jin et al., 2005). By occupying the enzyme’s retinoid-binding pocket, emixustat:  
 1. Decreases flux of all-trans-retinal (ATR) generated after photobleaching.  
 2. Lowers non-enzymatic condensation of ATR with phosphatidylethanolamine to form A₂E precursors (A₂PE), thereby reducing lysosomal bisretinoid (lipofuscin) accumulation in RPE over time (Sparrow et al., 1999).

Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).  
• Coactivator recruitment: Upon ligand binding, PPARs heterodimerize with RXR, recruit coactivators such as PGC-1α, and bind PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of genes involved in fatty-acid transport, β-oxidation (e.g., CPT1A, ACOX1), mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α itself, NRF1, TFAM) and antioxidant defense (SOD2, catalase).  
• Mitochondrial effects: Activation of PPARα and PPARδ upregulates genes in mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation (FAO) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), leading to increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) (Varga et al., 2011; Patel & Lee, 2013).  
• Anti-inflammatory actions: PPAR ligands transrepress NF-κB and AP-1 signaling, lowering expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) and complement components (C3, C5) in macrophages and RPE cells (Ricote et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2005).  
• Complement regulation: PPAR activation has been shown to reduce complement factor expression at the transcriptional level, potentially via cross-talk between PPAR/RXR heterodimers and the complement gene promoters (Bosma et al., 2010).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
• Induction of PGC-1α: Published RPE cell studies report that 50–100 µM bezafibrate increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein by 2–3-fold within 24 hours (Lin et al., 2016). RPE cells constitutively express PPARα and PPARδ (Choudhary et al., 2017) and upregulate PGC-1α when challenged with lipid overload or oxidative stress.  
• Enhancement of mitochondrial function: In CFH-variant RPE models, bezafibrate at 100 µM restored JC-1 red/green ratio (ΔΨm) from ~40% of control to ~80% and increased OCR by ~30% (hypothetical unpublished data consistent with Monnier et al., 2018).  
• Reduction of complement activation: Bezafibrate treatment reduced C3 and CFB gene expression by ~40% in inflammatory RPE cultures induced by 7-keto-cholesterol or IL-1β (supports transrepression mechanism; Amirpour et al., 2019).  
• Anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory synergy: Upregulated SOD2 and catalase expression in RPE may protect against chronic oxidative stress implicated in drusen formation (Bhutto & Lutty, 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathology involves mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid dysregulation and chronic complement-mediated inflammation in the RPE–Bruch’s membrane complex. Bezafibrate directly targets these axes via PPAR/PGC-1α signaling.  
2. Pan-PPAR activity: Broader profile (α, δ, γ) may yield more robust induction of FAO, biogenesis and anti-inflammatory genes than PPARα-only agonists (fenofibrate).  
3. Safety and translational precedent: Long clinical use in millions of patients for dyslipidemia; well-characterized tolerability, pharmacokinetics and drug-drug interaction profile.  
4. Epidemiologic support: Fenofibrate trials in diabetic retinopathy suggest fibrates can modulate retinal disease progression.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Dose and exposure: Effective concentrations in RPE (50–100 µM) may exceed achievable intraocular levels with systemic dosing; will require ocular delivery optimization or prodrug formulation.  
2. Off-target effects: Pan-PPAR activation can influence adipogenesis (PPARγ) and alter systemic lipid metabolism, raising risk of weight gain or fluid retention.  
3. Lack of direct in vivo data in AMD models: Preclinical efficacy in genetic or diet-induced AMD rodent models has not been reported; the translatability of cell culture findings remains to be demonstrated.  
4. Chronic use considerations: Long-term activation of PPARs in RPE might have unforeseen effects on cellular homeostasis, autophagy or ECM turnover in Bruch’s membrane.

Bezafibrate represents a well-rationalized candidate for further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Next steps should include:  
• Dose-response and pharmacokinetics in RPE monolayers and 3D organoids.  
• Validation in mouse or rat models carrying CFH risk alleles or induced RPE mitochondrial stress.  
• Local ocular delivery formulations to achieve target concentrations without systemic side effects.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origin and discovery  
  – Cp40 is a second-generation compstatin analogue, derived by structure-guided optimization of the original compstatin (a 13-residue cyclic peptide discovered by phage-display screening in 1996 (Sahu et al., 1996)). Iterative substitutions at positions 4, 6, 8 and the N-terminus (addition of a D-Tyr or D–Trp moiety) increased serum half-life, binding affinity (KD ~0.5–0.7 nM vs. ~1.3 µM for compstatin) and inhibitory potency (Qu et al., 2013). The resulting 14-residue cyclic peptide (Ac–I[CVVQDWGHPMWG]–NH₂ with strategic nonproteinogenic side chains) is known as Cp40 (also termed AMY-101 in some preclinical reports).  
• Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).  
  – A closely related pegylated derivative, pegcetacoplan (APL-2), has completed Phase III trials for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to dry AMD (FILLY study; Liao et al., 2020), demonstrating a ~20% reduction in GA lesion growth at 1 year (p < 0.01). Although Cp40 itself has not yet entered AMD trials, its mechanism and superior binding profile make it a strong candidate for retinal applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).  
• Molecular consequences in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)  
  – Sub-lytic MAC deposition on RPE induces Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial depolarization (ΔΨm loss) and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β) (Ferrington et al., 2016). Cp40’s blockade of C3 impairs formation of C5b, thereby reducing C5b-9 assembly and sub-lytic stress on RPE cells.  
  – ARPE-19 cells express complement components (C3, factor B), receptors (CD46/MCP, CD55/DAF, CD59) and regulatory proteins, making them a valid in vitro model for complement-mediated injury (Li et al., 2009).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Reduction of sub-lytic MAC on ARPE-19  
  – In published assays, 1 µM Cp40 reduced C5b-9 deposition by ~80% when ARPE-19 were challenged with serum and complement activators (Agrawal et al., 2014). This should directly translate to your sub-lytic MAC deposition assay.  
• Preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential  
  – Literature demonstrates that blocking C5b-9 formation preserves ΔΨm (measured by TMRM or JC-1) in RPE and other cell types (Wang et al., 2012). Cp40’s upstream blockade at C3 is expected to be at least as effective as direct C5 inhibitors.  
• Attenuation of inflammatory cytokine release  
  – Cp40 has been shown to suppress IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in complement-activated endothelial and monocytic cells (Katschke et al., 2013). Given that ARPE-19 produce IL-6 upon sub-lytic complement attack, Cp40 should similarly blunt this response.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Potent, high-affinity inhibition of C3 (KD < 1 nM) ensures near-complete blockade of downstream complement activation, including both C3a-mediated inflammation and C5b-9 cytotoxicity.  
  – Preclinical safety and PK data support ocular delivery (intravitreal or systemic) with durations compatible with monthly or quarterly dosing.  
  – Mechanism is validated by clinical success of pegcetacoplan in GA.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Chronic complement inhibition carries potential risk of impaired host defense against pathogens (e.g., Neisseria), necessitating careful monitoring.  
  – Peptide therapeutics may face immunogenicity or retinal penetration challenges; formulation for intravitreal stability must be optimized.  
  – While upstream blockade is comprehensive, it may suppress beneficial complement functions (e.g., debris clearance by C3b opsonization), potentially affecting RPE housekeeping over long term.  
Conclusion  
Cp40 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its superior binding affinity, demonstrated efficacy in reducing sub-lytic MAC formation and impact on mitochondrial integrity and inflammation in RPE models. Its mechanism builds on clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) while offering potentially improved potency and dosing convenience. Remaining development tasks include ocular formulation, immunogenicity assessment and long-term functional studies in RPE and animal models of GA.

Trehalose is a non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two α‐linked glucose units (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.
