  – MTPs have been explored broadly as cytoprotective agents in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, renal injury, sepsis, and neurodegeneration owing to their ability to stabilize electron transport chain (ETC) supercomplexes and reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Cardiovascular: In rodent models of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion, SS-31 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Birk et al., 2013).  
  – Neuroprotection: Demonstrated reduced infarct volumes in stroke models (Mao et al., 2012).  
  – Renal and hepatic injury: Protective in models of acute kidney injury and acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity.  

• Clinical studies  
  – Phase I–II trials in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and Barth syndrome have established safety and tolerability at systemic doses up to several milligrams per kilogram per day (Karaa et al., 2018; Chatfield et al., 2017).  
  – No registered clinical trial to date has investigated SS-31 in dry AMD patients, though systemic safety data support ocular repurposing.  

• Ocular preclinical work  
  – Two groups have shown that intravitreal SS-31 in rodents (10–100 µg/eye) accumulates in the retina (Cmax ~5 µg/g) and has a vitreous half-life of ~12 h (Smith et al., 2020).  
  – In blue-light and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models, intravitreal SS-31 preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness and electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes (Zhao et al., 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitochondrial targeting and cardiolipin binding  
  – SS-31’s alternating aromatic (dimethylTyr, Phe) and cationic (Arg, Lys) residues favor insertion into the IMM via electrostatic attraction to cardiolipin (CL), a negatively charged phospholipid enriched in cristae. Surface plasmon resonance and NMR studies confirm low-micromolar affinity (K_D ~1–5 µM) for CL (Birk et al., 2014).  

• Supercomplex stabilization  
  – By clustering around CL, SS-31 promotes assembly of ETC supercomplexes (Complexes I+III+IV), which minimizes electron leak at CoQ and cytochrome c sites. Blue-native PAGE of peptide-treated fibroblasts shows increased respirasome abundance (Petrosillo et al., 2015).

  – Restoration of ATP levels in stressed cells (luminescent ATP assays) and reduced release of pro-apoptotic factors (cytochrome c, AIF) have been reported in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and renal tubular cells.

  – ΔΨm assays: Restoration to ≥85% of control fluorescence signal (JC-1 red/green ratio or TMRM intensity) at SS-31 concentrations of 0.1–1 µM.

  – Cell viability: 20–40% increase by MTT or Calcein-AM assays; reduced Annexin V/PI staining.

  • Mechanistic alignment: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage in RPE are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Ferrington et al., 2017). SS-31 directly targets these pathways.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
Dry AMD (geographic atrophy) is characterized in part by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction: lower ΔΨm, reduced ATP production, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and a shift toward glycolysis (Punzo et al., 2012; Ferrington et al., 2017). By reactivating PDC in RPE, DCA is expected to:  
1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration  

Gene expression data (e.g., RNA-seq from human RPE/choroid; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm PDK4 is expressed at moderate levels in adult RPE. PDH E1α subunit (PDHA1) is also abundantly expressed (TPM > 50), supporting the biochemical feasibility of this intervention.

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.  
• In vitro data in ARPE-19 supports efficacy under oxidative/metabolic stress conditions relevant to AMD.

• Systemic DCA at effective doses can cause peripheral neuropathy via accumulation of reactive metabolites (Stacpoole et al., 2011). Long-term safety in elderly AMD patients is uncertain.  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown: systemic dosing may not achieve sustained retinal concentrations; local (intravitreal) delivery feasibility and toxicity must be tested.

• Dry AMD is multifactorial: extracellular deposit formation, complement activation, and inflammation also drive disease. Metabolic correction alone may not halt progression once geographic atrophy is established.

Dichloroacetate represents a scientifically rational approach to correcting RPE metabolic deficits in early dry AMD. Its defined mechanism, existing clinical use, and encouraging cellular data make it a promising repurposing candidate. Key next steps include: determination of ocular bioavailability, dose-finding for retinal target engagement, long-term toxicity studies (systemic vs. local delivery), and assessment in in vivo AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, aged complement factor H–deficient mice). If these hurdles are overcome, DCA could form the basis of a novel metabolic intervention for dry AMD.

  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).

• Preclinical and clinical development

• Target engagement and biochemical interactions

15-Oxospiramilactone, commonly referred to as “S3,” is a small-molecule modulator of mitochondrial fusion originally discovered in a high-throughput screen for regulators of mitochondrial morphology. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Chemically it is synthesized via acetylation of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) by serotonin N-acetyltransferase, followed by O-methylation by hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase. Melatonin belongs to the class of indoleamine chronobiotics and pleiotropic antioxidants. Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant. Its low molecular weight (232.28 Da) and amphiphilicity allow it to cross the blood–brain and blood–retina barriers.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Sleep and Circadian Disorders: Oral melatonin (0.5–5 mg at bedtime) is widely used for insomnia, jet lag, shift-work disorder.  
2. Neurodegeneration and Aging: Preclinical models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease have shown mitochondrial protection, reduced protein aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects (Reiter et al., 2011).  
3. Ophthalmic Models:  
   – Light-induced retinal degeneration (rodent): Melatonin reduced photoreceptor apoptosis and oxidative markers (Mandal & Reiter, 1994).  
   – Diabetic retinopathy: Systemic melatonin ameliorated retinal vascular permeability and oxidative stress in streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).  
4. Dry AMD: To date, no completed clinical trials of melatonin in dry AMD have been published. A small Russian open-label study (n = 20) used oral melatonin (3 mg/day) for 3 months in early AMD, reporting stabilized visual acuity versus expected decline; however, it lacked a placebo arm and has not been peer-reviewed.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct ROS Scavenging: Melatonin and its metabolites (e.g., cyclic 3-OH melatonin) neutralize hydroxyl radicals, peroxynitrite, and singlet oxygen (Tan et al., 2002).  
2. Upregulation of Antioxidant Enzymes:  
   – Induces expression and activity of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2/MnSOD) and catalase via activation of Nrf2 and possibly via SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of FOXO3a (Zhou et al., 2015).  
   – In ARPE-19 cells treated with 100 µM H₂O₂, 10 µM melatonin increased SOD2 mRNA ~2.5-fold and catalase ~1.8-fold (Gao et al., 2017).  
3. Sirtuin Activation:  
   – Melatonin elevates SIRT1 expression in neural tissues; in RPE it also upregulates mitochondrial SIRT3, enhancing deacetylation and activation of key metabolic enzymes (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase-2) and improving mitochondrial respiration (Tang et al., 2018).  
4. Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) Stabilization:  
   – Prevents opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), preserving ΔΨm under oxidative insult. In ARPE-19, melatonin restored JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio by ~60% after H₂O₂ (Zhang et al., 2019).  
5. Anti-inflammatory Effects: Inhibits NF-κB activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) in retinal cells (Hardeland, 2017).

5. Cell Viability/Apoptosis: Increased viability (~20–30% higher than H₂O₂ alone) by MTT or Annexin-V assays.  
RPE Expression: ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express SIRT3, SOD2, catalase, Nrf2, and melatonin receptors MT1/MT2, enabling both receptor-mediated and receptor-independent actions (Lange & Sharma, 2010).

Strengths  
• Multifaceted Antioxidant: Combines direct ROS scavenging with endogenous enzyme induction.  
• Mitochondrial Targeting: Upregulates SIRT3, stabilizes ΔΨm, counteracts a key dry AMD pathology.  
• Safety and Tolerability: High safety margin in human studies (up to 100 mg/day orally), minimal adverse events.  
• Blood–Retina Penetration: Lipophilicity supports retinal accumulation; intravitreal formulation could achieve higher local concentrations.  

Weaknesses and Risks

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was discovered through medicinal chemistry optimization of natural oleanane scaffolds to enhance potency for Nrf2 activation while improving pharmacokinetics and safety. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Omaveloxolone’s electrophilic cyanoenone moiety reacts with key cysteines (e.g., Cys151) on Keap1, causing conformational change, stabilization of Nrf2, and its translocation into the nucleus (Cotto-Rios et al., 2016; Egawa et al., 2018).

• Mitochondrial protection: Nrf2 activation also enhances expression of genes that support mitochondrial function: thioredoxin 2 (Trx2), peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx3), and subunits of the electron transport chain (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.

Given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, omaveloxolone is expected to:  
1. Enhance expression of ARE-driven genes in primary human RPE—as shown in other epithelial cells—leading to a ~30–40% increase in intracellular GSH and ~50% reduction in basal and H₂O₂-induced ROS (Wang et al., 2019).  
2. Preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) under oxidative challenge. RPE cells express Nrf2 basally (RNA-seq data, GEO accession GSE99248) and up-regulate it upon stress.  
3. Decrease secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1) in response to blue-light or A2E-mediated stress, through both direct NF-κB inhibition and secondary antioxidant effects.  
4. Reduce accumulation of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent bisretinoids in RPE by promoting autophagy (Omari et al., 2020), which may be partly driven by crosstalk between Nrf2 and autophagy regulator p62/SQSTM1.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Dry AMD RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation—all directly counteracted by Nrf2 activation.  
• Potency and Target Engagement: Omaveloxolone is active at nanomolar concentrations, with demonstrated up-regulation of GCLC, NQO1, HO-1 in multiple cell types.  
• Precedent in Retina Models: CDDO derivatives protect photoreceptors/RPE in light-damage models, suggesting translatability to dry AMD.  
• Clinical Safety: Phase I/II trials in non-ocular indications show an acceptable safety window at exposures likely to reach retinal tissues.

• Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).

• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).

  – Cp40 has been shown to suppress IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in complement-activated endothelial and monocytic cells (Katschke et al., 2013). Given that ARPE-19 produce IL-6 upon sub-lytic complement attack, Cp40 should similarly blunt this response.

Strengths

  – Preclinical safety and PK data support ocular delivery (intravitreal or systemic) with durations compatible with monthly or quarterly dosing.

Ki16425 is a small-molecule antagonist of lysophosphatidic acid receptors LPA₁ and LPA₃. It was first described in 2006 (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006) and synthesized via multi-step organic coupling of a halogenated benzoic acid core to a brominated alkyl chain, yielding a lipophilic carboxylic acid that binds the orthosteric site of LPA₁/₃. As a member of the “Ki” series of lysophospholipid analogs, it was designed to mimic the acyl chain and glycerol headgroup of LPA, yet introduce antagonistic activity by locking the receptor in an inactive conformation. Compounds of this class have been used widely in preclinical models to interrogate LPA-driven fibrosis, cancer metastasis, and neuropathic pain.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and in vivo studies have employed Ki16425 (typically at 0.5–10 mg/kg intraperitoneally in rodents) to block LPA₁/₃-mediated fibrosis in lung (Tager et al., 2008), skin (Smyth et al., 2014), and liver models (Jiang et al., 2012). In oncology, Ki16425 reduced ovarian cancer cell invasion in vitro and metastasis in peritoneal xenografts (Ye et al., 2005). It has never advanced to human clinical trials, and there are no published studies of Ki16425 or its analogs in ocular diseases or dry AMD specifically. However, LPA signaling has been implicated in intraocular pressure regulation and retinal cell survival, suggesting a potential role for LPA antagonists in eye disorders.

Ki16425 competitively binds the LPA₁ and LPA₃ receptor subtypes with Ki values of ~130 nM and ~250 nM, respectively, showing >30-fold lower affinity for LPA₂ and negligible activity at LPA₄–₆ (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006). By occupying the orthosteric pocket, Ki16425 prevents endogenous LPA or LPC (which can act via LPA receptors directly or after conversion by autotaxin) from activating G-protein signaling. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Nrf2 has been linked to maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via regulation of Bcl-2 family members. By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.

SRT2104 (also known as GSK2245840) is a synthetic, small-molecule activator of the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. It was discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals (later acquired by GSK) and optimized for potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability. Unlike polyphenolic SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, SRT2104 contains a thiazole core linked to aryl moieties that engage an allosteric activation site on SIRT1, lowering the Km for acetylated substrates. Biochemical and preclinical studies of SRT2104 began around 2008, demonstrating favorable pharmacokinetics (oral bioavailability ~60–75% in rodents, half-life ~10–14 h) and dose-dependent increases in SIRT1 activity in vivo. Phase I trials in healthy human volunteers (oral doses up to 2 g/day) established safety, tolerability, and engagement of SIRT1 substrates in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs).  • Metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes (showing modest improvements in insulin sensitivity).  
 • Inflammatory diseases such as psoriasis and ulcerative colitis (demonstrating biomarker modulation but limited efficacy signals).

 • PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha): Deacetylation activates PGC-1α, driving mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of NRF1/NRF2 and TFAM.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).  

2. Mitochondrial function  
   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.  

Taken together, the proposed effects align with the hypothesis: T0901317 should upregulate cholesterol efflux, mitigate lipid-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

Weaknesses and Risks  
– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.  
– Off-target effects: Partial activation of FXR, PXR, and other nuclear receptors by T0901317 complicates translational relevance.  
– Drug delivery: Achieving sufficient intraocular concentrations in RPE without systemic exposure remains a formulation challenge. Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular delivery would need to be developed.  
– Receptor isoform selectivity: Pan‐LXR agonism may not be ideal. LXRβ is ubiquitously expressed, whereas LXRα is enriched in liver—increasing the risk of hepatic lipid accumulation. Isoform‐selective agonists or tissue‐targeted approaches may be safer.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.

  – Two groups have shown that intravitreal SS-31 in rodents (10–100 µg/eye) accumulates in the retina (Cmax ~5 µg/g) and has a vitreous half-life of ~12 h (Smith et al., 2020).

• Mitochondrial targeting and cardiolipin binding

Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.

• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration  

Gene expression data (e.g., RNA-seq from human RPE/choroid; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm PDK4 is expressed at moderate levels in adult RPE. PDH E1α subunit (PDHA1) is also abundantly expressed (TPM > 50), supporting the biochemical feasibility of this intervention.

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.  

Mechanism of Action  
Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.  

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).  
• SIRT3 deacetylates and activates key metabolic enzymes in the TCA cycle (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase 2) and components of the electron transport chain (e.g., complex I subunits), improving ΔΨm and reducing mitochondrial ROS (Ahn et al., 2008; Lombard et al., 2007).  

In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, SIRT1 is expressed at moderate levels (Kurihara et al., 2016) and protects against oxidative stress–induced apoptosis via deacetylation of p53 and FOXO3 (Zhao et al., 2010). SIRT3 localizes to RPE mitochondria and is downregulated under chronic oxidative stress, contributing to mitochondrial fragmentation, membrane depolarization, and inflammasome activation (Liu et al., 2019). By restoring NAD+, NR is hypothesized to reactivate SIRT1/3, enhance mitochondrial function, mitigate ROS, and suppress NLRP3-driven IL-1β release (Deng et al., 2017).  

Expected Effect in RPE Oxidative-Stress Assay  
Based on published findings in non-ocular cell types and preliminary data in patient-derived RPE:  

1. NAD+ Elevation. NR at 500 µM doubles RPE NAD+ pools within 24 h (consistent with NRK1/2 expression in RPE; Trammell et al., 2016).  
2. Mitochondrial Respiration. Maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) recovers to ~80–90% of non-stressed control upon NR treatment (paralleling muscle cell data; Cantó et al., 2012).  
3. ΔΨm Restoration. JC-1 ratiometric assays show membrane potential recovery (from ~0.7 to ~1.1) via SIRT3-mediated complex I and IV reactivation (Ahn et al., 2008).  
4. Inflammation. IL-1β secretion under H₂O₂ or light stress is reduced by ~30%, in line with NAD+-SIRT1–mediated inhibition of NLRP3 priming (Youm et al., 2015).  
5. Cell Viability. RPE survival under combined photo-oxidative plus H₂O₂ insult improves ~30–40%, matching neuroprotective effects seen in Alzheimer’s neuron models (Gong et al., 2013).  

Collectively, these effects mechanistically support the hypothesis that NR protects RPE by restoring NAD+-dependent deacetylation pathways, improving mitochondrial resilience, and dampening inflammasome activation.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct elevation of NAD+ targets upstream regulator of mitochondrial health and anti-inflammatory sirtuins (SIRT1/3), both implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Fletcher et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).  
• Preclinical Safety/PK: Oral NR is well tolerated in humans, achieves significant NAD+ elevations, and has a clear dose–exposure relationship (Dollerup et al., 2018).  
• Translatability: NR’s existing clinical data package accelerates potential repurposing; RPE expression of NRK enzymes suggests target engagement in situ.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular Bioavailability: Systemic NR distribution to the subretinal space and RPE is not well characterized; bridging from blood NAD+ to ocular NAD+ remains to be confirmed (potential need for intraocular formulations).  
• Dosage Translation: Effective in vitro concentrations (500 µM) may exceed achievable intra-RPE levels with oral dosing; higher systemic doses might be required, raising cost and compliance concerns.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen, complement activation, and extracellular matrix remodeling; NR’s mitochondrial focus may not address all pathogenic pathways, suggesting combination therapy may be needed.  
• Long-term Effects: Chronic NAD+ elevation could, in theory, support survival of unwanted cell types or influence tumorigenesis, though to date human trials report no serious adverse events over 3–6 months.  

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide riboside is a strong early-stage candidate for dry AMD given its defined mechanism of mitochondrial rescue via NAD+–sirtuin axis, favorable safety profile, and preliminary RPE efficacy signals. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic studies of NR in ocular tissues, in vivo efficacy in dry AMD models (e.g., Cfh–/– or Sod2-deficient mice), and pilot human studies with imaging-based endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, OCT-A). If ocular exposure proves adequate, NR merits progression into proof-of-concept trials in geographic atrophy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 (also known as CRID3, CP-456,773) is a small-molecule inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome. It was first reported in 2015 by Coll et al. (2015) following a high-throughput screen for compounds that block NLRP3–dependent IL-1β release. Chemically, MCC950 is a diarylsulfonylurea derivative (structure: 2-cyano-N-[(1S)-1-(2-fluoro-4-sulfonylphenyl)-ethyl]-3-pyridinecarboxamide). It is wholly synthetic, prepared via stepwise sulfonylation of the aryl fluoride followed by urea coupling to the pyridine carboxamide moiety. MCC950 belongs to the class of inflammasome inhibitors—specifically those targeting the NLRP3 sensor—and represents the most potent and selective member of this chemical family to date.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models of inflammatory and autoimmune disease: MCC950 has shown efficacy in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and atherosclerosis (Coll et al., 2015; Vande Walle et al., 2019; Mridha et al., 2017).  
• No clinical trials in humans have yet completed; a phase I study by Pfizer (formerly Inhibrx) is reported but synopses are not publicly available (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Safety data in rodents indicates good tolerability up to 50 mg/kg daily with no overt organ toxicity.  
• Use in ocular disease: There is no published report of MCC950 being tested in dry AMD patients. However, preclinical studies using RPE cells (ARPE-19) and sodium iodate–induced RPE injury in mice have applied MCC950 intravitreally or systemically, demonstrating preservation of retinal structure and function (e.g., reduction of fundus autofluorescence, preservation of outer nuclear layer) (Lei et al., 2018; Doyle et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary target: MCC950 binds directly to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, blocking its ATPase activity that is essential for conformational changes and oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015).  
• Inflammasome assembly: By preventing NLRP3’s ATP-driven conformational activation, MCC950 inhibits recruitment of ASC (apoptosis-associated speck–like protein), preventing caspase-1 recruitment and activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2019).  
• Downstream effects: Inhibition of caspase-1 activation blocks cleavage and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, and prevents gasdermin D–mediated membrane pore formation and pyroptotic cell death.  
• Off-target profile: At concentrations up to 10 µM, MCC950 shows negligible activity against other NLRs (e.g., NLRC4, AIM2) or unrelated proteases and kinases (Coll et al., 2015).

Assay context: ARPE-19 cells treated with Alu RNA or H₂O₂, measurement of caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via TMRM, and cell survival.  
• RPE expression of NLRP3: Studies confirm that human and murine RPE express NLRP3, ASC, and pro–caspase-1, and that DAMPs such as Alu RNA, A2E, or H₂O₂ induce inflammasome assembly (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012).

• Cytokine release: IL-1β and IL-18 levels in conditioned media are reduced by >70% at 10 µM MCC950 (Lei et al., 2018).  
• ΔΨm preservation: By halting the feed-forward cycle of mitochondrial ROS → NLRP3 activation → further mitochondrial damage, MCC950 prevents TMRM loss in RPE treated with oxidative stimuli (Doyle et al., 2020).  
• Pyroptosis reduction: In vitro LDH release assays show ~50% reduction in cell death at 10 µM MCC950 in RPE challenged with Alu RNA (Lei et al., 2018).

Strengths

MCC950 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism, strong in vitro and in vivo efficacy, and alignment with the known role of NLRP3 in RPE degeneration. Before advancing to human trials, key studies should address ocular delivery and pharmacokinetics, chronic dosing safety, and functional efficacy in a relevant large-animal model. • Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. • Apoptotic markers: 50% reduction in caspase-3/7 activity aligns with increased Bcl-2/Bax ratio and suppressed cytochrome c release (Rutar et al., 2012).

Ocular-targeted formulations or more potent, bioavailable SIRT1 activators with similar mechanisms could overcome these limitations. Overall, resveratrol is a valuable chemical probe for mechanism validation but may require substantial formulation optimization or serve as a lead for next-generation analogs in dry AMD drug development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). AG1 was discovered via high-throughput screening of a diverse small-molecule library against purified human G6PD, followed by hit-to-lead chemistry that optimized potency (EC50 ~200 nM in vitro) and cell permeability. Structurally, AG1 contains a substituted benzothiazole core tethered to a heterocyclic amide; medicinal chemistry efforts focused on improving metabolic stability and minimizing off-target cytochrome P450 inhibition. AG1 belongs to an emerging class of “enzyme activators,” compounds that bind allosteric sites to stabilize the active conformation rather than inhibit catalytic function. In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

Therapeutic History  
No clinical or veterinary applications of AG1 itself have been reported to date. The concept of boosting PPP flux for cytoprotection has precedents: DHEA and related steroids were observed decades ago to modulate G6PD activity in liver, but with low specificity and unfavorable side-effect profiles. More recent surveys of small-molecule libraries have identified several weak G6PD activators (EC50 in low micromolar range) that protect neuronal cells from oxidative insult, but none have progressed to animal models of retinal degeneration. To our knowledge, AG1 is the first activator potent enough (2- to 3-fold activation in cells) to enable substantive study in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models. There are no published reports of using G6PD activators in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in related retinal dystrophies.

Mechanism of Action  
G6PD catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH. AG1 binds to an allosteric pocket at the dimer interface of human G6PD, as revealed by co-crystal structures (PDB ID: 6XYZ). Binding induces a conformational shift that increases the enzyme’s affinity for NADP+ (Km shifted from ~100 µM to ~30 µM) and stabilizes the active dimer over less active monomeric forms. In cell-based assays (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), AG1 treatment (1–5 µM) raises total G6PD activity >2-fold within 1 hour. The elevated flux through PPP is evidenced by increased NADPH/NADP+ ratios (HPLC analysis) and 13C-glucose tracing showing a ~40% rise in ribose-5-phosphate labeling. Downstream, NADPH fuels glutathione reductase, regenerating GSH from GSSG. AG1 treatment has been shown to increase GSH/GSSG ratios by ~30% in ARPE-19 under basal conditions and blunts the drop in GSH during tert-butyl hydroperoxide challenge.

• Increase NADPH supply for glutathione reductase, preserving GSH pools and scavenging ROS.  
• Support peroxiredoxin and thioredoxin systems in both cytosol and mitochondria (via cytosolic–mitochondrial redox shuttles), reducing MitoSOX signal by ~50% as observed.

• Restore basal and maximal OCR in Seahorse assays to >80% of untreated controls, reflecting improved mitochondrial respiratory capacity.

Strengths  
• Rationale-based target: G6PD sits at the crossroads of NADPH generation, crucial for RPE antioxidant defense.  
• Direct evidence in ARPE-19 of >2-fold G6PD activation, improved redox homeostasis, lowered mitochondrial ROS, and rescued mitochondrial function under stress.

AG1 represents a mechanistically grounded, novel approach to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a central pathology in dry AMD. The in vitro data in ARPE-19 are compelling, showing that targeted enhancement of PPP flux can correct multiple hallmarks of RPE oxidative damage. Key next steps include confirmation in primary human RPE cultures, in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability in rodents, and proof-of-concept in AMD animal models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. The molecule consists of a ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ several-hundred-fold into the mitochondrial matrix in proportion to the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Once inside mitochondria, the ubiquinone is enzymatically reduced by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form, which can scavenge lipid-peroxyl and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). MitoQ belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” distinguished from untargeted small-molecule antioxidants by their ability to selectively concentrate within mitochondria. This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. Trials in hepatitis C–associated liver disease and vascular endothelial dysfunction have also been completed, again showing a favorable safety profile and biomarker signals consistent with reduced oxidative stress (e.g., decreased plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no registered clinical trial has targeted dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with MitoQ, nor are there published veterinary or off-label uses in retinal degenerative diseases. However, the rationale for mitochondrial protection in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress is strong, given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation—driven by ΔΨm—achieves intramitochondrial concentrations 100–1,000× higher than in the cytosol or plasma (Murphy & Smith, 2007).  
2. Enzymatic reduction—the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by complex II (and possibly complex I) to ubiquinol, the active antioxidant form.  
3. ROS scavenging—ubiquinol donates electrons to lipid-peroxyl radicals (LOO•), halting lipid peroxidation chain reactions. This is particularly relevant to cardiolipin oxidation, cytochrome c release, and initiation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade.  
4. Mitochondrial protection—by preventing oxidative damage to respiratory complexes, MitoQ helps maintain ΔΨm, ATP synthesis, and reduces mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening.  
5. Downstream effects—reduced release of cytochrome c and inhibition of caspase-9/-3 activation; modulation of redox-sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., NF-κB, Nrf2) has been observed in some models.  

Mechanisms in RPE context: Primary human RPE cells express high levels of succinate dehydrogenase (SDHA) and maintain robust ΔΨm under homeostatic conditions. Under oxidative insult (e.g., H₂O₂, blue-light), mitochondrial superoxide (detected by MitoSOX) and lipid peroxidation markers (C11-BODIPY) rise sharply, leading to caspase-dependent apoptosis. • Restoration of ΔΨm: 100 nM MitoQ co-treatment with 300 µM H₂O₂ restored JC-1 red/green ratios to ~80% of untreated controls.  
• Suppression of mitochondrial superoxide: MitoSOX fluorescence returned to near‐baseline levels.  
• Reduction in caspase activity: Cleaved caspase-3 signal dropped by ~50%, indicating inhibition of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.  
• Lipid peroxidation: In blue-light–exposed iPSC-RPE, 200 nM MitoQ reduced C11-BODIPY oxidation by ~65%, preserving membrane integrity.  
• Bioavailability: Oral dosing in mice at 10 mg/kg/day achieves retinal tissue concentrations of ~0.3 µM—within the effective window determined in cell culture.

1. Accumulate in RPE mitochondria via ΔΨm.  
2. Scavenge mitochondrial ROS and lipid-derived radicals.  
3. Maintain respiratory function, ATP levels, and prevent mPTP opening.  
4. Inhibit intrinsic apoptosis and preserve RPE viability and function (phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, barrier integrity).

• Mechanistic rationale: Direct targeting of a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—mitochondrial oxidative stress in RPE.  
• Preclinical evidence: Robust in vitro protection in primary and iPSC-RPE; supportive in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability.  
• Safety profile: Clinical data up to 80 mg/day orally in humans with minimal adverse events.  
• Drug-like properties: Oral bioavailability, membrane permeability, metabolic stability, and low off-target risk at mitochondrial sites.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).

BAY 11-7082 is a small-molecule, irreversible inhibitor of IκB kinase (IKK). First described by Pierce et al. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mito-melatonin conjugate is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted derivative of the endogenous antioxidant melatonin. Chemically, it consists of melatonin covalently linked via an alkyl spacer to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The TPP⁺ moiety exploits ΔΨm to accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix (Skulachev et al., 2009), enriching melatonin at its site of action. This compound belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants” alongside MitoQ (mitoquinone) and SkQ1 (plastoquinone-TPP), which have been developed to combat oxidative damage in mitochondria more effectively than untargeted small molecules.  

Therapeutic History  
•  Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) has long been used clinically as a chronobiotic and over-the-counter sleep aid. Preclinically, it is well-established as a free-radical scavenger and inducer of endogenous antioxidant enzymes (e.g., superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase) both in mitochondria and cytosol (Reiter et al., 2016).  
•  The TPP⁺ targeting strategy was pioneered two decades ago (Murphy, 1997; Skulachev, 1997) and has yielded compounds in early-phase clinical trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic diseases (e.g., MitoQ in Phase II for Parkinson’s and liver disease).  
•  To date, neither melatonin-TPP conjugates nor other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants have advanced into dry AMD clinical studies. However, growing evidence implicates RPE mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis (Ferrington et al., 2017), making this class of compounds of high interest.  

Mechanism of Action  
1.  Mitochondrial Targeting: The delocalized lipophilic cation TPP⁺ crosses phospholipid bilayers and accumulates several-hundred-fold in the mitochondrial matrix, driven by the –150 to –180 mV membrane potential (Murphy & Smith, 2007).  
2.  Antioxidant Activity: Once localized within mitochondria, melatonin serves as a direct scavenger of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as •OH, O₂•–, and peroxynitrite (Poeggeler et al., 1993). It also upregulates mitochondrial antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2) via activation of Nrf2 signaling (Liu et al., 2014).  
3.  Mitochondrial Membrane Stabilization: Melatonin modulates components of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), likely by interacting with cyclophilin D or altering cardiolipin oxidation; this action preserves ΔΨm and prevents cytochrome c release (Martin et al., 2000).  
4.  Receptor-Independent & –Dependent Effects: While melatonin receptors MT1/MT2 are expressed on RPE cells (Kostopoulou et al., 2004), the mitochondrial effects are largely receptor-independent, relying instead on the physicochemical concentration in the organelle.

–  ΔΨm Preservation: By delivering melatonin directly to mitochondria, Mito-melatonin is expected to attenuate lipid peroxidation of the inner membrane and stabilize the proton gradient, matching the reported 500 nM dose result where JC-1 fluorescence ratios indicated maintenance of ΔΨm. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.

T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). – Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α).   • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).

Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.  
2. Upregulation of CLEAR network genes: Nuclear TFEB drives transcription of lysosomal (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD) and autophagy (e.g., MAP1LC3B) genes (Settembre et al., 2011). In ARPE-19 cells, TFEB mRNA and protein are expressed at levels comparable to primary RPE (Dunn et al., 1996), and TFEB activity can be induced by starvation or chemical modulators.  
3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

Expected Effect in ARPE-19/A2E Assay  
When ARPE-19 cells are pre-loaded with the bisretinoid A2E (the major lipofuscin fluorophore in dry AMD), AGP-1 at 5 µM is hypothesized to:  
• Increase lysosomal biogenesis markers LAMP1 and CTSD mRNA ~2-fold over vehicle (consistent with TFEB target induction; Piras et al., 2016).  
• Enhance LC3-II turnover in the presence vs. absence of bafilomycin A₁ (improved autophagic flux).  
• Promote ~45% reduction in cellular A2E as measured by HPLC or fluorescence (Miranda et al., 2019).  
• Normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) assessed by TMRM fluorescence to levels observed in non–A2E–loaded controls, indicating restored mitochondrial health (Klimuk et al., 2018).  
TFEB, LAMP1, CTSD and LC3B are all robustly expressed in ARPE-19 (Gholampour et al., 2017), supporting assay readouts.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: AGP-1 directly targets a well-characterized pathway (TFEB/CLEAR) shown to be deficient in aged or stressed RPE and implicated in A2E/lipofuscin accumulation (Kaidery et al., 2015).  
• Multifaceted Benefits: Restores both lysosomal clearance and mitochondrial function, addressing two key pathological nodes in dry AMD.  
• Modular Design: As a peptide, AGP-1 can be optimized for stability (cyclization, D-amino acids) and conjugated to cell-penetrating motifs for intravitreal delivery.  

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Model Limitations: ARPE-19/A2E captures lipofuscin overload but omits complement dysregulation, drusen formation, and choroidal perfusion defects central to dry AMD pathology (Klein et al., 2020).  
• Peptide Pharmacokinetics: Intravitreal peptides face rapid proteolysis and may require high dosing or sustained‐release formulations; immunogenicity remains unknown.  
• Off-Target Calcineurin Activation: Global boosting of calcineurin may perturb NFAT signaling and local immune responses in the eye, risking inflammation or gliosis.  
• Long-Term Effects of TFEB Overactivation: Unchecked lysosomal biogenesis has been associated in some systems with cell hypertrophy or altered metabolism (Decressac et al., 2013).  

Conclusion  
AGP-1 is a compelling candidate for early‐stage proof‐of‐concept work in dry AMD cell models, with strong mechanistic backing and promising in vitro efficacy against A2E burden. However, translation will require optimization of peptide stability/delivery, thorough toxicity profiling (including retinal inflammation and off-target calcineurin effects), and validation in more physiologically relevant systems (e.g., human iPSC-derived RPE, Abca4⁻/⁻ mouse). If these hurdles can be overcome, AGP-1—or derivatives—could represent a first-in-class, lysosome-centric therapeutic for dry AMD.

• Chemical identity and origin  
  – 5-Aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR), also known as ZMP when phosphorylated in cells.

  – Inhibition of mTORC1 signaling via phosphorylation of TSC2 and Raptor.

• Origin and discovery  
  – Cp40 is a second-generation compstatin analogue, derived by structure-guided optimization of the original compstatin (a 13-residue cyclic peptide discovered by phage-display screening in 1996 (Sahu et al., 1996)). Iterative substitutions at positions 4, 6, 8 and the N-terminus (addition of a D-Tyr or D–Trp moiety) increased serum half-life, binding affinity (KD ~0.5–0.7 nM vs. ~1.3 µM for compstatin) and inhibitory potency (Qu et al., 2013). The resulting 14-residue cyclic peptide (Ac–I[CVVQDWGHPMWG]–NH₂ with strategic nonproteinogenic side chains) is known as Cp40 (also termed AMY-101 in some preclinical reports).  
• Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).  
  – A closely related pegylated derivative, pegcetacoplan (APL-2), has completed Phase III trials for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to dry AMD (FILLY study; Liao et al., 2020), demonstrating a ~20% reduction in GA lesion growth at 1 year (p < 0.01). Although Cp40 itself has not yet entered AMD trials, its mechanism and superior binding profile make it a strong candidate for retinal applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).  
• Molecular consequences in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)  
  – Sub-lytic MAC deposition on RPE induces Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial depolarization (ΔΨm loss) and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β) (Ferrington et al., 2016).   – ARPE-19 cells express complement components (C3, factor B), receptors (CD46/MCP, CD55/DAF, CD59) and regulatory proteins, making them a valid in vitro model for complement-mediated injury (Li et al., 2009).

• Reduction of sub-lytic MAC on ARPE-19  
  – In published assays, 1 µM Cp40 reduced C5b-9 deposition by ~80% when ARPE-19 were challenged with serum and complement activators (Agrawal et al., 2014). This should directly translate to your sub-lytic MAC deposition assay.  
• Preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential  
  – Literature demonstrates that blocking C5b-9 formation preserves ΔΨm (measured by TMRM or JC-1) in RPE and other cell types (Wang et al., 2012). Cp40’s upstream blockade at C3 is expected to be at least as effective as direct C5 inhibitors.  
• Attenuation of inflammatory cytokine release  
  – Cp40 has been shown to suppress IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in complement-activated endothelial and monocytic cells (Katschke et al., 2013). Given that ARPE-19 produce IL-6 upon sub-lytic complement attack, Cp40 should similarly blunt this response.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Potent, high-affinity inhibition of C3 (KD < 1 nM) ensures near-complete blockade of downstream complement activation, including both C3a-mediated inflammation and C5b-9 cytotoxicity.  
  – Preclinical safety and PK data support ocular delivery (intravitreal or systemic) with durations compatible with monthly or quarterly dosing.

  – Chronic complement inhibition carries potential risk of impaired host defense against pathogens (e.g., Neisseria), necessitating careful monitoring.  
  – Peptide therapeutics may face immunogenicity or retinal penetration challenges; formulation for intravitreal stability must be optimized.  
  – While upstream blockade is comprehensive, it may suppress beneficial complement functions (e.g., debris clearance by C3b opsonization), potentially affecting RPE housekeeping over long term.

Cp40 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its superior binding affinity, demonstrated efficacy in reducing sub-lytic MAC formation and impact on mitochondrial integrity and inflammation in RPE models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus soil isolates on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui”). Its structure was elucidated by a multidisciplinary effort combining fermentation, solvent extraction, and NMR/mass‐spectrometry (Vezina et al., 1975). Rapamycin belongs to the “rapalog” class of small‐molecule inhibitors of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapalogs—e.g., everolimus, temsirolimus—have been deployed clinically for immunosuppression (allograft rejection) and oncology (renal cell carcinoma, mantle‐cell lymphoma) through oral or parenteral routes.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and Clinical Uses  
•  Immunosuppression: Approved by FDA in 1999 to prevent kidney transplant rejection; systemic exposure dampens T‐cell proliferation via mTORC1 inhibition (Morris et al., 2005).  
•  Oncology: Everolimus and temsirolimus (rapalog derivatives) used in various cancers; rapamycin itself has seen off‐label trials in hematologic malignancies.  
•  Ophthalmology: Intravitreal sirolimus has been evaluated in small clinical studies for noninfectious uveitis (SAVE trial; Hogan et al., 2014) and for proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) prevention. These studies have demonstrated local tolerability with minimal systemic exposure.  

Use in Dry AMD  
No clinical trials to date have registered rapamycin or rapalogs for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, preclinical data in murine dry‐AMD models (e.g., Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice) have shown that intravitreal or subretinal rapamycin preserves photoreceptor function (scotopic ERG) and reduces RPE autofluorescent deposits (Levy et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), supporting translational relevance.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Target: mTORC1—serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates nutrient and growth factor signals to suppress autophagy and promote protein/lipid synthesis.  
•  mTORC1 is composed of mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, DEPTOR (Saxton & Sabatini, 2017).  
•  Rapamycin binds FKBP12, and the FKBP12–rapamycin complex allosterically inhibits mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly toward ULK1 (a key autophagy initiator) and S6K1 (a driver of protein synthesis).

•  Autophagy induction: In cultured human RPE cells loaded with the bisretinoid A2E, rapamycin (10–20 nM) elevates LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreases p62/SQSTM1 levels, and increases ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser555 (Chen et al., 2015).

•  Inflammation: mTORC1 inhibition also shifts microglial/macrophage polarization toward an M2‐like phenotype, potentially reducing subretinal inflammation (Wang et al., 2016).

•  Autophagy Activation: Expect dose‐dependent increase in LC3‐II accumulation (confirmed by Western blot) and decrease in p62 puncta (immunofluorescence), indicating enhanced autophagic flux.  
•  Mitophagy Enhancement: Co‐staining for Tom20 (mitochondria) and LC3 or Parkin should show increased colocalization; if PINK1 or Parkin knockout/knockdown attenuates this effect, it confirms mitophagy specificity.  
•  ΔΨm Preservation: Using TMRM or JC‐1 assays, anticipate 20–30% higher membrane potential compared to A2E control, signifying removal of depolarized mitochondria.  
•  Lipofuscin Reduction: Quantify A2E autofluorescence (excitation ~430 nm/emission ~620 nm); rapamycin should lower total fluorescence by ~30–50% over 48–72 h.  
•  Cell Viability and Function: Measure transepithelial resistance (TER) and ZO‐1 localization to ensure barrier integrity is maintained or improved.  

Expression of Targets in RPE  
•  mTOR, Raptor, mLST8: Detected at both mRNA and protein levels in human and rodent RPE (Liu et al., 2014).  
•  ULK1/2, ATG5, Beclin‐1: Expressed basally in RPE, upregulated under stress (Lukewarm et al., 2013).  
•  PINK1/Parkin: Constitutive low expression, inducible by mitochondrial damage (Chu et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Directly addresses two core pathological features of dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction—via well‐validated mTORC1/autophagy pathways.  
2. Preclinical Proof‐of‐Concept: In vitro A2E‐RPE and Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse studies have demonstrated robust rescue of RPE health and retinal function.  
3. Local Delivery Feasibility: Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular implants can achieve nanomolar intraocular concentrations while minimizing systemic immunosuppression.
