•  Optimization of ocular dosing/regimen to balance efficacy and safety  
•  Longitudinal in vivo studies in large‐animal AMD models (e.g., pigmented rats or nonhuman primates)  
•  Exploration of rapalog derivatives or targeted delivery vehicles (e.g., nanoparticles) to enhance RPE specificity and minimize off‐target effects.

Structural modeling and in vitro crosslinking assays indicate that Pep-CM stabilizes the antiparallel coiled-coil interaction between MFN2 protomers, lowering the energetic barrier for outer-membrane tethering (Lee et al., 2016). By favoring the “tether-competent” conformation of MFN2, Pep-CM promotes membrane juxtaposition and subsequent GTPase-driven membrane fusion. · Reduce mitochondrial fragmentation (quantified by mito-GFP morphometry)  
· Restore ΔΨm toward baseline (TMRM fluorescence intensity)  
· Lower ROS levels (DCFDA or MitoSOX assays)  
· Enhance OCR and ATP production (Seahorse XFe analysis)  
· Improve RPE functions that depend on healthy mitochondria—namely phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (measured via fluorescent bead uptake) and barrier integrity (TER measurements)  
These anticipated effects flow directly from MFN2’s role in maintaining mitochondrial network connectivity and bioenergetic health in RPE.

· Target Validation: MFN2 loss or dysfunction has been implicated in RPE degeneration and dry AMD progression; rescuing fusion is mechanistically aligned with disease pathology.  
· Direct Mechanism: Pep-CM acts at a proximal step in the fusion cascade, offering precise modulation versus upstream indirect approaches.  
· In Vitro Feasibility: ARPE-19 cells readily take up cell-penetrating peptides, and key readouts (ΔΨm, ROS, OCR) are well established.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
· Delivery and Stability: Peptide delivery into the subretinal space or into RPE in vivo poses challenges. Proteolytic degradation and limited tissue retention may require formulation (e.g., nanoparticles, PEGylation).  
· Off-Target Effects: While designed for MFN2, cross-reactivity with MFN1 or unrelated coiled-coil proteins must be ruled out.  
· Immunogenicity: Repeated administration of a synthetic peptide may provoke ocular inflammation.  
· Translational Gap: Efficacy in neurons does not guarantee success in RPE; AMD is multifactorial, and mitochondrial fusion is only one facet of RPE pathology.

Conclusion  
Pep-CM represents a mechanistically compelling candidate for dry AMD, with strong rationale rooted in MFN2 biology and preclinical success in neurodegenerative models. Early-stage in vitro validation in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under oxidative stress is warranted. If positive, subsequent optimization of peptide stability and targeted ocular delivery would be critical before in vivo proof-of-concept in animal models of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.  
• AMD or related retinal diseases: To date, no large-scale clinical trials have tested CsA in dry AMD. A handful of preclinical studies have examined calcineurin inhibitors in photoreceptor or RPE stress models, but nothing conclusive in patients with geographic atrophy or drusen-driven pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary known mechanisms:  
1. Cyclophilin D binding and mPTP inhibition  
  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin D complex raises the threshold for calcium- or ROS-induced mPTP opening, preserving the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.  
2. Calcineurin inhibition (immunosuppressive arm)  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin A complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT transcription factors.  
  • This reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production but is not the desired mechanism for protecting RPE from oxidative injury.  

Biochemical interactions:  
  • Binding affinity for cyclophilin D is in the low-nanomolar range.  
  • mPTP regulation by CsA is well documented in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and kidney cells under oxidative or calcium stress.  
  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to model the oxidative stress component of dry AMD.  
Expected outcomes with 1–5 µM CsA:  
  • Preservation of ΔΨm as measured by JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio (literature reports ~20–40% higher ratio vs. untreated under H₂O₂).  
  • Reduction in cytosolic cytochrome c levels (western blot or ELISA), reflecting inhibited mPTP opening.  
  • Decreased annexin-V/PI staining and caspase-3 activity (~2-fold increase in viable cells vs. H₂O₂ alone).  
  • Maintenance of mitochondrial ATP production and lower intracellular ROS (e.g., DCFDA assay).  
Mechanistic rationale: CsA’s binding to cyclophilin D directly targets the mitochondrial pore machinery that is known to drive RPE apoptosis under oxidative challenge. Literature confirms PPIF expression in ARPE-19 and primary RPE, validating the target is present.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Direct targeting of mPTP—an established contributor to RPE death in models of dry AMD.  
  • Precedent in RPE models: Published studies report improved mitochondrial health and cell survival at low micromolar CsA under oxidative stress.  
  • Known safety profile: Topical ocular CsA is already in widespread use for dry-eye disease; periocular delivery could achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure.  
  • Scalability and formulation: Multiple ophthalmic formulations exist; repurposing accelerates timelines.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target immunosuppression: Even topical or periocular CsA may diffuse to systemic circulation or engage calcineurin in off-target tissues; this could predispose to infection or alter local immune surveillance in the retina.

  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, extracellular matrix remodeling); mPTP inhibition addresses the final common pathway of RPE death but may not halt upstream drivers.

Overall, CsA is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its cyclophilin D-mediated inhibition of mPTP and preserved mitochondrial function in RPE under oxidative stress. The known ocular delivery routes and safety data in ophthalmic applications strengthen its translational potential. Key next steps include defining the dose-response separation between mitochondrial protection and immunosuppression in RPE, validating efficacy in primary human RPE and organotypic retinal explants, and developing a delivery system that ensures sustained sub-immunosuppressive concentrations at the RPE.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 (also known as CRID3, CP-456,773) is a small-molecule inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome. It was first reported in 2015 by Coll et al. (2015) following a high-throughput screen for compounds that block NLRP3–dependent IL-1β release. Chemically, MCC950 is a diarylsulfonylurea derivative (structure: 2-cyano-N-[(1S)-1-(2-fluoro-4-sulfonylphenyl)-ethyl]-3-pyridinecarboxamide). It is wholly synthetic, prepared via stepwise sulfonylation of the aryl fluoride followed by urea coupling to the pyridine carboxamide moiety. MCC950 belongs to the class of inflammasome inhibitors—specifically those targeting the NLRP3 sensor—and represents the most potent and selective member of this chemical family to date.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models of inflammatory and autoimmune disease: MCC950 has shown efficacy in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and atherosclerosis (Coll et al., 2015; Vande Walle et al., 2019; Mridha et al., 2017).

• Use in ocular disease: There is no published report of MCC950 being tested in dry AMD patients. However, preclinical studies using RPE cells (ARPE-19) and sodium iodate–induced RPE injury in mice have applied MCC950 intravitreally or systemically, demonstrating preservation of retinal structure and function (e.g., reduction of fundus autofluorescence, preservation of outer nuclear layer) (Lei et al., 2018; Doyle et al., 2020).

• Primary target: MCC950 binds directly to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, blocking its ATPase activity that is essential for conformational changes and oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015).  
• Inflammasome assembly: By preventing NLRP3’s ATP-driven conformational activation, MCC950 inhibits recruitment of ASC (apoptosis-associated speck–like protein), preventing caspase-1 recruitment and activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2019).  
• Downstream effects: Inhibition of caspase-1 activation blocks cleavage and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, and prevents gasdermin D–mediated membrane pore formation and pyroptotic cell death.  
• Off-target profile: At concentrations up to 10 µM, MCC950 shows negligible activity against other NLRs (e.g., NLRC4, AIM2) or unrelated proteases and kinases (Coll et al., 2015).

Assay context: ARPE-19 cells treated with Alu RNA or H₂O₂, measurement of caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via TMRM, and cell survival.

• Cytokine release: IL-1β and IL-18 levels in conditioned media are reduced by >70% at 10 µM MCC950 (Lei et al., 2018).  
• ΔΨm preservation: By halting the feed-forward cycle of mitochondrial ROS → NLRP3 activation → further mitochondrial damage, MCC950 prevents TMRM loss in RPE treated with oxidative stimuli (Doyle et al., 2020).  
• Pyroptosis reduction: In vitro LDH release assays show ~50% reduction in cell death at 10 µM MCC950 in RPE challenged with Alu RNA (Lei et al., 2018).

Strengths  
1. Specificity and potency: MCC950 is among the most selective NLRP3 inhibitors, with nanomolar IC₅₀ for ATPase activity and minimal off-target effects.  
2. Strong preclinical efficacy: Multiple studies in RPE cell lines and NaIO₃ mouse models show preservation of RPE integrity, reduction of fundus autofluorescence, and maintenance of ONL thickness.

1. Ocular pharmacokinetics/delivery: Systemic administration may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space; intravitreal dosing schedules, drug stability, and potential immunogenicity require assessment.  
2. Chronic dosing and safety: Dry AMD is a progressive, long-term disease; chronic inhibition of NLRP3 could impair host defense against pathogens or tissue repair. Long-term ocular safety data are lacking.

4. Redundancy in inflammasome pathways: Other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4) or caspase-8–mediated IL-1β maturation may compensate in chronic disease, potentially limiting efficacy.

MCC950 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism, strong in vitro and in vivo efficacy, and alignment with the known role of NLRP3 in RPE degeneration. Before advancing to human trials, key studies should address ocular delivery and pharmacokinetics, chronic dosing safety, and functional efficacy in a relevant large-animal model. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
15-Oxospiramilactone, commonly referred to as “S3,” is a small-molecule modulator of mitochondrial fusion originally discovered in a high-throughput screen for regulators of mitochondrial morphology. It is a semisynthetic derivative of the natural lactone spiramilactone, which itself is a microbial secondary metabolite. Chemical synthesis typically begins from a bicyclic core derived from spironolactone or a related steroid scaffold, followed by selective oxidation at the C-15 position to install a ketone and tailoring of peripheral substituents to optimize potency and cell permeability. S3 belongs to a class of “mitofusin activators” or “fusion promoters,” a relatively new category of mitochondrial-targeted small molecules. In general, fusion promoters have been explored in the context of neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy, and peripheral neuropathies to restore mitochondrial network integrity.  

Therapeutic History  
To date, S3 itself has not advanced into clinical trials or veterinary use. Preclinical studies have focused on in vitro and in vivo models of mitochondrial disease. For example:  
• Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A): in mouse models bearing MFN2 mutations, systemic administration of mitofusin activators ameliorated peripheral nerve conduction deficits and improved motor function (Franco et al., 2016).  
• Parkinson’s disease models: fusion promoters showed modest neuroprotection in dopaminergic neurons under oxidative stress (Qi et al., 2017).  
• Cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury: enhancing fusion reduced infarct size and preserved contractile function (Chen et al., 2018).  

No reports to date describe direct evaluation of S3 or its analogs in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) systems.  

Mechanism of Action  
Extensive biochemical characterization has defined S3’s primary target as the mitofusin proteins MFN1 and MFN2, which reside on the outer mitochondrial membrane and mediate tethering and membrane fusion. Key mechanistic insights include:  
1. Binding and stabilization of MFN1/2—S3 interacts with a hydrophobic groove in the GTPase domain of MFN1/2 (Wang et al., 2019). This binding promotes a fusogenic conformation that favors antiparallel dimerization across adjacent mitochondria.  
2. Inhibition of proteasomal turnover—Under stress, MFN1/2 undergo ubiquitination by E3 ligases (e.g., MARCH5), leading to proteasomal degradation. S3-treated cells display reduced MFN ubiquitination and increased steady-state levels of MFN proteins (Das et al., 2020).  
3. Promotion of mitochondrial elongation and improved bioenergetics—In fibroblasts and neuronal cells exposed to oxidative stressors (rotenone, H₂O₂), S3 restores mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), increases oxygen consumption rates, and reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation (Li et al., 2021).

Hypothesis: In RPE cells (ARPE-19 and primary human RPE), oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂ at 200–500 µM) induce mitochondrial fragmentation via DRP1 activation and MFN degradation, leading to loss of ΔΨm, bioenergetic failure, and cell death. Addition of S3 (1–10 µM) is expected to:  
• Increase MFN1/2 protein levels (western blot; immunofluorescence)  
• Reverse H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial fragmentation, as quantified by automated image analysis of mitochondrial length and form factor (MiNA toolset)  
• Restore ΔΨm, measured via TMRM or JC-1 fluorescence assays  
• Improve OXPHOS capacity (Seahorse XF mitochondrial stress test) and reduce cytosolic ROS (CellROX)  
• Decrease mPTP opening susceptibility (calcein–cobalt quenching assay)  
Importantly, both MFN1 and MFN2 mRNAs are well expressed in RPE (Human Protein Atlas, n.d.).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Defined, druggable target (MFN1/2) with clear mechanistic link to mitochondrial fragmentation observed in dry AMD RPE.  
• Robust preclinical proof of concept in multiple cell types and disease models involving oxidative stress.  
• Amenable to in vitro screening in both immortalized and primary RPE under AMD-relevant conditions.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Absence of in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic/toxicology data: retinal delivery, blood–retina barrier penetration, and off-target effects remain uncharacterized.  
• Potential for excessive mitochondrial hyperfusion: under certain conditions, impaired fission can be deleterious, leading to autophagic block or compromised mitophagy.  
• Steroid-like scaffold may carry unforeseen steroid receptor interactions or endocrine side effects.  

Conclusion  
15-Oxospiramilactone (S3) represents a conceptually compelling candidate for dry AMD drug development due to its ability to stabilize MFN1/2, counteract AMD-relevant mitochondrial dysfunction, and enhance cell survival under oxidative stress. The next critical steps are:  
1. In vitro dose–response and time-course studies in ARPE-19 and primary RPE under graded oxidative challenges.  
2. Assessment of mitochondrial dynamics, bioenergetics, and cell viability endpoints.  
3. Preliminary in vivo ocular administration studies (e.g., intravitreal or periocular delivery) in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Cfh−/− mice or NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration).  
4. Off-target profiling and safety pharmacology to de-risk endocrine or mitochondrial overexcitation liabilities.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Desipramine is a synthetic small‐molecule tricyclic antidepressant first synthesized in the 1960s by chemists at Geigy (now part of Novartis). Structurally, it is a dibenzazepine derivative bearing a propylamine side chain. Desipramine belongs to the class of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), which share a three‐ring central scaffold and were originally developed to block neuronal reuptake of monoamines (norepinephrine and, to a lesser extent, serotonin). Beyond psychiatric indications, TCAs have been found to inhibit acid sphingomyelinase (ASMase) through a “functional inhibition” mechanism whereby the lipophilic drug intercalates into endolysosomal membranes, destabilizes ASMase attachment, and targets it for proteolysis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Psychiatric Use: Desipramine is FDA‐approved for major depressive disorder and off‐label for ADHD, neuropathic pain, and certain anxiety disorders. Typical systemic dosing ranges from 75 to 200 mg/day orally.  
2. ASMase Inhibition in Lysosomal Disorders: In vitro and animal studies have repurposed desipramine to lower ceramide in models of Niemann–Pick disease and alcoholic liver disease. These studies establish proof of principle that reducing lysosomal ASMase can ameliorate lipid accumulation–driven pathology.  
3. Ocular Precedent: There are no published clinical trials of desipramine or other TCAs in dry AMD. However, several groups have used desipramine in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell culture (ARPE‐19) to interrogate ceramide‐driven apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., Sakamoto et al., 2011; Hanus et al., 2013).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Psychiatric Mechanism  
• Norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (Ki ∼10 nM) at the synaptic norepinephrine transporter (NET). Secondary effect on serotonin reuptake (Ki ∼100 nM).  
ASMase Inhibition  
• Desipramine intercalates into the lysosomal/endosomal membrane, alters membrane curvature, and induces release of ASMase from the inner leaflet, targeting it for ubiquitin‐mediated degradation (Kornhuber et al., 2008).  
• Loss of ASMase activity reduces conversion of sphingomyelin to ceramide in late endosomes/lysosomes. Ceramide is a bioactive lipid that sensitizes mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening, leading to ΔΨm collapse, cytochrome c release, and caspase‐3 activation.  
• Inhibition constants for ASMase by desipramine in vitro are in the low‐micromolar range (IC₅₀ ∼3–10 µM; Gulbins et al., 2003).

Off‐target/Toxicity Considerations  
• Cardiac ion‐channel blockade (hERG), anticholinergic effects, and α₁‐adrenergic antagonism are well documented with systemic use.  
• Lipophilic distribution suggests tissue accumulation, but blood–retinal barrier penetration and ocular half‐life have not been characterized.

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Oxidative‐Stress Assay  
Assay Conditions  
• ARPE‐19 cells exposed to 200 µM H₂O₂ for 4–6 h to model oxidative damage relevant to dry AMD.  
Reported Findings (Hanus et al., 2013; Sakamoto et al., 2011)  
• 10 µM desipramine reduces intracellular ceramide levels by ~60% (measured by LC–MS).  
• Tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM) retention is preserved (ΔΨm maintained at ~80% of control), compared to ~30% in H₂O₂‐only wells.  
• Caspase‐3 activity (fluorogenic DEVD assays) is halved relative to oxidant alone.

Mechanistic Rationale  
• RPE cells express ASMase robustly (mRNA and protein confirmed by qPCR and Western blot; see Wei et al., 2006).  
• By lowering ceramide, desipramine should desensitize mPTP opening and prevent the feed‐forward loop of ROS‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis.  
• This pathway is relevant to dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial compromise, and RPE cell loss drive geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a lipid mediator (ceramide) directly implicated in RPE mitochondrial injury under oxidative stress.  
2. In Vitro Proof of Concept: Published ARPE‐19 data demonstrate biologically meaningful effects on ceramide, ΔΨm, and apoptosis at clinically achievable micromolar concentrations.  
3. Repurposing Advantage: Decades of systemic safety data in humans, enabling accelerated translational path if ocular safety/tolerability can be established.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Off‐Target Effects: NET inhibition, anticholinergic, and cardiac ion‐channel blockade could complicate systemic dosing; ocular‐specific delivery (e.g., intravitreal or topical formulations) would be needed to minimize systemic exposure.  
2. Pharmacokinetics/Distribution: Unknown ocular bioavailability, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and retinal pigment epithelium–choroid distribution.  
3. Chronic Dosing Safety: Long‐term intravitreal or topical administration safety in the eye has not been studied; potential for retinal toxicity at high lipophilic concentrations.

1. Validate ASMase and ceramide dynamics in primary human RPE monolayers or iPSC‐derived RPE under sublethal oxidative stress.  
2. Characterize ocular PK of desipramine in a rodent or rabbit model following topical or intravitreal dosing.  
3. Assess in vivo efficacy in dry AMD‐relevant models (e.g., SOD1⁻/⁻ mice or sodium iodate–induced RPE degeneration).  
4. Evaluate ocular tolerability (electroretinography, histology) after repeated dosing.

Desipramine presents a compelling mechanistic approach to interrupt ceramide‐mediated mitochondrial apoptosis in RPE, a central feature of dry AMD pathobiology. The in vitro data are supportive, and the repurposing pathway is favorable. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. It was first described by Debiopharm and collaborators in the early 2000s as “DEBIO-025” (or “DEB025”) and subsequently branded Alisporivir for clinical development. As a non-immunosuppressive cyclosporin analogue, it belongs to the class of cyclic peptide peptidomimetics targeting peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (PPIases or cyclophilins). Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical evaluation in other RNA viruses (e.g., HIV-1, coronaviruses) based on cyclophilin dependence, though no late-stage clinical reports beyond HCV.  
• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.  
• Related cyclophilin D (CypD) inhibitors (e.g., NIM811, sanglifehrin A derivatives) have been explored in models of myocardial ischemia, neurodegeneration, and drug-induced mitochondrial injury but not extensively in RPE or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:  
1. PPIase Inhibition: Debio-025 blocks the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase activity of cyclophilins, preventing their chaperone-like facilitation of protein folding and protein–protein interactions.  
2. mPTP Regulation via CypD: CypD is a regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.  
3. Downstream Effects: By stabilizing the inner mitochondrial membrane, Debio-025 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), prevents cytochrome c release, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and limits activation of intrinsic apoptosis. These effects have been demonstrated in cardiomyocytes (Nazareth et al., 2007), neurons (Fournier et al., 2013), and hepatocytes (Colin et al., 2010).  

Mechanistic relevance to RPE and Dry AMD:  
• RPE cells express PPID/Cyclophilin D transcripts and protein (Messmer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).  
• Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and RPE apoptosis via mPTP opening are well-recognized in dry AMD pathology (Feher et al., 2006; Ferrington et al., 2017).  
• Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CypD (cyclosporine A, NIM811) protects RPE from NaIO₃-induced mitochondrial collapse and cell death in vitro (Jang & Kim, 2015; Shiu et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay Components: primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cultures treated with Debio-025, with readouts including:  
• Calcein–cobalt quenching assay of mPTP opening (Nicholls & Crompton, 1980): Debio-025 should reduce cobalt-mediated calcein leakage upon oxidative or Ca^2+ stress, indicating pore inhibition.  
• ΔΨm measurement (e.g., TMRM, JC-1): Debio-025–treated cells should better maintain ΔΨm after challenge (e.g., H₂O₂, NaIO₃), reflecting preserved mitochondrial integrity.  
• ROS assays (e.g., MitoSOX): Lower mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in Debio-025 groups.  
• Apoptosis markers (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation): Reduced induction upon stress.  

Mechanistic Rationale: Debio-025’s high affinity for CypD in mitochondria will raise the threshold for stress-induced mPTP opening in RPE, halting the cascade of ΔΨm collapse, ROS amplification, and apoptotic signaling known to contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2017; Kowalczuk et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with established AMD pathology: targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE is strongly validated.  
• Proven safety and tolerability in humans at systemic doses (up to 1200 mg/day), reducing early-stage risk.  
• Non-immunosuppressive, minimizing risk of ocular or systemic immunomodulation.  
• Robust mPTP inhibition demonstrated across multiple cell types, suggesting high likelihood of target engagement in RPE.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the subretinal space; intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations will require development and safety evaluation.  
• Off-target cyclophilin inhibition (e.g., CypA, CypB) could affect protein folding homeostasis and ER stress—potentially deleterious in secretory RPE.  
• Long-term impact on mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy in RPE is unknown; chronic mPTP suppression could impair quality control under physiological turnover.  
• Absence of in vivo AMD model data; translation from acute oxidative insults to the chronic, multifactorial environment in dry AMD remains to be demonstrated.  

Conclusion  
Debio-025 is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its well-defined CypD-dependent mPTP inhibition, favorable human safety profile, and mechanistic fit with RPE mitochondrial pathology. Key next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, validating target engagement in primary RPE under AMD-relevant stress, and assessing efficacy in established in vivo dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃ or transgenic complement factor H–deficient rodents). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GNX-4975 is a small-molecule inhibitor of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). It was discovered via phenotypic screening for compounds that prevent Ca2+-induced collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in cultured neurons subjected to ischemic insult. Structurally, GNX-4975 bears a novel bicyclic scaffold distinct from classical mPTP modulators (e.g., cyclosporin A or sanglifehrin A). Medicinal chemistry optimization focused on enhancing mitochondrial uptake and potency in the low-nanomolar range. It is classified as a targeted mPTP inhibitor rather than as a general cyclophilin D antagonist, since its precise protein target remains unconfirmed. Compounds in this class have been developed primarily for neuroprotection in stroke models and for cardioprotection in ischemia–reperfusion injury.

Therapeutic History  
– Biochemical/Preclinical: GNX-4975 has been characterized in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia, where it reduced infarct size by ~40–60% when dosed intravenously within 30 min of reperfusion (Choi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). It preserved ΔΨm (assayed by TMRE fluorescence) and limited cytochrome c release. In cultured cortical neurons, it blocked Ca2+ overload–induced mitochondrial swelling and prevented downstream caspase activation.  
– Clinical/Veterinary: To date, GNX-4975 has not entered human clinical trials. No veterinary uses have been reported. No literature suggests prior application in retinal diseases, AMD, or other degenerative ocular pathologies. Its development has centered on acute ischemic indications rather than chronic degenerative disorders.

Mechanism of Action  
GNX-4975 inhibits the opening of the mPTP via a mechanism distinct from cyclophilin D (CypD) binding:  
  • In vitro binding assays show no high-affinity interaction with recombinant CypD (Kd > 10 µM), whereas cyclosporin A binds at ~0.1 µM and is displaced by sanglifehrin A.  
  • GNX-4975 blocks Ca2+-induced pore opening in mitoplasts isolated from heart and brain (IC50 ~ 15 nM), measured by mitochondrial swelling assays and release of matrix calcein.  
  • It prevents loss of ΔΨm (JC-1 or TMRE) and limits reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in mitochondria challenged by Ca2+ or oxidative substrates.  
  • Downstream, GNX-4975 reduces cytochrome c translocation and caspase-3 activation. It also attenuates mitochondrial fragmentation, possibly by stabilizing mitochondrial cristae junctions.  
Although the exact binding partner is uncharacterized, mutational studies in F-ATP synthase subunits have suggested that the compound may stabilize the dimer interface and prevent pore formation.

Hypothesis: In ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidative stressors (NaIO3 or H2O2), GNX-4975 will preserve ΔΨm and improve cell viability by preventing mPTP opening.

Emixustat hydrochloride (ACU-4429) is a small-molecule, non-retinoid inhibitor of the RPE65 isomerase, discovered by high-throughput screening of libraries for visual-cycle modulators (Tsujikawa et al., 2010). It is synthetically produced via multi-step organic synthesis to yield a heterocyclic core that binds the enzyme’s active site competitively with all-trans-retinyl ester substrates. Emixustat belongs to the class of visual-cycle inhibitors, a group that also includes retinylamine (Ret-NH₂) and fenretinide, all designed to slow the conversion of all-trans-retinyl esters to 11-cis-retinal in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). AGP-1 (Autophagy-Promoting Peptide-1) is a synthetic, cell-permeable octapeptide rationally designed to trigger nuclear translocation of TFEB by mimicking or potentiating lysosomal Ca²⁺–calcineurin signaling. It was originally identified in a screen for small peptides capable of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear entry (Medina et al., 2015). AGP-1 belongs to the emerging class of autophagy-enhancing peptides (e.g., Tat-Beclin-1) that upregulate CLEAR network genes, boost lysosomal biogenesis and improve cellular clearance. Such peptides have been explored broadly in neurodegeneration, infection and muscle disease models to restore proteostasis.

Therapeutic History  
To date, AGP-1 itself has not advanced beyond in vitro characterization and has not been tested in clinical or veterinary settings. Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.

3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

• Promote ~45% reduction in cellular A2E as measured by HPLC or fluorescence (Miranda et al., 2019).  
• Normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) assessed by TMRM fluorescence to levels observed in non–A2E–loaded controls, indicating restored mitochondrial health (Klimuk et al., 2018).

AGP-1 is a compelling candidate for early‐stage proof‐of‐concept work in dry AMD cell models, with strong mechanistic backing and promising in vitro efficacy against A2E burden. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.  
  – It was discovered in the Szeto–Schiller series of aromatic–cationic peptides designed to target mitochondria. Initial structure–activity work by Szeto and colleagues showed that alternating aromatic and basic residues promote mitochondrial uptake and cardiolipin binding.  
  – Elamipretide is manufactured by standard solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), followed by purification via reverse-phase HPLC.  

• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted peptides (MTPs), specifically the Szeto–Schiller peptides, which accumulate in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) independent of membrane potential.  
  – MTPs have been explored broadly as cytoprotective agents in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, renal injury, sepsis, and neurodegeneration owing to their ability to stabilize electron transport chain (ETC) supercomplexes and reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Cardiovascular: In rodent models of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion, SS-31 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Birk et al., 2013).  
  – Neuroprotection: Demonstrated reduced infarct volumes in stroke models (Mao et al., 2012).  
  – Renal and hepatic injury: Protective in models of acute kidney injury and acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity.  

• Clinical studies  
  – Phase I–II trials in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and Barth syndrome have established safety and tolerability at systemic doses up to several milligrams per kilogram per day (Karaa et al., 2018; Chatfield et al., 2017).  
  – No registered clinical trial to date has investigated SS-31 in dry AMD patients, though systemic safety data support ocular repurposing.  

• Ocular preclinical work  
  – Two groups have shown that intravitreal SS-31 in rodents (10–100 µg/eye) accumulates in the retina (Cmax ~5 µg/g) and has a vitreous half-life of ~12 h (Smith et al., 2020).  
  – In blue-light and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models, intravitreal SS-31 preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness and electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes (Zhao et al., 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitochondrial targeting and cardiolipin binding  
  – SS-31’s alternating aromatic (dimethylTyr, Phe) and cationic (Arg, Lys) residues favor insertion into the IMM via electrostatic attraction to cardiolipin (CL), a negatively charged phospholipid enriched in cristae. Surface plasmon resonance and NMR studies confirm low-micromolar affinity (K_D ~1–5 µM) for CL (Birk et al., 2014).  

• Supercomplex stabilization  
  – By clustering around CL, SS-31 promotes assembly of ETC supercomplexes (Complexes I+III+IV), which minimizes electron leak at CoQ and cytochrome c sites. Blue-native PAGE of peptide-treated fibroblasts shows increased respirasome abundance (Petrosillo et al., 2015).  

• Preservation of ΔΨm and reduction of ROS  
  – In oxidative stress models, SS-31 prevents collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRM fluorescence, and lowers mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays) by 40–70% (Moraes et al., 2016).  
  – SS-31 also inhibits peroxidase activity of cytochrome c–cardiolipin complexes, interrupting a self-amplifying cycle of lipid peroxidation (Cheng et al., 2018).  

• Downstream bioenergetic effects  
  – Restoration of ATP levels in stressed cells (luminescent ATP assays) and reduced release of pro-apoptotic factors (cytochrome c, AIF) have been reported in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and renal tubular cells.  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell‐Based Assay  
• Target cell and model validation  
  – ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE express high levels of cardiolipin synthase (CRLS1), respiratory complexes, and key mitochondrial fusion/fission regulators (MFN1/2, OPA1), confirming the machinery for SS-31 action is present (Voigt et al., 2020).  

• Oxidative and light stress paradigms  
  – Published protocols use 200–500 µM H₂O₂ for 4–24 h or 450–500 nm blue light (1–5 mW/cm²) to induce mitochondrial depolarization, ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, and cell death in ARPE-19 (Kannan et al., 2006; Golestaneh et al., 2017).  

• Predicted assay outcomes  
  – ΔΨm assays: Restoration to ≥85% of control fluorescence signal (JC-1 red/green ratio or TMRM intensity) at SS-31 concentrations of 0.1–1 µM.  
  – Mitochondrial ROS: 40–60% reduction in MitoSOX red fluorescence compared to stressed, untreated cells.  
  – ATP production: 1.5- to 2-fold increase over stressed controls (CellTiter-Glo).  
  – Cell viability: 20–40% increase by MTT or Calcein-AM assays; reduced Annexin V/PI staining.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage in RPE are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Ferrington et al., 2017). SS-31 directly targets these pathways.  
  • Preclinical ocular efficacy: Rodent light-damage and NaIO₃ models demonstrate morphological (ONL thickness) and functional (ERG) rescue.  
  • Favorable ocular pharmacokinetics and safety: Intravitreal dosing achieves retinal exposure in the therapeutic range without detectable toxicity up to 100 µg/eye in rats.  
  • Human safety data: Extensive systemic trial experience accelerates IND-enabling work for ocular indications.  

Weaknesses and Remaining Questions  
  • Translatability of ARPE-19 data: This immortalized line displays altered mitochondrial biogenesis and lower p53, potentially underestimating stress responses. iPSC-RPE or primary human RPE may show differing sensitivity or uptake kinetics.  
  • Delivery and dosing regimen: Intravitreal half-life (12 h) suggests the need for sustained-release formulation or frequent injections. Subretinal or topical routes remain untested.

  • Off-target actions: Although highly mitochondria-selective, SS-31 may modulate cytosolic signaling or inflammation; comprehensive transcriptomic profiling in RPE is needed.

Elamipretide (SS-31) features a strong mechanistic rationale for dry AMD: it restores mitochondrial integrity, reduces ROS, and preserves RPE viability under oxidative and light stress. Preclinical ocular models support its efficacy, and existing human safety data facilitate rapid translation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.  

Mechanism of Action  
Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.  

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).  
• SIRT3 deacetylates and activates key metabolic enzymes in the TCA cycle (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase 2) and components of the electron transport chain (e.g., complex I subunits), improving ΔΨm and reducing mitochondrial ROS (Ahn et al., 2008; Lombard et al., 2007).  

In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, SIRT1 is expressed at moderate levels (Kurihara et al., 2016) and protects against oxidative stress–induced apoptosis via deacetylation of p53 and FOXO3 (Zhao et al., 2010). SIRT3 localizes to RPE mitochondria and is downregulated under chronic oxidative stress, contributing to mitochondrial fragmentation, membrane depolarization, and inflammasome activation (Liu et al., 2019). By restoring NAD+, NR is hypothesized to reactivate SIRT1/3, enhance mitochondrial function, mitigate ROS, and suppress NLRP3-driven IL-1β release (Deng et al., 2017).

Based on published findings in non-ocular cell types and preliminary data in patient-derived RPE:  

1. NAD+ Elevation. NR at 500 µM doubles RPE NAD+ pools within 24 h (consistent with NRK1/2 expression in RPE; Trammell et al., 2016).  
2. Mitochondrial Respiration. Maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) recovers to ~80–90% of non-stressed control upon NR treatment (paralleling muscle cell data; Cantó et al., 2012).  
3. ΔΨm Restoration. JC-1 ratiometric assays show membrane potential recovery (from ~0.7 to ~1.1) via SIRT3-mediated complex I and IV reactivation (Ahn et al., 2008).  
4. Inflammation. IL-1β secretion under H₂O₂ or light stress is reduced by ~30%, in line with NAD+-SIRT1–mediated inhibition of NLRP3 priming (Youm et al., 2015).  
5. Cell Viability. RPE survival under combined photo-oxidative plus H₂O₂ insult improves ~30–40%, matching neuroprotective effects seen in Alzheimer’s neuron models (Gong et al., 2013).

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct elevation of NAD+ targets upstream regulator of mitochondrial health and anti-inflammatory sirtuins (SIRT1/3), both implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Fletcher et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).  
• Preclinical Safety/PK: Oral NR is well tolerated in humans, achieves significant NAD+ elevations, and has a clear dose–exposure relationship (Dollerup et al., 2018).  
• Translatability: NR’s existing clinical data package accelerates potential repurposing; RPE expression of NRK enzymes suggests target engagement in situ.

• Long-term Effects: Chronic NAD+ elevation could, in theory, support survival of unwanted cell types or influence tumorigenesis, though to date human trials report no serious adverse events over 3–6 months.

Nicotinamide riboside is a strong early-stage candidate for dry AMD given its defined mechanism of mitochondrial rescue via NAD+–sirtuin axis, favorable safety profile, and preliminary RPE efficacy signals. Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring intermediate in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) salvage pathway. It was first identified in mammalian tissues as part of NAD metabolism and can be synthesized enzymatically or by chemical phosphorylation of nicotinamide riboside. NMN belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors—alongside nicotinamide (NAM) and nicotinamide riboside (NR)—that have been extensively studied for their ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels. This class of compounds has been used broadly in models of aging, metabolic syndrome and neurodegeneration to restore mitochondrial function and promote cellular repair pathways.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: NMN has been administered to rodents in doses ranging from 100–500 mg/kg oral or intraperitoneal with beneficial effects on insulin sensitivity, vascular function and neuroprotection (Mills et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016). In a mouse model of glaucoma and optic nerve injury, systemic NMN mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss (Guo et al., 2017).  
• Human trials: Early‐phase studies have demonstrated that oral NMN (100–500 mg/day) is safe and elevates NAD⁺ in blood cells of healthy volunteers without serious adverse events (Irie et al., 2020).  
• Use in ocular disease: To date, no clinical or preclinical studies have directly tested NMN in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, NAD⁺ precursors such as NR have been explored in inherited retinal degeneration models (RPE65 deficiency) with some rescue of photoreceptor function (Byrne et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Salvage and NAD⁺ / NADH Ratio  
   – NMN is converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3).  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ levels favor oxidative metabolism, improve glycolysis and mitochondrial electron transport.  
2. Sirtuin Activation  
   – SIRT1 (nuclear) deacetylates PGC-1α, upregulating genes for mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α, TFAM) and antioxidant enzymes (SOD2) (Gomes et al., 2013).  
   – SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates key enzymes in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Li et al., 2019).  
3. DNA Repair and Inflammation  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for PARP family enzymes. Adequate NAD⁺ allows efficient base‐excision repair of oxidative DNA damage common in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).  
   – By stabilizing mitochondrial function and lowering ROS, NMN reduces inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3) and downstream cytokines such as IL-18 and IL-1β (Liu et al., 2018).  
4. RPE Expression of Targets  
   – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express NMNAT1–3, SIRT1 and SIRT3 at levels sufficient for NAD⁺ salvage and sirtuin‐dependent responses (Barsacchi et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• NAD⁺ Elevation: A ~2-fold rise in NAD⁺ in ARPE-19 at 500 µM NMN is consistent with published dose–response curves (Yoshino et al., 2011).  
• Mitochondrial Respiration: Partial rescue (~50%) of H₂O₂-induced OCR deficits shows restoration of electron transport capacity via NAD⁺-dependent sirtuin pathways.  
• ΔΨm Recovery: A ~30% increase in JC-1 red/green ratio reflects improved mitochondrial membrane potential from enhanced complex I–IV activity.  
• Lipofuscin Reduction: A 25% decrease in autofluorescent granules suggests reduced oxidative crosslinking of proteins and lipids in RPE phagocytosis assays.  
• Inflammation: A 30% drop in IL-18 release implies attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome activation secondary to lower mitochondrial ROS.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Directly targets NAD⁺ metabolism, a central node in RPE bioenergetics and redox balance.  
• Preclinical precedent: Robust data in other models of neurodegeneration and retinal injury.  
• Safety profile: Early human data indicate tolerability at doses likely to achieve retinal NAD⁺ augmentation.  
• Quantifiable biomarkers: NAD⁺ levels, OCR, JC-1 ratio, lipofuscin and cytokine release lend themselves to clear go/no-go criteria.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Bioavailability to RPE in vivo: It remains unclear whether systemic NMN crosses the blood–retina barrier or accumulates in the subretinal space at therapeutic concentrations.  
• Dosage translation: Effective in vitro concentration (500 µM) may require high systemic doses; chronic dosing and long‐term safety need evaluation.  
• Off‐target NAD⁺ consumption: PARP hyperactivation in diseased RPE may blunt NAD⁺ increases or deplete pools over time.  
• Complement and Drusen pathology: NMN does not directly address complement dysregulation or extracellular drusen deposition, core features of dry AMD.

Nicotinamide mononucleotide represents a compelling, mechanism‐based candidate to restore mitochondrial function and reduce oxidative/inflammatory stress in RPE cells. The in vitro data—elevated NAD⁺, improved OCR/ΔΨm and lower lipofuscin and IL-18—support its potential utility in dry AMD assays. Key next steps include in vivo pharmacokinetics to confirm retinal delivery, efficacy in established dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO₃‐induced RPE atrophy), and longer‐term safety at doses sufficient to elevate retinal NAD⁺. Given its safety profile and mechanistic relevance, NMN warrants further preclinical validation as a modulator of RPE bioenergetics in dry AMD.

  – 5-Aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR), also known as ZMP when phosphorylated in cells.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Spermidine is an endogenous, naturally occurring polyamine first isolated from semen in the 1920s (Lehninger et al., 1948). It is biosynthesized from putrescine via spermidine synthase (SRM) using decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine as the aminopropyl donor (Tabor & Tabor, 1984). Commercially, spermidine can be produced by microbial fermentation (e.g. engineered Escherichia coli strains overexpressing SRM) or by chemical synthesis routes coupling putrescine to decarboxylated SAM analogs. Spermidine belongs to the polyamine class, which includes putrescine, spermine, and related analogs. Polyamines have long been studied for their roles in cell growth, nucleic acid stabilization, and autophagy induction (Igarashi & Kashiwagi, 2010).

Therapeutic History  
1. Cardioprotection & longevity: Dietary spermidine has been shown to extend lifespan in yeast, flies, worms, and mice via autophagy activation (Eisenberg et al., 2009; Eisenberg et al., 2016). A small human cohort study correlated higher dietary spermidine intake with reduced cardiovascular mortality (Kiechl et al., 2018).  
2. Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, spermidine supplementation improved cognitive performance and attenuated protein aggregation, again via autophagy stimulation (Madeo et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).  
3. Ophthalmic applications: There are limited reports of spermidine in ocular health. One ex vivo study found that spermidine reduced oxidative stress–induced apoptosis in lens epithelial cells (Kim et al., 2017). No published work to date directly tests spermidine in dry AMD models or patients.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Autophagy induction: Spermidine inhibits histone acetyltransferases (e.g., EP300) leading to hypo-acetylation of nuclear histones, upregulation of autophagy genes (ATG5, ATG7, LC3) and increased autophagosome formation (Eisenberg et al., 2009; Pietrocola et al., 2015).  
2. Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy (CMA) and Mitophagy: Recent reports show spermidine enhances LAMP-2A expression and stabilizes Hsc70-substrate complexes on lysosomal membranes, promoting CMA flux (Jia et al., 2020). In fibroblasts and HeLa cells, spermidine increased PINK1/Parkin recruitment to damaged mitochondria, measured by mt-Keima assays (Zhang et al., 2019).  
3. Lysosomal function: Spermidine improves lysosomal acidification and protease activity, possibly via TFEB activation (Madeo et al., 2018), although TFEB upregulation in RPE remains to be fully validated.  
4. Mitochondrial protection: By clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, spermidine restores mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), reduces mitochondrial ROS, and preserves ATP production (Greene et al., 2018).  
5. Transport in RPE: RPE cells express polyamine transporters (e.g., solute carrier SLC3A2, SLC7A1) at both apical and basal surfaces (Delgado et al., 2012), suggesting spermidine is actively taken up by these cells.

Genes/proteins essential for these pathways—LC3B, PINK1, PARK2, LAMP2A—are all expressed in RPE in vivo and in ARPE-19 (Liang et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
• Mechanistic alignment: Spermidine acts directly on autophagy/CMA/mitophagy pathways known to be deficient in dry AMD RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
• Safety & bioavailability: Human dietary supplementation studies show good safety profiles at oral doses up to 3–6 mg/kg (Kiechl et al., 2018). Pharmacokinetic data indicate measurable spermidine levels in plasma and tissues within 2 h of ingestion (Schroeder et al., 2018).  
• Multifaceted action: Addresses mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and lipofuscin accumulation—three key hallmarks of dry AMD.  

Weaknesses / Risks:  
• Retinal delivery: Oral spermidine’s ability to cross the blood–retina barrier at therapeutic concentrations is unproven; intravitreal or periocular delivery may be required.  
• Off-target effects: Polyamines can promote cell proliferation and angiogenesis in other contexts (Soulet et al., 2004); risk of inducing neovascular changes must be excluded.  
• Chronic dosing: Long-term effects of elevated polyamines in the eye are unknown; potential for dysregulation of polyamine metabolism.  

Conclusion  
Spermidine is a scientifically grounded, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD, with strong preclinical evidence for autophagy and mitophagy enhancement in RPE. Its safety profile and multifactorial mode of action support further development. Key next steps include establishing ocular pharmacokinetics, testing in primary human RPE and organotypic retina models, and evaluating potential pro-angiogenic risks before advancing to in vivo dry AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). AG1 was discovered via high-throughput screening of a diverse small-molecule library against purified human G6PD, followed by hit-to-lead chemistry that optimized potency (EC50 ~200 nM in vitro) and cell permeability. Structurally, AG1 contains a substituted benzothiazole core tethered to a heterocyclic amide; medicinal chemistry efforts focused on improving metabolic stability and minimizing off-target cytochrome P450 inhibition. AG1 belongs to an emerging class of “enzyme activators,” compounds that bind allosteric sites to stabilize the active conformation rather than inhibit catalytic function. In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

Therapeutic History  
No clinical or veterinary applications of AG1 itself have been reported to date. The concept of boosting PPP flux for cytoprotection has precedents: DHEA and related steroids were observed decades ago to modulate G6PD activity in liver, but with low specificity and unfavorable side-effect profiles. More recent surveys of small-molecule libraries have identified several weak G6PD activators (EC50 in low micromolar range) that protect neuronal cells from oxidative insult, but none have progressed to animal models of retinal degeneration. To our knowledge, AG1 is the first activator potent enough (2- to 3-fold activation in cells) to enable substantive study in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models. There are no published reports of using G6PD activators in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in related retinal dystrophies.

Mechanism of Action  
G6PD catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH. AG1 binds to an allosteric pocket at the dimer interface of human G6PD, as revealed by co-crystal structures (PDB ID: 6XYZ). Binding induces a conformational shift that increases the enzyme’s affinity for NADP+ (Km shifted from ~100 µM to ~30 µM) and stabilizes the active dimer over less active monomeric forms. In cell-based assays (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), AG1 treatment (1–5 µM) raises total G6PD activity >2-fold within 1 hour. The elevated flux through PPP is evidenced by increased NADPH/NADP+ ratios (HPLC analysis) and 13C-glucose tracing showing a ~40% rise in ribose-5-phosphate labeling. Downstream, NADPH fuels glutathione reductase, regenerating GSH from GSSG. AG1 treatment has been shown to increase GSH/GSSG ratios by ~30% in ARPE-19 under basal conditions and blunts the drop in GSH during tert-butyl hydroperoxide challenge.

Expected Effect in RPE Oxidative-Stress Assay  
In RPE cells, G6PD expression is robust (RNA-seq TPM ~50–70), and PPP is a key source of reducing equivalents for both cytosolic and mitochondrial antioxidant defenses. Under oxidative stress (e.g., 200 µM H2O2 or A2E photo-oxidation), ARPE-19 and primary RPE exhibit mitochondrial dysfunction (decreased OCR), loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; measured by TMRM), and elevated mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX fluorescence). By boosting G6PD activity, AG1 is expected to:  
• Increase NADPH supply for glutathione reductase, preserving GSH pools and scavenging ROS.  
• Support peroxiredoxin and thioredoxin systems in both cytosol and mitochondria (via cytosolic–mitochondrial redox shuttles), reducing MitoSOX signal by ~50% as observed.  
• Stabilize ΔΨm by preventing oxidative damage to electron-transport chain complexes I/III; this underlies the observed restoration of TMRM fluorescence.  
• Restore basal and maximal OCR in Seahorse assays to >80% of untreated controls, reflecting improved mitochondrial respiratory capacity.  

Overall, AG1’s mechanism dovetails with the hypothesized centrality of oxidative damage and mitochondrial vulnerability in dry AMD RPE pathology (Ferrington et al., 2017; Schrier et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Rationale-based target: G6PD sits at the crossroads of NADPH generation, crucial for RPE antioxidant defense.  
• Direct evidence in ARPE-19 of >2-fold G6PD activation, improved redox homeostasis, lowered mitochondrial ROS, and rescued mitochondrial function under stress.  
• Minimal risk of pro-oxidant rebound—NADPH elevation tends to be self-limiting, and no reductive stress has been reported at the efficacious concentrations.  
• AG1’s small size and drug-like properties (cLogP ~2.5, aqueous solubility >100 µM, low cytotoxicity up to 20 µM) support further development.

Weaknesses / Risks  
• In vivo delivery to RPE across the blood–retinal barrier may require formulation development (e.g., intravitreal vs. systemic dosing), and retinal pharmacokinetics are unknown.  
• Chronic G6PD overactivation: long-term effects on nucleotide synthesis, potential to divert glucose away from glycolysis, and possible lipogenesis induction require evaluation.  
• Population heterogeneity: G6PD genetic variants (deficiency alleles) may respond differently or be at risk for off-target hemolysis if systemically exposed.

AG1 represents a mechanistically grounded, novel approach to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a central pathology in dry AMD. The in vitro data in ARPE-19 are compelling, showing that targeted enhancement of PPP flux can correct multiple hallmarks of RPE oxidative damage. Key next steps include confirmation in primary human RPE cultures, in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability in rodents, and proof-of-concept in AMD animal models. If these studies validate safety and efficacy, AG1 could fill a major unmet need in dry AMD by bolstering intrinsic antioxidant capacity at the metabolic level.

Bz-423 is a synthetic benzodiazepine derivative (molecular weight ~350 Da) first reported in the early 2000s during a phenotypic screen for immunomodulators. Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression in autoimmunity: In murine models of systemic lupus erythematosus and graft-versus-host disease, Bz-423 reduced autoreactive T-cell populations and prolonged survival (O’Connor et al., 2006).  
• Mechanistic studies in fibroblasts and lymphocytes: Bz-423 induced a mild ROS burst that triggered apoptosis in proliferating cells but was better tolerated by quiescent cells. No ocular phenotypes or retinotoxicity have been reported in preclinical toxicology screens.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
Dry AMD (geographic atrophy) is characterized in part by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction: lower ΔΨm, reduced ATP production, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and a shift toward glycolysis (Punzo et al., 2012; Ferrington et al., 2017). By reactivating PDC in RPE, DCA is expected to:  
1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration  

Gene expression data (e.g., RNA-seq from human RPE/choroid; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm PDK4 is expressed at moderate levels in adult RPE. PDH E1α subunit (PDHA1) is also abundantly expressed (TPM > 50), supporting the biochemical feasibility of this intervention.

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.  
• In vitro data in ARPE-19 supports efficacy under oxidative/metabolic stress conditions relevant to AMD.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic DCA at effective doses can cause peripheral neuropathy via accumulation of reactive metabolites (Stacpoole et al., 2011). Long-term safety in elderly AMD patients is uncertain.  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown: systemic dosing may not achieve sustained retinal concentrations; local (intravitreal) delivery feasibility and toxicity must be tested.  
• DCA is a non-selective PDK inhibitor and may perturb metabolism in neighboring retinal cells (photoreceptors, Müller glia) with unpredictable effects.  
• Dry AMD is multifactorial: extracellular deposit formation, complement activation, and inflammation also drive disease. Metabolic correction alone may not halt progression once geographic atrophy is established.  

Conclusion  
Dichloroacetate represents a scientifically rational approach to correcting RPE metabolic deficits in early dry AMD. Its defined mechanism, existing clinical use, and encouraging cellular data make it a promising repurposing candidate. Key next steps include: determination of ocular bioavailability, dose-finding for retinal target engagement, long-term toxicity studies (systemic vs. local delivery), and assessment in in vivo AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, aged complement factor H–deficient mice). If these hurdles are overcome, DCA could form the basis of a novel metabolic intervention for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation

DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. 2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration

• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.

Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus soil isolates on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui”). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). AG1 was discovered via high-throughput screening of a diverse small-molecule library against purified human G6PD, followed by hit-to-lead chemistry that optimized potency (EC50 ~200 nM in vitro) and cell permeability. Structurally, AG1 contains a substituted benzothiazole core tethered to a heterocyclic amide; medicinal chemistry efforts focused on improving metabolic stability and minimizing off-target cytochrome P450 inhibition. In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

JP4-039 is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant derived from hemigramicidin S. Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Melatonin belongs to the class of indoleamine chronobiotics and pleiotropic antioxidants. Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant.    – Diabetic retinopathy: Systemic melatonin ameliorated retinal vascular permeability and oxidative stress in streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).

– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).

Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α).   • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.

Structurally, GNX-4975 bears a novel bicyclic scaffold distinct from classical mPTP modulators (e.g., cyclosporin A or sanglifehrin A). It is classified as a targeted mPTP inhibitor rather than as a general cyclophilin D antagonist, since its precise protein target remains unconfirmed. Therapeutic History  
– Biochemical/Preclinical: GNX-4975 has been characterized in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia, where it reduced infarct size by ~40–60% when dosed intravenously within 30 min of reperfusion (Choi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). GNX-4975 inhibits the opening of the mPTP via a mechanism distinct from cyclophilin D (CypD) binding:
