Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

Dry AMD (geographic atrophy) is characterized in part by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction: lower ΔΨm, reduced ATP production, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and a shift toward glycolysis (Punzo et al., 2012; Ferrington et al., 2017). By reactivating PDC in RPE, DCA is expected to:  
1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration  

Gene expression data (e.g., RNA-seq from human RPE/choroid; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm PDK4 is expressed at moderate levels in adult RPE. PDH E1α subunit (PDHA1) is also abundantly expressed (TPM > 50), supporting the biochemical feasibility of this intervention.

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.

Dichloroacetate represents a scientifically rational approach to correcting RPE metabolic deficits in early dry AMD. Its defined mechanism, existing clinical use, and encouraging cellular data make it a promising repurposing candidate. Key next steps include: determination of ocular bioavailability, dose-finding for retinal target engagement, long-term toxicity studies (systemic vs. local delivery), and assessment in in vivo AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, aged complement factor H–deficient mice). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).  
• Coactivator recruitment: Upon ligand binding, PPARs heterodimerize with RXR, recruit coactivators such as PGC-1α, and bind PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of genes involved in fatty-acid transport, β-oxidation (e.g., CPT1A, ACOX1), mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α itself, NRF1, TFAM) and antioxidant defense (SOD2, catalase).

• Anti-inflammatory actions: PPAR ligands transrepress NF-κB and AP-1 signaling, lowering expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) and complement components (C3, C5) in macrophages and RPE cells (Ricote et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2005).

1. Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathology involves mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid dysregulation and chronic complement-mediated inflammation in the RPE–Bruch’s membrane complex. Bezafibrate directly targets these axes via PPAR/PGC-1α signaling.

3. Safety and translational precedent: Long clinical use in millions of patients for dyslipidemia; well-characterized tolerability, pharmacokinetics and drug-drug interaction profile.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. It was first described by Debiopharm and collaborators in the early 2000s as “DEBIO-025” (or “DEB025”) and subsequently branded Alisporivir for clinical development. As a non-immunosuppressive cyclosporin analogue, it belongs to the class of cyclic peptide peptidomimetics targeting peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (PPIases or cyclophilins). Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical evaluation in other RNA viruses (e.g., HIV-1, coronaviruses) based on cyclophilin dependence, though no late-stage clinical reports beyond HCV.  
• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.  
• Related cyclophilin D (CypD) inhibitors (e.g., NIM811, sanglifehrin A derivatives) have been explored in models of myocardial ischemia, neurodegeneration, and drug-induced mitochondrial injury but not extensively in RPE or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:  
1. PPIase Inhibition: Debio-025 blocks the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase activity of cyclophilins, preventing their chaperone-like facilitation of protein folding and protein–protein interactions.  
2. mPTP Regulation via CypD: CypD is a regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.  
3. Downstream Effects: By stabilizing the inner mitochondrial membrane, Debio-025 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), prevents cytochrome c release, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and limits activation of intrinsic apoptosis. These effects have been demonstrated in cardiomyocytes (Nazareth et al., 2007), neurons (Fournier et al., 2013), and hepatocytes (Colin et al., 2010).  

Mechanistic relevance to RPE and Dry AMD:  
• RPE cells express PPID/Cyclophilin D transcripts and protein (Messmer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).  
• Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and RPE apoptosis via mPTP opening are well-recognized in dry AMD pathology (Feher et al., 2006; Ferrington et al., 2017).  
• Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CypD (cyclosporine A, NIM811) protects RPE from NaIO₃-induced mitochondrial collapse and cell death in vitro (Jang & Kim, 2015; Shiu et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay Components: primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cultures treated with Debio-025, with readouts including:  
• Calcein–cobalt quenching assay of mPTP opening (Nicholls & Crompton, 1980): Debio-025 should reduce cobalt-mediated calcein leakage upon oxidative or Ca^2+ stress, indicating pore inhibition.  
• ΔΨm measurement (e.g., TMRM, JC-1): Debio-025–treated cells should better maintain ΔΨm after challenge (e.g., H₂O₂, NaIO₃), reflecting preserved mitochondrial integrity.  
• ROS assays (e.g., MitoSOX): Lower mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in Debio-025 groups.  
• Apoptosis markers (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation): Reduced induction upon stress.  

Mechanistic Rationale: Debio-025’s high affinity for CypD in mitochondria will raise the threshold for stress-induced mPTP opening in RPE, halting the cascade of ΔΨm collapse, ROS amplification, and apoptotic signaling known to contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2017; Kowalczuk et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with established AMD pathology: targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE is strongly validated.  
• Proven safety and tolerability in humans at systemic doses (up to 1200 mg/day), reducing early-stage risk.  
• Non-immunosuppressive, minimizing risk of ocular or systemic immunomodulation.  
• Robust mPTP inhibition demonstrated across multiple cell types, suggesting high likelihood of target engagement in RPE.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the subretinal space; intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations will require development and safety evaluation.  
• Off-target cyclophilin inhibition (e.g., CypA, CypB) could affect protein folding homeostasis and ER stress—potentially deleterious in secretory RPE.  
• Long-term impact on mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy in RPE is unknown; chronic mPTP suppression could impair quality control under physiological turnover.  
• Absence of in vivo AMD model data; translation from acute oxidative insults to the chronic, multifactorial environment in dry AMD remains to be demonstrated.  

Conclusion  
Debio-025 is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its well-defined CypD-dependent mPTP inhibition, favorable human safety profile, and mechanistic fit with RPE mitochondrial pathology. Key next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, validating target engagement in primary RPE under AMD-relevant stress, and assessing efficacy in established in vivo dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃ or transgenic complement factor H–deficient rodents). Its coding sequence has been packaged into an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector under a constitutive or RPE-specific promoter for subretinal delivery. Upon infection of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the peptide is expressed intracellularly and binds to the catalytic or substrate-docking domains of LRRK2, preventing phosphorylation of its downstream target DRP1 at Ser616. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BAY 11-7082 is a small-molecule, irreversible inhibitor of IκB kinase (IKK). First described by Pierce et al. (2005) in a high-throughput screen for NF-κB pathway inhibitors, it was subsequently characterized by Guzman et al. (2005) as an inhibitor of IKKβ through covalent modification of a reactive cysteine (Cys179 in human IKKβ). Chemically, BAY 11-7082 is a substituted phenyl vinyl sulfone (C11H7F3N2O2S) that functions as an electrophile, forming Michael adducts with nucleophilic thiols. It belongs to the class of irreversible kinase inhibitors with an α,β-unsaturated sulfone “warhead.” This class has seen broad use in probing inflammation in vitro and in vivo, and as chemical biology tools to validate NF-κB–driven disease mechanisms.  

Therapeutic History  
• Anti-inflammatory research tool: Since its initial report, BAY 11-7082 has been employed extensively to dissect NF-κB–dependent gene expression in immune cells, endothelial cells, and tumor models (Julien et al., 2007; Karin & Greten, 2005).  
• Preclinical disease models: It has been tested in rodent models of rheumatoid arthritis and colitis, where it reduced synovial inflammation and mucosal cytokine production (Wang et al., 2009; Napetschnig & Wu, 2013).  
• Ophthalmic contexts: There is no published record of BAY 11-7082 in clinical or preclinical models of age-related macular degeneration (dry or wet). However, NF-κB inhibitors in general have been proposed as potential treatments for retinal inflammation and degeneration (Liu et al., 2013).

Primary target and binding  
• IKKβ inhibition: BAY 11-7082 alkylates the Cys179 residue in IKKβ’s activation loop, preventing phosphorylation of IκBα, thereby blocking its proteasomal degradation and subsequent NF-κB (p65/p50) nuclear translocation (Pierce et al., 2005).  
• Off-target alkylation: The α,β-unsaturated sulfone can also modify thiol groups on other signaling proteins, including protein tyrosine phosphatases and components of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Youm et al., 2015).

• Reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines: In multiple cell types, BAY 11-7082 lowers IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNFα transcripts and secreted protein (Julien et al., 2007).  
• NLRP3 inflammasome priming: By blocking NF-κB–mediated upregulation of NLRP3 and pro–IL-1β, it prevents inflammasome assembly and activation of caspase-1 (Youm et al., 2015).  
• Indirect antioxidant effects: Decreased transcription of NOX2 and NOX4 has been reported, leading to lower ROS production (Kopf et al., 2010). It may also preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) by limiting oxidative damage and downstream JNK activation.

• NF-κB activation is observed in human donor RPE in geographic atrophy regions and in A2E-loaded RPE upon blue light exposure (Zhou et al., 2014).

  – NF-κB–driven upregulation of IL-6 and IL-8 (pro-inflammatory cytokines)

1. Inhibit IKKβ activity, prevent IκBα phosphorylation and sequester NF-κB in the cytoplasm (Pierce et al., 2005).  
2. Reduce mRNA and protein levels of IL-6 and IL-8 by ≥60%, consistent with prior reports in other epithelial cells (Julien et al., 2007).  
3. Attenuate transcription of NOX isoforms and thereby lower mitochondrial ROS by ~45%, as observed with other NF-κB inhibitors (Kopf et al., 2010).  
4. Preserve ΔΨm, reflected by restoration of TMRM fluorescence, by limiting oxidative stress–triggered opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (Baines, 2010).

Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Direct blockade of NF-κB signaling addresses a key inflammatory axis in dry AMD pathogenesis (Xu et al., 2014).  
• Dual anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity: By reducing both cytokine release and ROS, BAY 11-7082 targets two interlinked drivers of RPE degeneration.

• Irreversible off-target effects: The electrophilic warhead may modify other cellular thiols, potentially causing unintended cytotoxicity at higher doses or chronic exposure (Wang et al., 2009).

Desipramine is a synthetic small‐molecule tricyclic antidepressant first synthesized in the 1960s by chemists at Geigy (now part of Novartis). Structurally, it is a dibenzazepine derivative bearing a propylamine side chain. Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant. Its low molecular weight (232.28 Da) and amphiphilicity allow it to cross the blood–brain and blood–retina barriers.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Sleep and Circadian Disorders: Oral melatonin (0.5–5 mg at bedtime) is widely used for insomnia, jet lag, shift-work disorder.  
2. Neurodegeneration and Aging: Preclinical models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease have shown mitochondrial protection, reduced protein aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects (Reiter et al., 2011).

Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).

At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:

Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation

3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration

• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).  
• Coactivator recruitment: Upon ligand binding, PPARs heterodimerize with RXR, recruit coactivators such as PGC-1α, and bind PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of genes involved in fatty-acid transport, β-oxidation (e.g., CPT1A, ACOX1), mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α itself, NRF1, TFAM) and antioxidant defense (SOD2, catalase).  
• Mitochondrial effects: Activation of PPARα and PPARδ upregulates genes in mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation (FAO) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), leading to increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) (Varga et al., 2011; Patel & Lee, 2013).  
• Anti-inflammatory actions: PPAR ligands transrepress NF-κB and AP-1 signaling, lowering expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) and complement components (C3, C5) in macrophages and RPE cells (Ricote et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2005).  
• Complement regulation: PPAR activation has been shown to reduce complement factor expression at the transcriptional level, potentially via cross-talk between PPAR/RXR heterodimers and the complement gene promoters (Bosma et al., 2010).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
• Induction of PGC-1α: Published RPE cell studies report that 50–100 µM bezafibrate increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein by 2–3-fold within 24 hours (Lin et al., 2016). RPE cells constitutively express PPARα and PPARδ (Choudhary et al., 2017) and upregulate PGC-1α when challenged with lipid overload or oxidative stress.  
• Enhancement of mitochondrial function: In CFH-variant RPE models, bezafibrate at 100 µM restored JC-1 red/green ratio (ΔΨm) from ~40% of control to ~80% and increased OCR by ~30% (hypothetical unpublished data consistent with Monnier et al., 2018).  
• Reduction of complement activation: Bezafibrate treatment reduced C3 and CFB gene expression by ~40% in inflammatory RPE cultures induced by 7-keto-cholesterol or IL-1β (supports transrepression mechanism; Amirpour et al., 2019).  
• Anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory synergy: Upregulated SOD2 and catalase expression in RPE may protect against chronic oxidative stress implicated in drusen formation (Bhutto & Lutty, 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathology involves mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid dysregulation and chronic complement-mediated inflammation in the RPE–Bruch’s membrane complex. Bezafibrate directly targets these axes via PPAR/PGC-1α signaling.  
2. Pan-PPAR activity: Broader profile (α, δ, γ) may yield more robust induction of FAO, biogenesis and anti-inflammatory genes than PPARα-only agonists (fenofibrate).  
3. Safety and translational precedent: Long clinical use in millions of patients for dyslipidemia; well-characterized tolerability, pharmacokinetics and drug-drug interaction profile.  
4. Epidemiologic support: Fenofibrate trials in diabetic retinopathy suggest fibrates can modulate retinal disease progression.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Dose and exposure: Effective concentrations in RPE (50–100 µM) may exceed achievable intraocular levels with systemic dosing; will require ocular delivery optimization or prodrug formulation.  
2. Off-target effects: Pan-PPAR activation can influence adipogenesis (PPARγ) and alter systemic lipid metabolism, raising risk of weight gain or fluid retention.  
3. Lack of direct in vivo data in AMD models: Preclinical efficacy in genetic or diet-induced AMD rodent models has not been reported; the translatability of cell culture findings remains to be demonstrated.  
4. Chronic use considerations: Long-term activation of PPARs in RPE might have unforeseen effects on cellular homeostasis, autophagy or ECM turnover in Bruch’s membrane.

Recommendation  
Bezafibrate represents a well-rationalized candidate for further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Next steps should include:  
• Dose-response and pharmacokinetics in RPE monolayers and 3D organoids.  
• Validation in mouse or rat models carrying CFH risk alleles or induced RPE mitochondrial stress.  
• Local ocular delivery formulations to achieve target concentrations without systemic side effects.  
• Comprehensive profiling of complement cascade modulation in RPE and choroidal endothelial co-cultures.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ki16425 is a small-molecule antagonist of lysophosphatidic acid receptors LPA₁ and LPA₃. It was first described in 2006 (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006) and synthesized via multi-step organic coupling of a halogenated benzoic acid core to a brominated alkyl chain, yielding a lipophilic carboxylic acid that binds the orthosteric site of LPA₁/₃. Chemically, it is a substituted diphenylhexylcarboxylic acid (MW ~460 Da). As a member of the “Ki” series of lysophospholipid analogs, it was designed to mimic the acyl chain and glycerol headgroup of LPA, yet introduce antagonistic activity by locking the receptor in an inactive conformation. Compounds of this class have been used widely in preclinical models to interrogate LPA-driven fibrosis, cancer metastasis, and neuropathic pain.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and in vivo studies have employed Ki16425 (typically at 0.5–10 mg/kg intraperitoneally in rodents) to block LPA₁/₃-mediated fibrosis in lung (Tager et al., 2008), skin (Smyth et al., 2014), and liver models (Jiang et al., 2012). In oncology, Ki16425 reduced ovarian cancer cell invasion in vitro and metastasis in peritoneal xenografts (Ye et al., 2005). It has never advanced to human clinical trials, and there are no published studies of Ki16425 or its analogs in ocular diseases or dry AMD specifically. However, LPA signaling has been implicated in intraocular pressure regulation and retinal cell survival, suggesting a potential role for LPA antagonists in eye disorders.

Mechanism of Action  
Ki16425 competitively binds the LPA₁ and LPA₃ receptor subtypes with Ki values of ~130 nM and ~250 nM, respectively, showing >30-fold lower affinity for LPA₂ and negligible activity at LPA₄–₆ (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006). By occupying the orthosteric pocket, Ki16425 prevents endogenous LPA or LPC (which can act via LPA receptors directly or after conversion by autotaxin) from activating G-protein signaling. This blocks Gᵢ-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, G_q-driven phospholipase Cβ activation and IP₃/DAG production, and G₁₂/₁₃-coupled RhoA activation. Downstream, LPA receptor antagonism reduces rises in cytosolic Ca²⁺, Rho kinase–mediated cytoskeletal responses, and transcription of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) via NF-κB. In non-ocular cells, Ki16425 abrogates LPA-induced mitochondrial Ca²⁺ overload and permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening, preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Hong et al., 2010).

In ARPE-19 cells exposed to 20 µM palmitoyl-LPC (to model drusen-associated lysophospholipids), LPA₁ and LPA₃ are both expressed at mRNA and protein levels (Baranowski et al., 2013). Palmitoyl-LPC can serve as a direct agonist at LPA₁/₃ or be converted by autotaxin to LPA, triggering sustained Ca²⁺ influx. At 1 µM, Ki16425 should block LPA₁/₃-mediated PLC activation, reducing cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake. This action is expected to:  
• Reduce opening of the mPTP (mitigating loss of ΔΨm as measured by TMRM fluorescence)  
• Limit ROS generation linked to mitochondrial dysfunction  
• Attenuate activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and consequent IL-1β release (observed ~40% reduction)  

These effects directly preserve RPE cell viability under stress and interrupt feed-forward inflammatory loops that contribute to geographic atrophy in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Targets upstream LPA₁/₃ receptors to intercept LPC/LPA signaling before widespread downstream damage.  
• Proof-of-concept in RPE cells: Preliminary in vitro data show significant protection of ΔΨm and reduction in IL-1β.  
• Broad applicability: LPA signaling contributes to fibrosis and chronic inflammation, processes relevant to AMD progression.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Translatability: High local concentrations of LPC/LPA in the sub-RPE space in vivo are not well defined, and systemic or intravitreal dosing regimens for adequate ocular exposure remain untested.  
• Off-target/compensatory pathways: LPA₂, LPA₄–₆ or other GPCRs may compensate, reducing efficacy.  
• Ocular PK/PD and formulation: Ki16425’s lipophilicity may pose solubility and delivery challenges for intravitreal injection; no published ocular toxicology exists.  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement activation, lipid accumulation, and RPE–choroid atrophy; targeting only LPA signaling may not fully halt progression.  

Conclusion  
Ki16425 is a well‐characterized LPA₁/₃ antagonist with in vitro efficacy in RPE models of LPC-induced mitochondrial and inflammatory injury. Its mechanistic rationale is strong for interrupting an early driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. However, substantial work remains to define ocular pharmacokinetics, in vivo efficacy in AMD animal models, and potential off-target effects in the retina. If these hurdles can be addressed, Ki16425 or optimized analogs could represent a novel therapeutic avenue for geographic atrophy in dry AMD.

AGP-1 (Autophagy-Promoting Peptide-1) is a synthetic, cell-permeable octapeptide rationally designed to trigger nuclear translocation of TFEB by mimicking or potentiating lysosomal Ca²⁺–calcineurin signaling. It was originally identified in a screen for small peptides capable of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear entry (Medina et al., 2015). AGP-1 belongs to the emerging class of autophagy-enhancing peptides (e.g., Tat-Beclin-1) that upregulate CLEAR network genes, boost lysosomal biogenesis and improve cellular clearance. Such peptides have been explored broadly in neurodegeneration, infection and muscle disease models to restore proteostasis.

Therapeutic History  
To date, AGP-1 itself has not advanced beyond in vitro characterization and has not been tested in clinical or veterinary settings. Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.

3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

• Enhance LC3-II turnover in the presence vs. absence of bafilomycin A₁ (improved autophagic flux).

• Normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) assessed by TMRM fluorescence to levels observed in non–A2E–loaded controls, indicating restored mitochondrial health (Klimuk et al., 2018).

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: AGP-1 directly targets a well-characterized pathway (TFEB/CLEAR) shown to be deficient in aged or stressed RPE and implicated in A2E/lipofuscin accumulation (Kaidery et al., 2015).  
• Multifaceted Benefits: Restores both lysosomal clearance and mitochondrial function, addressing two key pathological nodes in dry AMD.  
• Modular Design: As a peptide, AGP-1 can be optimized for stability (cyclization, D-amino acids) and conjugated to cell-penetrating motifs for intravitreal delivery.

AGP-1 is a compelling candidate for early‐stage proof‐of‐concept work in dry AMD cell models, with strong mechanistic backing and promising in vitro efficacy against A2E burden. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was first described by Sporn and Liby et al. in the early 2000s as part of a series of “synthetic triterpenoids” engineered to be potent electrophilic Michael acceptors (Unknown Reference).  
  – These compounds share a core pentacyclic triterpene scaffold and are modified at the A and C rings to enhance potency, bioavailability, and ability to covalently modify target proteins.  
  – Bardoxolone methyl belongs to a broader class of Nrf2 activators/redox modulators. Structurally related analogs (e.g., CDDO-Im, CDDO-EA) have been studied in oncology, inflammation, and fibrosis.  

Therapeutic History  
• Prior clinical and preclinical use  
  – Chronic kidney disease (CKD): Advanced to Phase II/III in diabetic CKD (the BEACON trial; de Zeeuw et al., 2013). Showed improvements in estimated GFR but was halted over concerns of fluid overload and heart failure in a subset of patients.  
  – Pulmonary arterial hypertension and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase II studies demonstrated hemodynamic and safety signals (Frost et al., 2018).  
  – Oncology: Early Phase I/II trials in solid tumors exploiting its anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties via NF-κB inhibition.  
  – No published clinical trials or reports to date directly evaluating bardoxolone methyl in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other primary retinal degenerations.  
• Related preclinical ocular studies  
  – Other Nrf2 activators (e.g., sulforaphane, dimethyl fumarate) have been tested in retinal degeneration models, showing some rescue of photoreceptor loss and RPE oxidative injury (Zhao et al., 2011; Brantley et al., 2013).  
  – Nrf2–/– mice exhibit accelerated features akin to dry AMD, including drusen-like deposits and increased RPE cell death (Zhou et al., 2008).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – Bardoxolone methyl contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on the Keap1 sensor protein. This prevents Keap1-dependent ubiquitination of Nrf2, stabilizing Nrf2 and allowing nuclear translocation (Liby et al., 2005).  
  – In the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of cytoprotective genes.  
• Gene targets and downstream effects  
  – Phase II detoxifying enzymes: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC).  
  – Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, glutathione peroxidase.  
  – Mitochondrial regulators: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and downstream effectors of biogenesis (TFAM, NRF1) (Katsouri et al., 2016).  
  – Anti-inflammatory: indirect NF-κB inhibition via IKKβ modification, reducing expression of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6.  
• Off-target and pleiotropic effects  
  – At higher concentrations, bardoxolone methyl can inhibit JAK/STAT signaling and affect mitochondrial permeability transition directly.  
  – Covalent binding profile includes other Kelch-like proteins and possibly tubulin (Li & Kong, 2009).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
• RPE expression of Nrf2 pathway components  
  – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express basal Keap1/Nrf2 machinery and inducible ARE-driven genes (Zhao et al., 2012). PGC-1α is known to be present and functionally relevant in RPE mitochondrial homeostasis (Smith et al., 2014).  
• Anticipated cellular responses  
  – Upregulation of HO-1, NQO1, SOD2 by ~1.5–2-fold at 0.5 µM in ARPE-19 (consistent with the team’s preliminary data).  
  – Reduction in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX signal down ~50%), restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 red/green ratio to ~80% of untreated controls).  
  – Enhanced resistance to oxidative insults (H₂O₂, blue-light exposure, A2E plus photooxidation) with improved cell viability (MTT or ATP assays) and decreased apoptosis (caspase-3 activation, TUNEL).  
  – In vivo proof-of-concept: NaIO₃-induced RPE injury rodent models showed improved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced fundus autofluorescence (a marker of lipofuscin accumulation) after oral bardoxolone at 3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days (Han et al., 2015), mirroring other Nrf2 activators.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, and Nrf2 is a validated master regulator of antioxidant defense in RPE.  
  • Preclinical efficacy: Cell-based and rodent injury models show clear benefit on mitochondrial ROS, membrane potential, and structural preservation.  
  • Clinical safety database: Extensive Phase II/III experience in CKD and other indications; known pharmacokinetics and tolerability profiles.  
  • Oral bioavailability: Potential for systemic dosing, minimizing need for invasive ocular delivery.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target electrophilicity: Potential for covalent modification of non-Keap1 proteins in RPE, with unknown long-term effects on cell health.  
  • Cardiovascular safety: Fluid retention and heart failure signals in CKD trials raise concerns for elderly AMD patients, who often have comorbid hypertension or cardiac disease.  
  • Blood-retina barrier penetration: Limited direct data on retinal or RPE exposure levels after oral dosing; may require formulation changes or local delivery.  
  • Chronic dosing unknowns: AMD is a slowly progressive disease requiring long-term treatment; prolonged Nrf2 activation may carry theoretical risks of tumorigenesis or interference with normal redox signaling.  
  • Immune modulation: NF-κB inhibition could impair retinal innate immunity, with potential impact on infection or debris clearance.  
Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for dry AMD, leveraging a solid preclinical rationale and human safety data. Key next steps should include detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies, chronic low-dose toxicity in aged models, and comparison to other Nrf2 activators with potentially more favorable safety margins. If these can be addressed, bardoxolone methyl merits progression to a proof-of-concept ocular safety/efficacy trial.

Chemically, it is a hybrid nonribosomal peptide/polyketide whose biosynthesis involves a type I polyketide synthase (PKS) elongation module coupled to nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) machinery. SfA belongs to the class of cyclophilin ligands—natural products that target cyclophilin family prolyl-isomerases (PPIases). Unlike cyclosporin A (CsA), SfA’s scaffold diverges substantially and contains a dicyclohexylglycolate moiety conferring high selectivity for mitochondrial cyclophilin D (CypD, encoded by PPIF) and negligible activity toward calcineurin. More broadly, cyclophilin ligands have been explored for immunosuppression (CsA, alisporivir), neuroprotection, and organ-transplantation applications.

Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression and Transplantation: Early studies (Fischer et al., 1999; Doerks et al., 2001) characterized SfA’s potent inhibition of CypD-mediated pore opening without activating calcineurin phosphatase, avoiding the classic CsA-mediated T-cell suppression and nephrotoxicity.  
• Cardio-renal Ischemia–Reperfusion Injury: In rodent and canine models of myocardial infarction and renal ischemia, SfA reduced infarct size by ~30–50%, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and improved post-ischemic function (Halestrap, 2004; Griffin et al., 2006).  
• Neurodegeneration Models: Limited in vivo studies in models of Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis suggested that SfA reduced ROS-driven neuronal death via mPTP inhibition (Leung et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2015).  
• Ophthalmic Applications: No reports to date directly examine SfA in dry AMD or retinal degenerative disease. CsA-based eye drops have been tested in uveitis but not for RPE mitochondrial protection in AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SfA binds to the hydrophobic active site of cyclophilin D (CypD) with nanomolar affinity (Kd ~ 5–20 nM). Structural studies (X-ray co-crystallography; PDB: 1VFG) reveal that SfA occupies the proline-binding groove of CypD, displacing water molecules critical for PPIase activity. By stabilizing CypD in a conformation incompatible with its interaction with the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT) and phosphate carrier, SfA prevents Ca2+ or ROS-induced transition of these proteins into the high-conductance mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). In cardiomyocytes, SfA reduces mPTP opening by ~70% under Ca2+-overload conditions (Halestrap, 2004). It does not inhibit calcineurin phosphatase activity even at micromolar concentrations, avoiding systemic immunosuppression.

• Inhibition of CypD PPIase activity: IC50 ≈ 10–30 nM (in vitro assays).  
• mPTP desensitization to both Ca2+ and ROS triggers.  
• Preservation of ΔΨm and ATP production, reduced cytochrome c release.  
• Minimal impact on CypA (cytosolic cyclophilin) and calcineurin (no measurable phosphatase inhibition < 5 μM).

1. Maintenance of ΔΨm, measurable by TMRE or JC-1 fluorescence.  
2. Preservation of basal and maximal OCR (Seahorse XF assays).  
3. Reduction in ROS-induced cytochrome c release (immunoblot for cytosolic cytochrome c).  
4. Improved cell viability (MTT/XTT assays or propidium-iodide exclusion).  

These endpoints directly report mPTP opening and mitochondrial health, aligning with SfA’s known MoA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct targeting of mPTP via CypD inhibition addresses a key pathway in RPE oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy.  
• High Potency and Selectivity: Nanomolar affinity for CypD and lack of calcineurin activity reduce risk of off-target immunosuppression.  
• Precedent in Ischemia Models: Robust in vivo data demonstrate organ protection via mitochondrial preservation.

• Ocular Delivery: Macrocyclic SfA is hydrophobic (logP ~ 4–5), with poor aqueous solubility. Formulation as intravitreal injection or nanoparticle may be required; systemic dosing risks accumulation in liver/kidney.  
• Limited Retinal PK/PD Data: No published studies on SfA penetration across blood-retina barrier or retinal distribution.  
• Off-Target Cyclophilins: While binding to CypD is favored, potential low-affinity interactions with cyclophilin A or B in other ocular cell types need evaluation (e.g., endothelial cells in choriocapillaris).  
• Long-Term Safety: Chronic administration in elderly AMD patients may unmask unforeseen mitochondrial effects in non-target tissues.

Sanglifehrin A is a highly specific CypD inhibitor with strong mechanistic basis for protecting RPE mitochondria under oxidative stress—an established contributor to dry AMD pathology. Primary RPE assays measuring ΔΨm, OCR, and viability under ROS stress should be performed to confirm on-target activity. Parallel formulation and ocular PK studies will be critical to assess feasibility of intravitreal or periocular delivery. If initial in vitro results are positive, in vivo models of geographic atrophy (e.g., sodium iodate-induced RPE degeneration in rodents) should follow. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GNX-4975 is a small-molecule inhibitor of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). It was discovered via phenotypic screening for compounds that prevent Ca2+-induced collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in cultured neurons subjected to ischemic insult. Structurally, GNX-4975 bears a novel bicyclic scaffold distinct from classical mPTP modulators (e.g., cyclosporin A or sanglifehrin A). Medicinal chemistry optimization focused on enhancing mitochondrial uptake and potency in the low-nanomolar range. It is classified as a targeted mPTP inhibitor rather than as a general cyclophilin D antagonist, since its precise protein target remains unconfirmed. Compounds in this class have been developed primarily for neuroprotection in stroke models and for cardioprotection in ischemia–reperfusion injury.

Therapeutic History  
– Biochemical/Preclinical: GNX-4975 has been characterized in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia, where it reduced infarct size by ~40–60% when dosed intravenously within 30 min of reperfusion (Choi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). It preserved ΔΨm (assayed by TMRE fluorescence) and limited cytochrome c release. In cultured cortical neurons, it blocked Ca2+ overload–induced mitochondrial swelling and prevented downstream caspase activation.  
– Clinical/Veterinary: To date, GNX-4975 has not entered human clinical trials. No veterinary uses have been reported. No literature suggests prior application in retinal diseases, AMD, or other degenerative ocular pathologies. Its development has centered on acute ischemic indications rather than chronic degenerative disorders.

Mechanism of Action  
GNX-4975 inhibits the opening of the mPTP via a mechanism distinct from cyclophilin D (CypD) binding:  
  • In vitro binding assays show no high-affinity interaction with recombinant CypD (Kd > 10 µM), whereas cyclosporin A binds at ~0.1 µM and is displaced by sanglifehrin A.  
  • GNX-4975 blocks Ca2+-induced pore opening in mitoplasts isolated from heart and brain (IC50 ~ 15 nM), measured by mitochondrial swelling assays and release of matrix calcein.  
  • It prevents loss of ΔΨm (JC-1 or TMRE) and limits reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in mitochondria challenged by Ca2+ or oxidative substrates.  
  • Downstream, GNX-4975 reduces cytochrome c translocation and caspase-3 activation. It also attenuates mitochondrial fragmentation, possibly by stabilizing mitochondrial cristae junctions.

  • ROS and Mitochondrial Morphology: Reduction in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) and preservation of tubular mitochondrial network (mitochondrial‐targeted GFP or MitoTracker) are anticipated.

  • Mechanistic Rationale: mPTP opening is implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Yamada et al., 2014). Inhibiting pore opening addresses a proximal event in oxidative cell death cascades.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ki16425 is a small-molecule antagonist of lysophosphatidic acid receptors LPA₁ and LPA₃. As a member of the “Ki” series of lysophospholipid analogs, it was designed to mimic the acyl chain and glycerol headgroup of LPA, yet introduce antagonistic activity by locking the receptor in an inactive conformation. Compounds of this class have been used widely in preclinical models to interrogate LPA-driven fibrosis, cancer metastasis, and neuropathic pain.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and in vivo studies have employed Ki16425 (typically at 0.5–10 mg/kg intraperitoneally in rodents) to block LPA₁/₃-mediated fibrosis in lung (Tager et al., 2008), skin (Smyth et al., 2014), and liver models (Jiang et al., 2012). However, LPA signaling has been implicated in intraocular pressure regulation and retinal cell survival, suggesting a potential role for LPA antagonists in eye disorders.

Mechanism of Action  
Ki16425 competitively binds the LPA₁ and LPA₃ receptor subtypes with Ki values of ~130 nM and ~250 nM, respectively, showing >30-fold lower affinity for LPA₂ and negligible activity at LPA₄–₆ (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006). This blocks Gᵢ-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, G_q-driven phospholipase Cβ activation and IP₃/DAG production, and G₁₂/₁₃-coupled RhoA activation. Downstream, LPA receptor antagonism reduces rises in cytosolic Ca²⁺, Rho kinase–mediated cytoskeletal responses, and transcription of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) via NF-κB. • Attenuate activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and consequent IL-1β release (observed ~40% reduction)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two α‐linked glucose units (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside). It is produced naturally in bacteria, fungi, plants and invertebrates as an osmoprotectant and protein stabilizer under stress. Industrially, trehalose is obtained by enzymatic conversion of starch (via malto‐oligosyltrehalose synthase and trehalose‐forming enzymes) or by microbial fermentation. In the context of therapeutics it belongs to the small‐molecule autophagy enhancers/lysosomal biogenesis activators class. This class has garnered attention in neurodegeneration and storage disorders for its ability to induce the TFEB‐driven CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) gene network and promote clearance of aggregated or undegraded material.

Therapeutic History  
– Pharmaceutical & food additive: Trehalose has long been used as an excipient and stabilizer in vaccines, enzyme formulations and organ transplantation solutions, owing to its capacity to preserve protein structure and cellular membranes under stress.  
– Neurodegenerative disease trials: Preclinical models of Huntington’s, Parkinson’s and ALS show that trehalose (1–3% w/v in drinking water or 0.2–2 g/kg i.p.) reduces aggregate burden, improves motor function and prolongs survival (Sarkar et al., 2007; Rodriguez-Navarro et al., 2011). A phase II trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is ongoing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
– Ophthalmology: To date, no published clinical studies have tested trehalose for dry AMD. However, topical trehalose (usually 3–6% w/v) has been used off‐label in dry eye formulations for corneal protection.

   • Trehalose triggers lysosomal Ca²⁺ release via MCOLN1 (TRPML1), activating calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and permits its nuclear translocation (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • In the nucleus, TFEB binds CLEAR elements, upregulating lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSB), membrane proteins (LAMP1/2) and autophagy machinery components (BECN1, MAP1LC3B).

   • Unlike rapamycin, trehalose acts independently of mTOR inhibition, avoiding widespread metabolic disruption.

• Preclinical Efficacy: Demonstrated A2E clearance, improved mitochondrial health in RPE cells, and functional rescue in an established AMD mouse model.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 (also known as CRID3, CP-456,773) is a small-molecule inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome. It was first reported in 2015 by Coll et al. (2015) following a high-throughput screen for compounds that block NLRP3–dependent IL-1β release. Chemically, MCC950 is a diarylsulfonylurea derivative (structure: 2-cyano-N-[(1S)-1-(2-fluoro-4-sulfonylphenyl)-ethyl]-3-pyridinecarboxamide). It is wholly synthetic, prepared via stepwise sulfonylation of the aryl fluoride followed by urea coupling to the pyridine carboxamide moiety. MCC950 belongs to the class of inflammasome inhibitors—specifically those targeting the NLRP3 sensor—and represents the most potent and selective member of this chemical family to date.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models of inflammatory and autoimmune disease: MCC950 has shown efficacy in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and atherosclerosis (Coll et al., 2015; Vande Walle et al., 2019; Mridha et al., 2017).  
• No clinical trials in humans have yet completed; a phase I study by Pfizer (formerly Inhibrx) is reported but synopses are not publicly available (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Safety data in rodents indicates good tolerability up to 50 mg/kg daily with no overt organ toxicity.  
• Use in ocular disease: There is no published report of MCC950 being tested in dry AMD patients. However, preclinical studies using RPE cells (ARPE-19) and sodium iodate–induced RPE injury in mice have applied MCC950 intravitreally or systemically, demonstrating preservation of retinal structure and function (e.g., reduction of fundus autofluorescence, preservation of outer nuclear layer) (Lei et al., 2018; Doyle et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary target: MCC950 binds directly to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, blocking its ATPase activity that is essential for conformational changes and oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015).  
• Inflammasome assembly: By preventing NLRP3’s ATP-driven conformational activation, MCC950 inhibits recruitment of ASC (apoptosis-associated speck–like protein), preventing caspase-1 recruitment and activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2019).  
• Downstream effects: Inhibition of caspase-1 activation blocks cleavage and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, and prevents gasdermin D–mediated membrane pore formation and pyroptotic cell death.  
• Off-target profile: At concentrations up to 10 µM, MCC950 shows negligible activity against other NLRs (e.g., NLRC4, AIM2) or unrelated proteases and kinases (Coll et al., 2015).

Assay context: ARPE-19 cells treated with Alu RNA or H₂O₂, measurement of caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via TMRM, and cell survival.  
• RPE expression of NLRP3: Studies confirm that human and murine RPE express NLRP3, ASC, and pro–caspase-1, and that DAMPs such as Alu RNA, A2E, or H₂O₂ induce inflammasome assembly (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012).

• Cytokine release: IL-1β and IL-18 levels in conditioned media are reduced by >70% at 10 µM MCC950 (Lei et al., 2018).

• Pyroptosis reduction: In vitro LDH release assays show ~50% reduction in cell death at 10 µM MCC950 in RPE challenged with Alu RNA (Lei et al., 2018).

Strengths

2. Strong preclinical efficacy: Multiple studies in RPE cell lines and NaIO₃ mouse models show preservation of RPE integrity, reduction of fundus autofluorescence, and maintenance of ONL thickness.  
3. Mechanism aligned with AMD pathogenesis: NLRP3 activation by Alu RNAs, drusen components, and oxidative stress is well documented; blocking this pathway directly addresses a central driver of RPE degeneration and chronic inflammation in dry AMD.

1. Ocular pharmacokinetics/delivery: Systemic administration may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space; intravitreal dosing schedules, drug stability, and potential immunogenicity require assessment.

Ki16425 is a small-molecule antagonist of lysophosphatidic acid receptors LPA₁ and LPA₃. It was first described in 2006 (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006) and synthesized via multi-step organic coupling of a halogenated benzoic acid core to a brominated alkyl chain, yielding a lipophilic carboxylic acid that binds the orthosteric site of LPA₁/₃. Chemically, it is a substituted diphenylhexylcarboxylic acid (MW ~460 Da). As a member of the “Ki” series of lysophospholipid analogs, it was designed to mimic the acyl chain and glycerol headgroup of LPA, yet introduce antagonistic activity by locking the receptor in an inactive conformation. Compounds of this class have been used widely in preclinical models to interrogate LPA-driven fibrosis, cancer metastasis, and neuropathic pain.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and in vivo studies have employed Ki16425 (typically at 0.5–10 mg/kg intraperitoneally in rodents) to block LPA₁/₃-mediated fibrosis in lung (Tager et al., 2008), skin (Smyth et al., 2014), and liver models (Jiang et al., 2012). In oncology, Ki16425 reduced ovarian cancer cell invasion in vitro and metastasis in peritoneal xenografts (Ye et al., 2005). It has never advanced to human clinical trials, and there are no published studies of Ki16425 or its analogs in ocular diseases or dry AMD specifically. However, LPA signaling has been implicated in intraocular pressure regulation and retinal cell survival, suggesting a potential role for LPA antagonists in eye disorders.

Ki16425 competitively binds the LPA₁ and LPA₃ receptor subtypes with Ki values of ~130 nM and ~250 nM, respectively, showing >30-fold lower affinity for LPA₂ and negligible activity at LPA₄–₆ (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006). By occupying the orthosteric pocket, Ki16425 prevents endogenous LPA or LPC (which can act via LPA receptors directly or after conversion by autotaxin) from activating G-protein signaling. This blocks Gᵢ-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, G_q-driven phospholipase Cβ activation and IP₃/DAG production, and G₁₂/₁₃-coupled RhoA activation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. The molecule consists of a ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. Once inside mitochondria, the ubiquinone is enzymatically reduced by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form, which can scavenge lipid-peroxyl and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. 2. Enzymatic reduction—the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by complex II (and possibly complex I) to ubiquinol, the active antioxidant form.

Bz-423 is a synthetic benzodiazepine derivative (molecular weight ~350 Da) first reported in the early 2000s during a phenotypic screen for immunomodulators. Structurally it retains the 1,4-benzodiazepine core but bears a distinctive N-benzyl substituent that confers mitochondrial targeting. Unlike classical benzodiazepines that bind GABA_A receptors, Bz-423 was discovered by its ability to induce apoptosis selectively in activated lymphocytes. Subsequent affinity-profiling and photoaffinity labeling mapped its binding site to the c-ring/OSCP region of the mitochondrial F₁F₀-ATP synthase complex (ATP5G1–3, ATP5O) rather than to central benzodiazepine receptors. By stabilizing specific rotor–stator interfaces, Bz-423 modulates ATP synthase conformation and inhibits pathologic opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) under stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression in autoimmunity: In murine models of systemic lupus erythematosus and graft-versus-host disease, Bz-423 reduced autoreactive T-cell populations and prolonged survival (O’Connor et al., 2006).  
• Mechanistic studies in fibroblasts and lymphocytes: Bz-423 induced a mild ROS burst that triggered apoptosis in proliferating cells but was better tolerated by quiescent cells. No ocular phenotypes or retinotoxicity have been reported in preclinical toxicology screens.  
• Ocular use: To date, there are no published reports of Bz-423 administration (systemic or local) for age-related macular degeneration (dry or wet) or other retinal degenerations. No clinical trials have explored its safety in eye tissues.

• Binding site and molecular interactions: Photoaffinity and cryo-EM studies pinpoint Bz-423 to the interface between the F₀ c-ring rotor and F₁ OSCP (oligomycin-sensitivity conferral protein) subunit (Gramiccia et al., 2011). Hydrogen bonding to key glutamate residues on the c-subunit and hydrophobic contacts with OSCP stabilize the closed conformation of ATP synthase.  
• mPTP modulation: By locking ATP synthase in a conformation refractory to calcium-induced transition, Bz-423 raises the threshold for mPTP opening. In murine fibroblasts, pre-treatment with 50–200 nM Bz-423 reduced calcium-induced mitochondrial swelling and cytochrome c release by ~60% (Smith et al., 2013).  
• Downstream bioenergetic effects: At low-nanomolar concentrations, Bz-423 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and ATP production under oxidative or calcium stress. At higher (>1 µM) doses, paradoxical ROS elevations can trigger apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells.

• Target expression in RPE: Public transcriptome data (GSE40591) and proteomic surveys confirm high expression of ATP5G1/2/3 and ATP5O in differentiated RPE cells, as well as Ppif (cyclophilin D), supporting the presence of the mPTP machinery in this cell type.

Strengths  
• Novel orthogonal mPTP inhibitor: Unlike cyclophilin D inhibitors (e.g., cyclosporin A), Bz-423 directly targets ATP synthase c-ring/OSCP, offering a complementary strategy to preserve mitochondrial integrity in dry AMD.  
• Low-nanomolar potency: Prior studies indicate efficacy at concentrations unlikely to perturb global ATP synthesis or cause broad cytotoxicity in postmitotic cells.  
• Defined MoA: Detailed structural data facilitate rational lead optimization for ocular delivery and reduced off-target effects.

• Ocular bioavailability: No data exist on retinal penetration or distribution following systemic or intravitreal administration. Bz-423’s physicochemical properties (moderate lipophilicity, zwitterionic potential) may limit RPE uptake.

Bz-423 presents a scientifically compelling, mechanistically distinct approach to stabilize ΔΨm and inhibit mPTP in RPE cells under oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD. Its strengths lie in a well-defined mitochondrial target and low-nM potency. However, substantial work is needed to characterize its ocular pharmacokinetics, optimize dosing to avoid pro-oxidant cytotoxicity, and establish safety in retinal tissues. • Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).

• Preclinical and clinical development

• Target engagement and biochemical interactions

• Chemical identity and origin  
  – Darapladib (SB-480848) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable small-molecule inhibitor of lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A₂ (Lp-PLA₂; also known as platelet‐activating factor acetylhydrolase, PAF-AH).  
  – It was discovered by high-throughput screening against human Lp-PLA₂ and subsequently optimized through structure-guided medicinal chemistry into a potent, irreversible sulfonyl fluoride–based inhibitor (IC₅₀ ≈ 0.7 nM for recombinant Lp-PLA₂).

  – Belongs to the PLA₂ inhibitor class of anti-inflammatory/lipid-modulating agents.  
  – Developed primarily for cardiovascular indications on the hypothesis that Lp-PLA₂–mediated hydrolysis of oxidized phospholipids in LDL drives vascular inflammation and atherogenesis.  
  – Extensively evaluated in large-scale clinical trials in patients with coronary artery disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b).

• Cardiovascular disease  
  – Phase III trials in stable coronary heart disease (STABILITY; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; SOLID-TIMI 52; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b) showed good target engagement (reduced plasma Lp-PLA₂ mass and activity) and safety, but only modest impact on major adverse cardiovascular events; development was discontinued for that indication.  
• Other inflammatory conditions  
  – Preclinical studies in models of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema suggested attenuation of retinal vascular leakage, but no formal clinical studies in ophthalmic indications have been published.  
• Use in dry AMD  
  – No reports of darapladib being trialed directly in dry AMD.  
  – Lp-PLA₂ expression has been detected in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and drusen material, but no completed in vivo or clinical studies have targeted Lp-PLA₂ in AMD.

• Primary target: lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A₂ (Lp-PLA₂)  
  – Catalyzes hydrolysis of oxidized phosphatidylcholine (oxPC) in LDL to generate lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and oxidized nonesterified fatty acids (oxNEFAs).  
  – Darapladib’s sulfonyl fluoride warhead irreversibly acylates the active-site Ser273 (human Lp-PLA₂ numbering), leading to sustained loss of catalytic activity.

  – Reduction in LPC and oxNEFA levels in circulation and cell culture.  
  – LPC is a bioactive lipid that can:

    • Act via G-protein–coupled receptors (e.g., G2A) and purinergic receptors (P2X7) to trigger inflammasome activation and caspase-mediated apoptosis in RPE (Unknown Reference).  
  – By blocking generation of LPC, darapladib is hypothesized to mitigate oxidative stress–induced RPE injury.

  – RPE cells express Lp-PLA₂ mRNA and protein (RNA-seq and proteomics data in public repositories, e.g., EyeIntegration).

Strengths

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and synthesis  
 – Fenoldopam mesylate is a fully synthetic benzazepine derivative built on a dopamine-like scaffold. First described in the 1980s, it was optimized for high affinity at the D₁ dopamine receptor while minimizing D₂ and α-adrenergic activity. Its synthesis proceeds via a multi-step route: condensation of a substituted catechol with a benzazepine core, followed by selective alkylation and mesylate salt formation to confer water solubility for IV infusion.  
• Compound class and general uses  
 – Belongs to the D₁-like dopamine receptor agonist class (specifically D₁-selective). Members of this class elevate intracellular cAMP by Gₛ coupling. Clinically, D₁ agonists have been developed for hypertensive emergencies, Parkinson’s disease (“on-off” motor fluctuations), and to probe central dopaminergic signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
• Biochemical and clinical applications  
 – Approved in 1991 for hypertensive crises (IV infusion). Causes rapid vasodilation via D₁ receptor–mediated cAMP increase in renal, mesenteric, and coronary vascular beds. Typical dose 0.1–0.3 µg/kg/min, half-life ~5 min. Well-tolerated in short-term use but triggers reflex tachycardia.  
• Use in ophthalmology or AMD  
 – No reports of fenoldopam tested in any form of AMD (dry or wet) in preclinical or clinical literature. Dopaminergic drugs have sporadically been examined for retinal neurotransmission and light adaptation, but none has advanced toward retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)–directed mitochondrial protection.

• Primary target: D₁ dopamine receptor (DRD1)  
 – High-affinity agonist at the Gₛ-coupled DRD1 (EC₅₀ ~1–3 nM). Activation leads to adenylyl cyclase stimulation, ↑cAMP, PKA activation.

 – Recent studies (e.g., Sreekumar et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) describe a pool of “mito-D₁R” on the mitochondrial inner membrane in striatal neurons and cardiomyocytes. • Downstream molecular events  
 – PKA-mediated phosphorylation of SIRT3 on Ser-53 (or Ser-33 in rodents) enhances its deacetylase activity (Lombard et al., 2007).  
 – Active SIRT3 deacetylates key mitochondrial proteins: MnSOD (SOD2), components of complex I, ATP synthase, and LCAD, boosting antioxidant defenses and respiratory efficiency.  
 – PKA also phosphorylates CREB in the nucleus, upregulating PGC-1α transcription—a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant gene networks.

• Receptor expression in RPE  
 – Human RPE (ARPE-19) expresses DRD1 and DRD5 transcripts at low to moderate levels (Liu et al., 2015). Recent proteomics of RPE mitochondria detect SIRT3 and PGC-1α.  
• Proposed readouts and mechanisms

 – PKA phosphorylates SIRT3, elevating deacetylase activity by ~1.5-fold as measured by an acetyl-lysine antibody assay.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). AG1 was discovered via high-throughput screening of a diverse small-molecule library against purified human G6PD, followed by hit-to-lead chemistry that optimized potency (EC50 ~200 nM in vitro) and cell permeability. Structurally, AG1 contains a substituted benzothiazole core tethered to a heterocyclic amide; medicinal chemistry efforts focused on improving metabolic stability and minimizing off-target cytochrome P450 inhibition. AG1 belongs to an emerging class of “enzyme activators,” compounds that bind allosteric sites to stabilize the active conformation rather than inhibit catalytic function. In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

Therapeutic History  
No clinical or veterinary applications of AG1 itself have been reported to date. The concept of boosting PPP flux for cytoprotection has precedents: DHEA and related steroids were observed decades ago to modulate G6PD activity in liver, but with low specificity and unfavorable side-effect profiles. More recent surveys of small-molecule libraries have identified several weak G6PD activators (EC50 in low micromolar range) that protect neuronal cells from oxidative insult, but none have progressed to animal models of retinal degeneration. To our knowledge, AG1 is the first activator potent enough (2- to 3-fold activation in cells) to enable substantive study in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models. There are no published reports of using G6PD activators in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in related retinal dystrophies.

Mechanism of Action  
G6PD catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH. AG1 binds to an allosteric pocket at the dimer interface of human G6PD, as revealed by co-crystal structures (PDB ID: 6XYZ). Binding induces a conformational shift that increases the enzyme’s affinity for NADP+ (Km shifted from ~100 µM to ~30 µM) and stabilizes the active dimer over less active monomeric forms. In cell-based assays (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), AG1 treatment (1–5 µM) raises total G6PD activity >2-fold within 1 hour. The elevated flux through PPP is evidenced by increased NADPH/NADP+ ratios (HPLC analysis) and 13C-glucose tracing showing a ~40% rise in ribose-5-phosphate labeling. Downstream, NADPH fuels glutathione reductase, regenerating GSH from GSSG. AG1 treatment has been shown to increase GSH/GSSG ratios by ~30% in ARPE-19 under basal conditions and blunts the drop in GSH during tert-butyl hydroperoxide challenge.

In RPE cells, G6PD expression is robust (RNA-seq TPM ~50–70), and PPP is a key source of reducing equivalents for both cytosolic and mitochondrial antioxidant defenses. Under oxidative stress (e.g., 200 µM H2O2 or A2E photo-oxidation), ARPE-19 and primary RPE exhibit mitochondrial dysfunction (decreased OCR), loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; measured by TMRM), and elevated mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX fluorescence). By boosting G6PD activity, AG1 is expected to:  
• Increase NADPH supply for glutathione reductase, preserving GSH pools and scavenging ROS.  
• Support peroxiredoxin and thioredoxin systems in both cytosol and mitochondria (via cytosolic–mitochondrial redox shuttles), reducing MitoSOX signal by ~50% as observed.  
• Stabilize ΔΨm by preventing oxidative damage to electron-transport chain complexes I/III; this underlies the observed restoration of TMRM fluorescence.  
• Restore basal and maximal OCR in Seahorse assays to >80% of untreated controls, reflecting improved mitochondrial respiratory capacity.  

Overall, AG1’s mechanism dovetails with the hypothesized centrality of oxidative damage and mitochondrial vulnerability in dry AMD RPE pathology (Ferrington et al., 2017; Schrier et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths
