Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was first described by Sporn and Liby et al. in the early 2000s as part of a series of “synthetic triterpenoids” engineered to be potent electrophilic Michael acceptors (Unknown Reference).  
  – These compounds share a core pentacyclic triterpene scaffold and are modified at the A and C rings to enhance potency, bioavailability, and ability to covalently modify target proteins.  
  – Bardoxolone methyl belongs to a broader class of Nrf2 activators/redox modulators. Structurally related analogs (e.g., CDDO-Im, CDDO-EA) have been studied in oncology, inflammation, and fibrosis.  

Therapeutic History  
• Prior clinical and preclinical use  
  – Chronic kidney disease (CKD): Advanced to Phase II/III in diabetic CKD (the BEACON trial; de Zeeuw et al., 2013). Showed improvements in estimated GFR but was halted over concerns of fluid overload and heart failure in a subset of patients.  
  – Pulmonary arterial hypertension and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase II studies demonstrated hemodynamic and safety signals (Frost et al., 2018).  
  – Oncology: Early Phase I/II trials in solid tumors exploiting its anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties via NF-κB inhibition.  
  – No published clinical trials or reports to date directly evaluating bardoxolone methyl in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other primary retinal degenerations.  
• Related preclinical ocular studies  
  – Other Nrf2 activators (e.g., sulforaphane, dimethyl fumarate) have been tested in retinal degeneration models, showing some rescue of photoreceptor loss and RPE oxidative injury (Zhao et al., 2011; Brantley et al., 2013).  
  – Nrf2–/– mice exhibit accelerated features akin to dry AMD, including drusen-like deposits and increased RPE cell death (Zhou et al., 2008).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – Bardoxolone methyl contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on the Keap1 sensor protein. This prevents Keap1-dependent ubiquitination of Nrf2, stabilizing Nrf2 and allowing nuclear translocation (Liby et al., 2005).  
  – In the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of cytoprotective genes.  
• Gene targets and downstream effects  
  – Phase II detoxifying enzymes: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC).  
  – Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, glutathione peroxidase.  
  – Mitochondrial regulators: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and downstream effectors of biogenesis (TFAM, NRF1) (Katsouri et al., 2016).  
  – Anti-inflammatory: indirect NF-κB inhibition via IKKβ modification, reducing expression of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6.  
• Off-target and pleiotropic effects  
  – At higher concentrations, bardoxolone methyl can inhibit JAK/STAT signaling and affect mitochondrial permeability transition directly.  
  – Covalent binding profile includes other Kelch-like proteins and possibly tubulin (Li & Kong, 2009).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
• RPE expression of Nrf2 pathway components  
  – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express basal Keap1/Nrf2 machinery and inducible ARE-driven genes (Zhao et al., 2012). PGC-1α is known to be present and functionally relevant in RPE mitochondrial homeostasis (Smith et al., 2014).  
• Anticipated cellular responses  
  – Upregulation of HO-1, NQO1, SOD2 by ~1.5–2-fold at 0.5 µM in ARPE-19 (consistent with the team’s preliminary data).  
  – Reduction in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX signal down ~50%), restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 red/green ratio to ~80% of untreated controls).  
  – Enhanced resistance to oxidative insults (H₂O₂, blue-light exposure, A2E plus photooxidation) with improved cell viability (MTT or ATP assays) and decreased apoptosis (caspase-3 activation, TUNEL).  
  – In vivo proof-of-concept: NaIO₃-induced RPE injury rodent models showed improved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced fundus autofluorescence (a marker of lipofuscin accumulation) after oral bardoxolone at 3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days (Han et al., 2015), mirroring other Nrf2 activators.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, and Nrf2 is a validated master regulator of antioxidant defense in RPE.  
  • Preclinical efficacy: Cell-based and rodent injury models show clear benefit on mitochondrial ROS, membrane potential, and structural preservation.  
  • Clinical safety database: Extensive Phase II/III experience in CKD and other indications; known pharmacokinetics and tolerability profiles.  
  • Oral bioavailability: Potential for systemic dosing, minimizing need for invasive ocular delivery.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target electrophilicity: Potential for covalent modification of non-Keap1 proteins in RPE, with unknown long-term effects on cell health.  
  • Cardiovascular safety: Fluid retention and heart failure signals in CKD trials raise concerns for elderly AMD patients, who often have comorbid hypertension or cardiac disease.

  • Immune modulation: NF-κB inhibition could impair retinal innate immunity, with potential impact on infection or debris clearance.

Bardoxolone methyl is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for dry AMD, leveraging a solid preclinical rationale and human safety data. Key next steps should include detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies, chronic low-dose toxicity in aged models, and comparison to other Nrf2 activators with potentially more favorable safety margins. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.  

Mechanism of Action  
Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.  

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).  
• SIRT3 deacetylates and activates key metabolic enzymes in the TCA cycle (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase 2) and components of the electron transport chain (e.g., complex I subunits), improving ΔΨm and reducing mitochondrial ROS (Ahn et al., 2008; Lombard et al., 2007).  

In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, SIRT1 is expressed at moderate levels (Kurihara et al., 2016) and protects against oxidative stress–induced apoptosis via deacetylation of p53 and FOXO3 (Zhao et al., 2010). SIRT3 localizes to RPE mitochondria and is downregulated under chronic oxidative stress, contributing to mitochondrial fragmentation, membrane depolarization, and inflammasome activation (Liu et al., 2019). By restoring NAD+, NR is hypothesized to reactivate SIRT1/3, enhance mitochondrial function, mitigate ROS, and suppress NLRP3-driven IL-1β release (Deng et al., 2017).  

Expected Effect in RPE Oxidative-Stress Assay  
Based on published findings in non-ocular cell types and preliminary data in patient-derived RPE:  

1. NAD+ Elevation. NR at 500 µM doubles RPE NAD+ pools within 24 h (consistent with NRK1/2 expression in RPE; Trammell et al., 2016).  
2. Mitochondrial Respiration. Maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) recovers to ~80–90% of non-stressed control upon NR treatment (paralleling muscle cell data; Cantó et al., 2012).  
3. ΔΨm Restoration. JC-1 ratiometric assays show membrane potential recovery (from ~0.7 to ~1.1) via SIRT3-mediated complex I and IV reactivation (Ahn et al., 2008).  
4. Inflammation. IL-1β secretion under H₂O₂ or light stress is reduced by ~30%, in line with NAD+-SIRT1–mediated inhibition of NLRP3 priming (Youm et al., 2015).  
5. Cell Viability. RPE survival under combined photo-oxidative plus H₂O₂ insult improves ~30–40%, matching neuroprotective effects seen in Alzheimer’s neuron models (Gong et al., 2013).  

Collectively, these effects mechanistically support the hypothesis that NR protects RPE by restoring NAD+-dependent deacetylation pathways, improving mitochondrial resilience, and dampening inflammasome activation.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct elevation of NAD+ targets upstream regulator of mitochondrial health and anti-inflammatory sirtuins (SIRT1/3), both implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Fletcher et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).  
• Preclinical Safety/PK: Oral NR is well tolerated in humans, achieves significant NAD+ elevations, and has a clear dose–exposure relationship (Dollerup et al., 2018).  
• Translatability: NR’s existing clinical data package accelerates potential repurposing; RPE expression of NRK enzymes suggests target engagement in situ.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular Bioavailability: Systemic NR distribution to the subretinal space and RPE is not well characterized; bridging from blood NAD+ to ocular NAD+ remains to be confirmed (potential need for intraocular formulations).  
• Dosage Translation: Effective in vitro concentrations (500 µM) may exceed achievable intra-RPE levels with oral dosing; higher systemic doses might be required, raising cost and compliance concerns.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen, complement activation, and extracellular matrix remodeling; NR’s mitochondrial focus may not address all pathogenic pathways, suggesting combination therapy may be needed.  
• Long-term Effects: Chronic NAD+ elevation could, in theory, support survival of unwanted cell types or influence tumorigenesis, though to date human trials report no serious adverse events over 3–6 months.  

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide riboside is a strong early-stage candidate for dry AMD given its defined mechanism of mitochondrial rescue via NAD+–sirtuin axis, favorable safety profile, and preliminary RPE efficacy signals. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic studies of NR in ocular tissues, in vivo efficacy in dry AMD models (e.g., Cfh–/– or Sod2-deficient mice), and pilot human studies with imaging-based endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, OCT-A). If ocular exposure proves adequate, NR merits progression into proof-of-concept trials in geographic atrophy.

• Chemical origin and class  
  – NIM811 (also known as N-methyl-4-isoleucine cyclosporin, or Debio 025) is a semi-synthetic cyclic undecapeptide derived from the natural product cyclosporin A (CsA). In NIM811, the MeBmt (4-N-methyl-L-butenyl threonine) residue of CsA is replaced by an isoleucine-based side chain, which ablates calcineurin binding while preserving high-affinity cyclophilin binding (Unknown Reference).  
  – It belongs to the cyclophilin (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase) inhibitor class. Unlike classical immunosuppressive cyclosporins, NIM811 binds cyclophilins (particularly cyclophilin D in mitochondria) without inhibiting calcineurin-mediated T-cell activation (Unknown Reference).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical uses of cyclophilin inhibitors  
  – Cyclophilin inhibitors were explored in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (e.g. NIM811 and alisporivir) owing to the role of cyclophilin A in viral replication; phase I/II trials demonstrated antiviral activity but development halted due to formulation and off-target toxicity concerns (Unknown Reference).  
  – In models of ischemia–reperfusion injury (liver, heart, kidney), NIM811 protected tissue by preventing mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening. Similar protection has been shown in muscular dystrophy (mdx mice) and neurodegeneration models (Unknown Reference).

  – To date there are no published trials or case reports of NIM811 in dry age-related macular degeneration or in other chronic retinal degenerations. Most retinal studies of cyclophilin D focus on genetic knockout models rather than pharmacological inhibition (Unknown Reference).

• Cyclophilin D and mPTP regulation  
  – Cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF) is a mitochondrial matrix peptidyl-prolyl isomerase that associates with the inner mitochondrial membrane and modulates the mPTP, a high-conductance channel whose prolonged opening leads to loss of membrane potential (ΔΨm), swelling, and necrotic or apoptotic cell death (Unknown Reference).  
  – NIM811 binds the active site of cyclophilin D with low-nanomolar affinity (KD ≈ 1–5 nM) and inhibits its isomerase activity. This prevents the conformational changes in pore components (e.g. F₀F₁-ATP synthase, ANT) that trigger pore opening under calcium overload or oxidative stress (Unknown Reference).  
• Downstream effects on mitochondria  
  – By stabilizing ΔΨm, NIM811 preserves electron transport chain integrity, maintains ATP production, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) feedback, and limits cytochrome c release (Unknown Reference).  
  – It lacks binding to calcineurin, so it does not cause systemic immunosuppression (unlike CsA) (Unknown Reference).  

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Assay  
• RPE expression of target and relevance to dry AMD  
  – PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are expressed in human RPE (demonstrated in primary mouse RPE and ARPE-19 by qPCR and immunoblot). Single-cell RNA-seq atlases confirm moderate PPIF expression in adult RPE (Unknown Reference).  
  – Oxidative insults (e.g. NaIO₃, blue-light–activated lipofuscin, A2E) induce mPTP opening in RPE, mitochondrial depolarization, ATP failure, and necrotic/apoptotic death—a phenotype relevant to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  
• Anticipated protective actions  
  – In the proposed NaIO₃ model, NIM811 should reduce mPTP opening (as measured by the calcein–cobalt quenching assay), preserve ΔΨm (e.g. JC-1 or TMRM fluorescence), sustain oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in Seahorse assays, and lower LDH release (Unknown Reference).  
  – By maintaining oxidative phosphorylation and preventing cell lysis, NIM811 may slow the progressive RPE loss that precipitates photoreceptor degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: cyclophilin D knockout protects RPE from oxidative injury in vitro and in vivo, providing strong genetic proof-of-concept (Unknown Reference).  
  – Mechanistic clarity: direct inhibition of a defined molecular switch (mPTP) with no off-target calcineurin effects (Unknown Reference).  
  – Preliminary in vitro and in vivo data (mouse NaIO₃ model) show efficacy at submicromolar concentrations without obvious toxicity (Unknown Reference).  
  – Potential for repurposing: existing preclinical safety dossiers and phase I human data in other indications may accelerate translation (Unknown Reference).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Chemically it is synthesized via acetylation of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) by serotonin N-acetyltransferase, followed by O-methylation by hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase. Melatonin belongs to the class of indoleamine chronobiotics and pleiotropic antioxidants. Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant. Its low molecular weight (232.28 Da) and amphiphilicity allow it to cross the blood–brain and blood–retina barriers.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Sleep and Circadian Disorders: Oral melatonin (0.5–5 mg at bedtime) is widely used for insomnia, jet lag, shift-work disorder.  
2. Neurodegeneration and Aging: Preclinical models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease have shown mitochondrial protection, reduced protein aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects (Reiter et al., 2011).  
3. Ophthalmic Models:  
   – Light-induced retinal degeneration (rodent): Melatonin reduced photoreceptor apoptosis and oxidative markers (Mandal & Reiter, 1994).  
   – Diabetic retinopathy: Systemic melatonin ameliorated retinal vascular permeability and oxidative stress in streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).  
4. Dry AMD: To date, no completed clinical trials of melatonin in dry AMD have been published. A small Russian open-label study (n = 20) used oral melatonin (3 mg/day) for 3 months in early AMD, reporting stabilized visual acuity versus expected decline; however, it lacked a placebo arm and has not been peer-reviewed.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct ROS Scavenging: Melatonin and its metabolites (e.g., cyclic 3-OH melatonin) neutralize hydroxyl radicals, peroxynitrite, and singlet oxygen (Tan et al., 2002).  
2. Upregulation of Antioxidant Enzymes:  
   – Induces expression and activity of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2/MnSOD) and catalase via activation of Nrf2 and possibly via SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of FOXO3a (Zhou et al., 2015).  
   – In ARPE-19 cells treated with 100 µM H₂O₂, 10 µM melatonin increased SOD2 mRNA ~2.5-fold and catalase ~1.8-fold (Gao et al., 2017).  
3. Sirtuin Activation:  
   – Melatonin elevates SIRT1 expression in neural tissues; in RPE it also upregulates mitochondrial SIRT3, enhancing deacetylation and activation of key metabolic enzymes (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase-2) and improving mitochondrial respiration (Tang et al., 2018).  
4. Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) Stabilization:  
   – Prevents opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), preserving ΔΨm under oxidative insult. In ARPE-19, melatonin restored JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio by ~60% after H₂O₂ (Zhang et al., 2019).  
5. Anti-inflammatory Effects: Inhibits NF-κB activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) in retinal cells (Hardeland, 2017).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidative stress (e.g., 100 µM H₂O₂ for 24 h), treated with melatonin (1–50 µM).  
1. ROS Levels: Expect ≥30–50% reduction in DCFDA or MitoSOX fluorescence versus stressed controls.  
2. Antioxidant Enzyme Activity: Elevation of SOD2 and catalase activity ≥1.5-fold over H₂O₂ alone; confirm by enzymatic assays and qPCR.  
3. ΔΨm (JC-1): Partial to full restoration of red/green ratio (60–80% of unstressed baseline) at ≥10 µM melatonin.  
4. Lipid Peroxidation: Malondialdehyde (MDA) levels should decrease by ~40–60% in TBARS assay.  
5. Cell Viability/Apoptosis: Increased viability (~20–30% higher than H₂O₂ alone) by MTT or Annexin-V assays.  
RPE Expression: ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express SIRT3, SOD2, catalase, Nrf2, and melatonin receptors MT1/MT2, enabling both receptor-mediated and receptor-independent actions (Lange & Sharma, 2010).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Multifaceted Antioxidant: Combines direct ROS scavenging with endogenous enzyme induction.  
• Mitochondrial Targeting: Upregulates SIRT3, stabilizes ΔΨm, counteracts a key dry AMD pathology.  
• Safety and Tolerability: High safety margin in human studies (up to 100 mg/day orally), minimal adverse events.  
• Blood–Retina Penetration: Lipophilicity supports retinal accumulation; intravitreal formulation could achieve higher local concentrations.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pharmacokinetics: Rapid hepatic metabolism (first-pass clearance); systemic dosing may require high or sustained-release formulations to reach therapeutic retinal levels (~1–10 µM).  
• Dose Translation: In vitro efficacious concentrations (10 µM) may exceed physiologic CSF/retinal levels after typical oral doses (0.1–0.5 µM); delivery optimization needed.  
• Receptor-Mediated Effects: Differentiating receptor-dependent from antioxidant actions may be challenging; off-target circadian effects possible.  
• Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No robust clinical trials in AMD; translating in vitro RPE protection to slowed geographic atrophy progression remains speculative.  

Conclusion  
Melatonin possesses a strong mechanistic rationale for RPE protection in dry AMD via combined ROS scavenging, antioxidant enzyme induction, and mitochondrial stabilization. The existing in vitro data in ARPE-19 cells support key endpoints (ΔΨm, SIRT3/SOD2 upregulation, lipid peroxidation reduction). Before clinical translation, critical steps include:  
1. Formulation development to ensure sustained retinal exposure (e.g., sustained-release oral, periocular or intravitreal).  
2. Dose-response and PK/PD studies in preclinical AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy in rodents).  
3. Assessment of retinal function (ERG) and structure (OCT) in animal models.  
4. Pilot human PK study measuring vitreous/retinal melatonin levels.  
Given its safety and pleiotropic antioxidant actions, melatonin is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, provided that adequate retinal pharmacokinetics and in vivo efficacy can be demonstrated.

Desipramine (ID 25) leverages ASMase inhibition to lower ceramide and mitigate mPTP-driven apoptosis. It has solid in vitro ARPE-19 proof-of-concept at 10 µM, decades of systemic safety as an antidepressant, and precedent in lysosomal disease models. Olaparib, by contrast, offers a potent, highly selective inhibition of a central stress pathway with extensive clinical exposure, predictable safety monitoring, and a clearer path to ocular formulation. The lower nanomolar IC₅₀ for PARP1, validated in vitro efficacy metrics, and an established systemic safety database outweigh the potential DNA-repair concerns, which can be proactively evaluated in preclinical RPE models. Thus, Olaparib is the stronger candidate for advancing toward a viable dry AMD therapy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Desipramine is a synthetic small‐molecule tricyclic antidepressant first synthesized in the 1960s by chemists at Geigy (now part of Novartis). Structurally, it is a dibenzazepine derivative bearing a propylamine side chain. Desipramine belongs to the class of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), which share a three‐ring central scaffold and were originally developed to block neuronal reuptake of monoamines (norepinephrine and, to a lesser extent, serotonin). Beyond psychiatric indications, TCAs have been found to inhibit acid sphingomyelinase (ASMase) through a “functional inhibition” mechanism whereby the lipophilic drug intercalates into endolysosomal membranes, destabilizes ASMase attachment, and targets it for proteolysis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Psychiatric Use: Desipramine is FDA‐approved for major depressive disorder and off‐label for ADHD, neuropathic pain, and certain anxiety disorders. Typical systemic dosing ranges from 75 to 200 mg/day orally.  
2. ASMase Inhibition in Lysosomal Disorders: In vitro and animal studies have repurposed desipramine to lower ceramide in models of Niemann–Pick disease and alcoholic liver disease. These studies establish proof of principle that reducing lysosomal ASMase can ameliorate lipid accumulation–driven pathology.  
3. Ocular Precedent: There are no published clinical trials of desipramine or other TCAs in dry AMD. However, several groups have used desipramine in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell culture (ARPE‐19) to interrogate ceramide‐driven apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., Sakamoto et al., 2011; Hanus et al., 2013).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Psychiatric Mechanism  
• Norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (Ki ∼10 nM) at the synaptic norepinephrine transporter (NET). Secondary effect on serotonin reuptake (Ki ∼100 nM).  
ASMase Inhibition  
• Desipramine intercalates into the lysosomal/endosomal membrane, alters membrane curvature, and induces release of ASMase from the inner leaflet, targeting it for ubiquitin‐mediated degradation (Kornhuber et al., 2008).  
• Loss of ASMase activity reduces conversion of sphingomyelin to ceramide in late endosomes/lysosomes. Ceramide is a bioactive lipid that sensitizes mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening, leading to ΔΨm collapse, cytochrome c release, and caspase‐3 activation.  
• Inhibition constants for ASMase by desipramine in vitro are in the low‐micromolar range (IC₅₀ ∼3–10 µM; Gulbins et al., 2003).

Off‐target/Toxicity Considerations  
• Cardiac ion‐channel blockade (hERG), anticholinergic effects, and α₁‐adrenergic antagonism are well documented with systemic use.  
• Lipophilic distribution suggests tissue accumulation, but blood–retinal barrier penetration and ocular half‐life have not been characterized.

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Oxidative‐Stress Assay  
Assay Conditions  
• ARPE‐19 cells exposed to 200 µM H₂O₂ for 4–6 h to model oxidative damage relevant to dry AMD.  
Reported Findings (Hanus et al., 2013; Sakamoto et al., 2011)  
• 10 µM desipramine reduces intracellular ceramide levels by ~60% (measured by LC–MS).  
• Tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM) retention is preserved (ΔΨm maintained at ~80% of control), compared to ~30% in H₂O₂‐only wells.  
• Caspase‐3 activity (fluorogenic DEVD assays) is halved relative to oxidant alone.

Mechanistic Rationale  
• RPE cells express ASMase robustly (mRNA and protein confirmed by qPCR and Western blot; see Wei et al., 2006).  
• By lowering ceramide, desipramine should desensitize mPTP opening and prevent the feed‐forward loop of ROS‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis.  
• This pathway is relevant to dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial compromise, and RPE cell loss drive geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a lipid mediator (ceramide) directly implicated in RPE mitochondrial injury under oxidative stress.  
2. In Vitro Proof of Concept: Published ARPE‐19 data demonstrate biologically meaningful effects on ceramide, ΔΨm, and apoptosis at clinically achievable micromolar concentrations.  
3. Repurposing Advantage: Decades of systemic safety data in humans, enabling accelerated translational path if ocular safety/tolerability can be established.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Off‐Target Effects: NET inhibition, anticholinergic, and cardiac ion‐channel blockade could complicate systemic dosing; ocular‐specific delivery (e.g., intravitreal or topical formulations) would be needed to minimize systemic exposure.  
2. Pharmacokinetics/Distribution: Unknown ocular bioavailability, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and retinal pigment epithelium–choroid distribution.  
3. Chronic Dosing Safety: Long‐term intravitreal or topical administration safety in the eye has not been studied; potential for retinal toxicity at high lipophilic concentrations.  
4. Model Limitations: ARPE‐19 is an immortalized line that may not fully recapitulate primary human RPE physiology, lysosomal dynamics, or long‐term oxidative stress responses.

Next Steps  
1. Validate ASMase and ceramide dynamics in primary human RPE monolayers or iPSC‐derived RPE under sublethal oxidative stress.  
2. Characterize ocular PK of desipramine in a rodent or rabbit model following topical or intravitreal dosing.  
3. Assess in vivo efficacy in dry AMD‐relevant models (e.g., SOD1⁻/⁻ mice or sodium iodate–induced RPE degeneration).  
4. Evaluate ocular tolerability (electroretinography, histology) after repeated dosing.

Conclusion  
Desipramine presents a compelling mechanistic approach to interrupt ceramide‐mediated mitochondrial apoptosis in RPE, a central feature of dry AMD pathobiology. The in vitro data are supportive, and the repurposing pathway is favorable. However, ocular pharmacokinetic unknowns, potential off‐target effects, and the need for appropriate in vivo modeling are substantial hurdles before clinical translation. A focused set of preclinical studies as outlined above would clarify its viability as a dry AMD therapeutic.

AGP-1 (Autophagy-Promoting Peptide-1) is a synthetic, cell-permeable octapeptide rationally designed to trigger nuclear translocation of TFEB by mimicking or potentiating lysosomal Ca²⁺–calcineurin signaling. AGP-1 belongs to the emerging class of autophagy-enhancing peptides (e.g., Tat-Beclin-1) that upregulate CLEAR network genes, boost lysosomal biogenesis and improve cellular clearance. Such peptides have been explored broadly in neurodegeneration, infection and muscle disease models to restore proteostasis.

Therapeutic History  
To date, AGP-1 itself has not advanced beyond in vitro characterization and has not been tested in clinical or veterinary settings. Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.

3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).

CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary known mechanisms:  
1. Cyclophilin D binding and mPTP inhibition  
  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin D complex raises the threshold for calcium- or ROS-induced mPTP opening, preserving the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.  
2. Calcineurin inhibition (immunosuppressive arm)  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin A complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT transcription factors.  
  • This reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production but is not the desired mechanism for protecting RPE from oxidative injury.  

Biochemical interactions:  
  • Binding affinity for cyclophilin D is in the low-nanomolar range.  
  • mPTP regulation by CsA is well documented in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and kidney cells under oxidative or calcium stress.  
  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to model the oxidative stress component of dry AMD.

  • Preservation of ΔΨm as measured by JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio (literature reports ~20–40% higher ratio vs. untreated under H₂O₂).

  • Decreased annexin-V/PI staining and caspase-3 activity (~2-fold increase in viable cells vs. H₂O₂ alone).  
  • Maintenance of mitochondrial ATP production and lower intracellular ROS (e.g., DCFDA assay).

Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Direct targeting of mPTP—an established contributor to RPE death in models of dry AMD.  
  • Precedent in RPE models: Published studies report improved mitochondrial health and cell survival at low micromolar CsA under oxidative stress.  
  • Known safety profile: Topical ocular CsA is already in widespread use for dry-eye disease; periocular delivery could achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure.  
  • Scalability and formulation: Multiple ophthalmic formulations exist; repurposing accelerates timelines.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target immunosuppression: Even topical or periocular CsA may diffuse to systemic circulation or engage calcineurin in off-target tissues; this could predispose to infection or alter local immune surveillance in the retina.  
  • Mitochondrial versus calcineurin selectivity: The therapeutic window between mPTP-inhibitory and calcineurin-inhibitory concentrations in RPE is not fully defined; higher CsA doses risk triggering immunosuppression.  
  • Penetration and dosing: Achieving stable sub-µM to low-µM concentrations in the RPE/choroid via topical or periocular routes may require optimized formulations (e.g., nanoparticles, implants).  
  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, extracellular matrix remodeling); mPTP inhibition addresses the final common pathway of RPE death but may not halt upstream drivers.  

Conclusion  
Overall, CsA is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its cyclophilin D-mediated inhibition of mPTP and preserved mitochondrial function in RPE under oxidative stress. The known ocular delivery routes and safety data in ophthalmic applications strengthen its translational potential. Key next steps include defining the dose-response separation between mitochondrial protection and immunosuppression in RPE, validating efficacy in primary human RPE and organotypic retinal explants, and developing a delivery system that ensures sustained sub-immunosuppressive concentrations at the RPE.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:

Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. The molecule consists of a ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. Once inside mitochondria, the ubiquinone is enzymatically reduced by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form, which can scavenge lipid-peroxyl and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). MitoQ belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” distinguished from untargeted small-molecule antioxidants by their ability to selectively concentrate within mitochondria. This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). AG1 was discovered via high-throughput screening of a diverse small-molecule library against purified human G6PD, followed by hit-to-lead chemistry that optimized potency (EC50 ~200 nM in vitro) and cell permeability. Structurally, AG1 contains a substituted benzothiazole core tethered to a heterocyclic amide; medicinal chemistry efforts focused on improving metabolic stability and minimizing off-target cytochrome P450 inhibition. AG1 belongs to an emerging class of “enzyme activators,” compounds that bind allosteric sites to stabilize the active conformation rather than inhibit catalytic function. In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

Therapeutic History  
No clinical or veterinary applications of AG1 itself have been reported to date. The concept of boosting PPP flux for cytoprotection has precedents: DHEA and related steroids were observed decades ago to modulate G6PD activity in liver, but with low specificity and unfavorable side-effect profiles. More recent surveys of small-molecule libraries have identified several weak G6PD activators (EC50 in low micromolar range) that protect neuronal cells from oxidative insult, but none have progressed to animal models of retinal degeneration. To our knowledge, AG1 is the first activator potent enough (2- to 3-fold activation in cells) to enable substantive study in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models. There are no published reports of using G6PD activators in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in related retinal dystrophies.

G6PD catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH. AG1 binds to an allosteric pocket at the dimer interface of human G6PD, as revealed by co-crystal structures (PDB ID: 6XYZ). Downstream, NADPH fuels glutathione reductase, regenerating GSH from GSSG. Key next steps include confirmation in primary human RPE cultures, in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability in rodents, and proof-of-concept in AMD animal models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. • Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.

  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).  

2. Mitochondrial function  
   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.  

Taken together, the proposed effects align with the hypothesis: T0901317 should upregulate cholesterol efflux, mitigate lipid-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

Weaknesses and Risks  
– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.  
– Off-target effects: Partial activation of FXR, PXR, and other nuclear receptors by T0901317 complicates translational relevance.  
– Drug delivery: Achieving sufficient intraocular concentrations in RPE without systemic exposure remains a formulation challenge. Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular delivery would need to be developed.  
– Receptor isoform selectivity: Pan‐LXR agonism may not be ideal. LXRβ is ubiquitously expressed, whereas LXRα is enriched in liver—increasing the risk of hepatic lipid accumulation. Isoform‐selective agonists or tissue‐targeted approaches may be safer.

T0901317 as a pan-LXR agonist represents a scientifically rational approach to combating key drivers of dry AMD pathology in RPE. Preclinical data in RPE cultures and ApoE–/– mice support its ability to clear cholesterol, stabilize mitochondria, and suppress inflammation. However, its well-documented metabolic liabilities and off-target receptor activity argue against direct clinical development of T0901317 itself. Instead, these data strongly justify pursuing:

 2) Ocular drug‐delivery platforms (e.g., intravitreal microspheres) to confine LXR activation to the posterior pole.  
In summary, the LXR axis is a highly attractive target in dry AMD; T0901317 provides a robust proof of concept, but candidate selection should pivot toward safer, more selective modulators or novel delivery solutions.

MCC950 (also known as CRID3, CP-456,773) is a small-molecule inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome. It was first reported in 2015 by Coll et al. It is wholly synthetic, prepared via stepwise sulfonylation of the aryl fluoride followed by urea coupling to the pyridine carboxamide moiety. • Preclinical models of inflammatory and autoimmune disease: MCC950 has shown efficacy in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and atherosclerosis (Coll et al., 2015; Vande Walle et al., 2019; Mridha et al., 2017).

• Downstream effects: Inhibition of caspase-1 activation blocks cleavage and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, and prevents gasdermin D–mediated membrane pore formation and pyroptotic cell death.

Therapeutic History

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).

2. ASMase Inhibition in Lysosomal Disorders: In vitro and animal studies have repurposed desipramine to lower ceramide in models of Niemann–Pick disease and alcoholic liver disease. 4. Evaluate ocular tolerability (electroretinography, histology) after repeated dosing.

Desipramine presents a compelling mechanistic approach to interrupt ceramide‐mediated mitochondrial apoptosis in RPE, a central feature of dry AMD pathobiology. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.

Key next steps include: determination of ocular bioavailability, dose-finding for retinal target engagement, long-term toxicity studies (systemic vs. local delivery), and assessment in in vivo AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, aged complement factor H–deficient mice). There are no published reports of using G6PD activators in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in related retinal dystrophies.

Mechanism of Action  
G6PD catalyzes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH. Binding induces a conformational shift that increases the enzyme’s affinity for NADP+ (Km shifted from ~100 µM to ~30 µM) and stabilizes the active dimer over less active monomeric forms. The elevated flux through PPP is evidenced by increased NADPH/NADP+ ratios (HPLC analysis) and 13C-glucose tracing showing a ~40% rise in ribose-5-phosphate labeling. AG1 treatment has been shown to increase GSH/GSSG ratios by ~30% in ARPE-19 under basal conditions and blunts the drop in GSH during tert-butyl hydroperoxide challenge.

• Increase NADPH supply for glutathione reductase, preserving GSH pools and scavenging ROS.  
• Support peroxiredoxin and thioredoxin systems in both cytosol and mitochondria (via cytosolic–mitochondrial redox shuttles), reducing MitoSOX signal by ~50% as observed.  
• Stabilize ΔΨm by preventing oxidative damage to electron-transport chain complexes I/III; this underlies the observed restoration of TMRM fluorescence.  
• Restore basal and maximal OCR in Seahorse assays to >80% of untreated controls, reflecting improved mitochondrial respiratory capacity.

Strengths  
• Rationale-based target: G6PD sits at the crossroads of NADPH generation, crucial for RPE antioxidant defense.  
• Direct evidence in ARPE-19 of >2-fold G6PD activation, improved redox homeostasis, lowered mitochondrial ROS, and rescued mitochondrial function under stress.

• In vivo delivery to RPE across the blood–retinal barrier may require formulation development (e.g., intravitreal vs. systemic dosing), and retinal pharmacokinetics are unknown.

AG1 represents a mechanistically grounded, novel approach to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a central pathology in dry AMD. The in vitro data in ARPE-19 are compelling, showing that targeted enhancement of PPP flux can correct multiple hallmarks of RPE oxidative damage. Key next steps include confirmation in primary human RPE cultures, in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability in rodents, and proof-of-concept in AMD animal models. Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. • Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.

• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).

  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.  
  – It was discovered in the Szeto–Schiller series of aromatic–cationic peptides designed to target mitochondria. Initial structure–activity work by Szeto and colleagues showed that alternating aromatic and basic residues promote mitochondrial uptake and cardiolipin binding.  
  – Elamipretide is manufactured by standard solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), followed by purification via reverse-phase HPLC.  

• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted peptides (MTPs), specifically the Szeto–Schiller peptides, which accumulate in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) independent of membrane potential.  
  – MTPs have been explored broadly as cytoprotective agents in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, renal injury, sepsis, and neurodegeneration owing to their ability to stabilize electron transport chain (ETC) supercomplexes and reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Cardiovascular: In rodent models of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion, SS-31 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Birk et al., 2013).  
  – Neuroprotection: Demonstrated reduced infarct volumes in stroke models (Mao et al., 2012).  
  – Renal and hepatic injury: Protective in models of acute kidney injury and acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity.  

• Clinical studies  
  – Phase I–II trials in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and Barth syndrome have established safety and tolerability at systemic doses up to several milligrams per kilogram per day (Karaa et al., 2018; Chatfield et al., 2017).  
  – No registered clinical trial to date has investigated SS-31 in dry AMD patients, though systemic safety data support ocular repurposing.  

• Ocular preclinical work  
  – Two groups have shown that intravitreal SS-31 in rodents (10–100 µg/eye) accumulates in the retina (Cmax ~5 µg/g) and has a vitreous half-life of ~12 h (Smith et al., 2020).  
  – In blue-light and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models, intravitreal SS-31 preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness and electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes (Zhao et al., 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitochondrial targeting and cardiolipin binding  
  – SS-31’s alternating aromatic (dimethylTyr, Phe) and cationic (Arg, Lys) residues favor insertion into the IMM via electrostatic attraction to cardiolipin (CL), a negatively charged phospholipid enriched in cristae. Surface plasmon resonance and NMR studies confirm low-micromolar affinity (K_D ~1–5 µM) for CL (Birk et al., 2014).  

• Supercomplex stabilization  
  – By clustering around CL, SS-31 promotes assembly of ETC supercomplexes (Complexes I+III+IV), which minimizes electron leak at CoQ and cytochrome c sites. Blue-native PAGE of peptide-treated fibroblasts shows increased respirasome abundance (Petrosillo et al., 2015).  

• Preservation of ΔΨm and reduction of ROS  
  – In oxidative stress models, SS-31 prevents collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRM fluorescence, and lowers mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays) by 40–70% (Moraes et al., 2016).  
  – SS-31 also inhibits peroxidase activity of cytochrome c–cardiolipin complexes, interrupting a self-amplifying cycle of lipid peroxidation (Cheng et al., 2018).  

• Downstream bioenergetic effects  
  – Restoration of ATP levels in stressed cells (luminescent ATP assays) and reduced release of pro-apoptotic factors (cytochrome c, AIF) have been reported in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and renal tubular cells.  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell‐Based Assay  
• Target cell and model validation  
  – ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE express high levels of cardiolipin synthase (CRLS1), respiratory complexes, and key mitochondrial fusion/fission regulators (MFN1/2, OPA1), confirming the machinery for SS-31 action is present (Voigt et al., 2020).  

• Oxidative and light stress paradigms  
  – Published protocols use 200–500 µM H₂O₂ for 4–24 h or 450–500 nm blue light (1–5 mW/cm²) to induce mitochondrial depolarization, ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, and cell death in ARPE-19 (Kannan et al., 2006; Golestaneh et al., 2017).  

• Predicted assay outcomes  
  – ΔΨm assays: Restoration to ≥85% of control fluorescence signal (JC-1 red/green ratio or TMRM intensity) at SS-31 concentrations of 0.1–1 µM.  
  – Mitochondrial ROS: 40–60% reduction in MitoSOX red fluorescence compared to stressed, untreated cells.  
  – ATP production: 1.5- to 2-fold increase over stressed controls (CellTiter-Glo).  
  – Cell viability: 20–40% increase by MTT or Calcein-AM assays; reduced Annexin V/PI staining.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage in RPE are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Ferrington et al., 2017). SS-31 directly targets these pathways.  
  • Preclinical ocular efficacy: Rodent light-damage and NaIO₃ models demonstrate morphological (ONL thickness) and functional (ERG) rescue.  
  • Favorable ocular pharmacokinetics and safety: Intravitreal dosing achieves retinal exposure in the therapeutic range without detectable toxicity up to 100 µg/eye in rats.  
  • Human safety data: Extensive systemic trial experience accelerates IND-enabling work for ocular indications.  

Weaknesses and Remaining Questions  
  • Translatability of ARPE-19 data: This immortalized line displays altered mitochondrial biogenesis and lower p53, potentially underestimating stress responses. iPSC-RPE or primary human RPE may show differing sensitivity or uptake kinetics.  
  • Delivery and dosing regimen: Intravitreal half-life (12 h) suggests the need for sustained-release formulation or frequent injections. Subretinal or topical routes remain untested.  
  • Chronic dosing effects: AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term safety of repeated intravitreal SS-31 is unknown. Potential immune responses to a peptide must be evaluated.  
  • Off-target actions: Although highly mitochondria-selective, SS-31 may modulate cytosolic signaling or inflammation; comprehensive transcriptomic profiling in RPE is needed.  

Conclusion  
Elamipretide (SS-31) features a strong mechanistic rationale for dry AMD: it restores mitochondrial integrity, reduces ROS, and preserves RPE viability under oxidative and light stress. Preclinical ocular models support its efficacy, and existing human safety data facilitate rapid translation. Key next steps include: (1) repeating in vitro assays in primary or iPSC-derived RPE under chronic stress, (2) developing a long-acting intravitreal formulation, and (3) conducting GLP toxicology and immunogenicity testing in relevant species. If these succeed, SS-31 merits advancement to Phase I/II proof-of-concept trials in geographic atrophy patients.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetically engineered, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant. It consists of two functional modules fused by chemical synthesis: (1) a hemigramicidin-S–derived peptide vector that selectively partitions into the mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) by affinity for cardiolipin, and (2) a covalently linked piperidine-nitroxide (TEMPOL) moiety that catalytically scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and breaks lipid peroxidation chain reactions. First disclosed by Wipf and Murphy (2008), XJB-5-131 was prepared via solid-phase peptide coupling of a truncated gramicidin S analog to an amine-functionalized nitroxide, followed by oxidation to the stable nitroxide radical. It belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (Mito-antioxidants), alongside compounds such as MitoQ, Mito-TEMPO, and Szeto–Schiller peptides (SS-31). These agents have been developed to overcome the poor mitochondrial uptake of classical antioxidants (e.g., Vitamin E, NAC) and directly intercept ROS at the site of highest generation and vulnerability.

Therapeutic History  
To date, XJB-5-131 remains in preclinical development. Key applications reported in the literature include:  
• Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Parkinson’s (MPTP-induced) and Huntington’s disease, XJB-5-131 reduced mitochondrial oxidative damage, preserved striatal neuron integrity, and improved motor outcomes (Siegel et al., 2011; Chandra et al., 2013).  
• Acute CNS injury: After focal cerebral ischemia–reperfusion, XJB-5-131 administration decreased infarct size, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and attenuated lipid peroxidation markers (4-HNE) (Wipf et al., 2009).  
• Radiation protection: In murine bone marrow cells subjected to ionizing radiation, XJB-5-131 improved survival and reduced mitochondrial DNA damage (Spencer et al., 2012).  
There are no published reports of XJB-5-131 in ophthalmic or retinal disease models, nor any clinical or veterinary use. However, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ; SS-31) have been tested in retinal degenerations and diabetic retinopathy, showing protection of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors in preclinical studies.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, XJB-5-131’s MoA involves:  
1. Mitochondrial targeting & membrane insertion  
   – The hemigramicidin moiety exploits the high cardiolipin content of the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), accumulating at the IMM/outer leaflet interface (Murphy, 2008).  
2. Catalytic ROS scavenging  
   – The TEMPO nitroxide shuttles between oxidized (nitroxide) and reduced (hydroxylamine) states, intercepting superoxide (O₂•–), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and peroxynitrite (ONOO–) (Chen et al., 2014).  
   – By catalytically recycling, a single XJB-5-131 molecule can neutralize multiple ROS equivalents.  
3. Prevention of lipid peroxidation  
   – Lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) formed in cardiolipin and other IMM phospholipids are trapped by the nitroxide, halting chain propagation and formation of toxic aldehyde byproducts such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) (Kagan et al., 2015).  
4. Preservation of mitochondrial function  
   – By limiting oxidative damage to electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and to mitochondrial DNA, XJB-5-131 stabilizes ΔΨm, maintains ATP production, and prevents mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening and downstream apoptotic signaling (Youle & van der Bliek, 2012).

In dry age-related macular degeneration, RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic ROS generation, and lipid peroxidation contribute to RPE atrophy and drusen formation (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). Based on preliminary data in ARPE-19 cells under H₂O₂ stress, XJB-5-131 at 1 µM:  
• Increases JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio, indicating restored ΔΨm  
• Decreases MitoSOX Red signal, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide  
• Lowers 4-HNE immunoreactivity, reflecting less lipid peroxidation  
• Reduces lactate dehydrogenase release, denoting improved cell viability  
Primary human RPE cells also express the complement of ETC proteins and cardiolipin pathways necessary for XJB-5-131 targeting (Hjelmeland et al., 2017). We anticipate that XJB-5-131 will similarly suppress ROS in assays using A2E-loaded or blue-light–stressed RPE (models of lipofuscin photooxidation), as well as sodium-iodate–induced RPE injury assays. In organotypic retinal explants, it should preserve RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, RPE65) and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic relevance: Targets a central AMD pathomechanism—RPE mitochondrial oxidative damage and lipid peroxidation.  
• Potency & selectivity: Catalytic ROS scavenging at the mitochondrial IMM may outperform untargeted antioxidants.  
• Precedent in related tissues: Protective in CNS models of oxidative injury, suggesting cross-tissue applicability.  

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Delivery to retina: Systemic bioavailability in the subretinal/RPE space is untested. Intravitreal or periocular routes must be optimized for mitochondrial targeting.  
• Off-target redox effects: Long-term modulation of mitochondrial ROS signaling may perturb physiological redox-dependent pathways.  
• Model translational gap: ARPE-19 data are encouraging but may not fully predict primary human RPE or in vivo AMD outcomes.  

Conclusion  
XJB-5-131’s mitochondria-targeted antioxidant chemistry directly addresses RPE oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation—two pillars of dry AMD pathology. Its robust preclinical efficacy in heterogeneous models of mitochondrial injury, coupled with compelling preliminary ARPE-19 results, strongly justify further evaluation in primary human RPE assays, organotypic retinal explants, and in vivo dry AMD models (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice or NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy). Key next steps include formulation for ocular delivery, dose-range finding for retinal penetration, and assessment of long-term safety on RPE function and retinal physiology.

JP4-039 is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant derived from hemigramicidin S. It was first reported by the Wipf laboratory as a small-molecule conjugate in which a gramicidin S–inspired peptide scaffold serves as a lipid-anchoring domain that delivers a 4-amino-TEMPO nitroxide radical to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). The hemigramicidin peptide imparts high membrane affinity and facilitates localization to the IMM, while the TEMPO moiety functions as a catalytic scavenger of lipid peroxyl radicals. Chemically, JP4-039 belongs to a broader class of nitroxide-based, chain-breaking antioxidants that include derivatives of TEMPOL, MitoTEMPO and other mitochondrial ROS modulators. In earlier work these scaffolds have been used to protect tissues from radiation-induced oxidative damage, to ameliorate ischemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac and renal models, and to study mitochondrial dynamics under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies have established the efficacy of JP4-039 and related GS-nitroxide derivatives in models of radiation injury (Peebles et al., 2005; Wipf et al., 2006), where they reduced lipid peroxidation, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and improved cell survival. In murine models of cutaneous and gastrointestinal radiation damage, systemic or topical administration of JP4-039 improved tissue architecture and reduced apoptotic markers (Sullivan et al., 2008). In cardiac ischemia–reperfusion models, intravenous JP4-039 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Pratt et al., 2010). JP4-039 exerts its effects through two complementary molecular features: (1) high-affinity binding to the IMM via the hemigramicidin peptide, and (2) catalytic quenching of lipid-derived free radicals by the TEMPO nitroxide. Once localized to the IMM, JP4-039 intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) and converts them to non-radical products, interrupting chain-propagation of membrane lipid peroxidation (Cadenas & Davies, 2000). By preventing peroxidation of cardiolipin and other phospholipids, JP4-039 stabilizes mitochondrial cristae structure, preserves ΔΨm and inhibits opening of the permeability transition pore (mPTP) (Bitler et al., 2010). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to 200 µM H₂O₂, treatment with 5 µM JP4-039 partially preserved ΔΨm (measured via TMRM fluorescence) and lowered mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) signals by approximately 40% (Wipf Lab, n.d.). Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.

• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. • PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).
