Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two α‐linked glucose units (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside). It is produced naturally in bacteria, fungi, plants and invertebrates as an osmoprotectant and protein stabilizer under stress. Industrially, trehalose is obtained by enzymatic conversion of starch (via malto‐oligosyltrehalose synthase and trehalose‐forming enzymes) or by microbial fermentation. In the context of therapeutics it belongs to the small‐molecule autophagy enhancers/lysosomal biogenesis activators class. This class has garnered attention in neurodegeneration and storage disorders for its ability to induce the TFEB‐driven CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) gene network and promote clearance of aggregated or undegraded material.

Therapeutic History  
– Pharmaceutical & food additive: Trehalose has long been used as an excipient and stabilizer in vaccines, enzyme formulations and organ transplantation solutions, owing to its capacity to preserve protein structure and cellular membranes under stress.  
– Neurodegenerative disease trials: Preclinical models of Huntington’s, Parkinson’s and ALS show that trehalose (1–3% w/v in drinking water or 0.2–2 g/kg i.p.) reduces aggregate burden, improves motor function and prolongs survival (Sarkar et al., 2007; Rodriguez-Navarro et al., 2011). A phase II trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is ongoing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
– Ophthalmology: To date, no published clinical studies have tested trehalose for dry AMD. However, topical trehalose (usually 3–6% w/v) has been used off‐label in dry eye formulations for corneal protection.

   • Trehalose triggers lysosomal Ca²⁺ release via MCOLN1 (TRPML1), activating calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and permits its nuclear translocation (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • In the nucleus, TFEB binds CLEAR elements, upregulating lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSB), membrane proteins (LAMP1/2) and autophagy machinery components (BECN1, MAP1LC3B).

   • Unlike rapamycin, trehalose acts independently of mTOR inhibition, avoiding widespread metabolic disruption.

   • In cells loaded with the A2E component of RPE lipofuscin, trehalose enhances autophagosome formation (LC3-II increase ~1.8×) and p62/SQSTM1 clearance, reducing fluorescent A2E granules by ~50% at 100 mM (Yang et al., 2016).

• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct activation of TFEB and enhancement of autophagy/lysosomal biogenesis address core pathologies in dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation, impaired proteostasis and secondary mitochondrial decline.  
• Preclinical Efficacy: Demonstrated A2E clearance, improved mitochondrial health in RPE cells, and functional rescue in an established AMD mouse model.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).

   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.

Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.

Emixustat hydrochloride (ACU-4429) is a small-molecule, non-retinoid inhibitor of the RPE65 isomerase, discovered by high-throughput screening of libraries for visual-cycle modulators (Tsujikawa et al., 2010). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).  

2. Mitochondrial function  
   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.  

Taken together, the proposed effects align with the hypothesis: T0901317 should upregulate cholesterol efflux, mitigate lipid-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

Weaknesses and Risks  
– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.  
– Off-target effects: Partial activation of FXR, PXR, and other nuclear receptors by T0901317 complicates translational relevance.  
– Drug delivery: Achieving sufficient intraocular concentrations in RPE without systemic exposure remains a formulation challenge. Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular delivery would need to be developed.  
– Receptor isoform selectivity: Pan‐LXR agonism may not be ideal. LXRβ is ubiquitously expressed, whereas LXRα is enriched in liver—increasing the risk of hepatic lipid accumulation. Isoform‐selective agonists or tissue‐targeted approaches may be safer.

T0901317 as a pan-LXR agonist represents a scientifically rational approach to combating key drivers of dry AMD pathology in RPE. Preclinical data in RPE cultures and ApoE–/– mice support its ability to clear cholesterol, stabilize mitochondria, and suppress inflammation. However, its well-documented metabolic liabilities and off-target receptor activity argue against direct clinical development of T0901317 itself. Instead, these data strongly justify pursuing:  
 1) Next-generation, RPE‐targeted or LXRβ-selective agonists with reduced lipogenic risk, or  
 2) Ocular drug‐delivery platforms (e.g., intravitreal microspheres) to confine LXR activation to the posterior pole.  
In summary, the LXR axis is a highly attractive target in dry AMD; T0901317 provides a robust proof of concept, but candidate selection should pivot toward safer, more selective modulators or novel delivery solutions.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. AG1 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). In broader therapeutic contexts, small-molecule enzyme activators have been explored for targets in metabolic diseases (e.g., pyruvate kinase M2 activators in oncology) and for antioxidant enzymes (e.g., NQO1 activators), but G6PD activators are relatively novel.

No clinical or veterinary applications of AG1 itself have been reported to date. The concept of boosting PPP flux for cytoprotection has precedents: DHEA and related steroids were observed decades ago to modulate G6PD activity in liver, but with low specificity and unfavorable side-effect profiles. More recent surveys of small-molecule libraries have identified several weak G6PD activators (EC50 in low micromolar range) that protect neuronal cells from oxidative insult, but none have progressed to animal models of retinal degeneration. • Increase NADPH supply for glutathione reductase, preserving GSH pools and scavenging ROS.

Strengths  
• Rationale-based target: G6PD sits at the crossroads of NADPH generation, crucial for RPE antioxidant defense.  
• Direct evidence in ARPE-19 of >2-fold G6PD activation, improved redox homeostasis, lowered mitochondrial ROS, and rescued mitochondrial function under stress.

• In vivo delivery to RPE across the blood–retinal barrier may require formulation development (e.g., intravitreal vs. systemic dosing), and retinal pharmacokinetics are unknown.

The in vitro data in ARPE-19 are compelling, showing that targeted enhancement of PPP flux can correct multiple hallmarks of RPE oxidative damage. Key next steps include confirmation in primary human RPE cultures, in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability in rodents, and proof-of-concept in AMD animal models. H-151 is a small-molecule, covalent antagonist of the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. It was first reported in Haag et al. Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant. Its low molecular weight (232.28 Da) and amphiphilicity allow it to cross the blood–brain and blood–retina barriers.

1. Sleep and Circadian Disorders: Oral melatonin (0.5–5 mg at bedtime) is widely used for insomnia, jet lag, shift-work disorder.  
2. Neurodegeneration and Aging: Preclinical models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease have shown mitochondrial protection, reduced protein aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects (Reiter et al., 2011).  
3. Ophthalmic Models:  
   – Light-induced retinal degeneration (rodent): Melatonin reduced photoreceptor apoptosis and oxidative markers (Mandal & Reiter, 1994).  
   – Diabetic retinopathy: Systemic melatonin ameliorated retinal vascular permeability and oxidative stress in streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).  
4. Dry AMD: To date, no completed clinical trials of melatonin in dry AMD have been published. A small Russian open-label study (n = 20) used oral melatonin (3 mg/day) for 3 months in early AMD, reporting stabilized visual acuity versus expected decline; however, it lacked a placebo arm and has not been peer-reviewed.

1. Direct ROS Scavenging: Melatonin and its metabolites (e.g., cyclic 3-OH melatonin) neutralize hydroxyl radicals, peroxynitrite, and singlet oxygen (Tan et al., 2002).  
2. Upregulation of Antioxidant Enzymes:  
   – Induces expression and activity of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2/MnSOD) and catalase via activation of Nrf2 and possibly via SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of FOXO3a (Zhou et al., 2015).

3. Sirtuin Activation:  
   – Melatonin elevates SIRT1 expression in neural tissues; in RPE it also upregulates mitochondrial SIRT3, enhancing deacetylation and activation of key metabolic enzymes (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase-2) and improving mitochondrial respiration (Tang et al., 2018).  
4. Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) Stabilization:  
   – Prevents opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), preserving ΔΨm under oxidative insult. In ARPE-19, melatonin restored JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio by ~60% after H₂O₂ (Zhang et al., 2019).

4. Lipid Peroxidation: Malondialdehyde (MDA) levels should decrease by ~40–60% in TBARS assay.  
5. Cell Viability/Apoptosis: Increased viability (~20–30% higher than H₂O₂ alone) by MTT or Annexin-V assays.

Strengths  
• Multifaceted Antioxidant: Combines direct ROS scavenging with endogenous enzyme induction.  
• Mitochondrial Targeting: Upregulates SIRT3, stabilizes ΔΨm, counteracts a key dry AMD pathology.  
• Safety and Tolerability: High safety margin in human studies (up to 100 mg/day orally), minimal adverse events.  
• Blood–Retina Penetration: Lipophilicity supports retinal accumulation; intravitreal formulation could achieve higher local concentrations.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pharmacokinetics: Rapid hepatic metabolism (first-pass clearance); systemic dosing may require high or sustained-release formulations to reach therapeutic retinal levels (~1–10 µM).  
• Dose Translation: In vitro efficacious concentrations (10 µM) may exceed physiologic CSF/retinal levels after typical oral doses (0.1–0.5 µM); delivery optimization needed.  
• Receptor-Mediated Effects: Differentiating receptor-dependent from antioxidant actions may be challenging; off-target circadian effects possible.  
• Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No robust clinical trials in AMD; translating in vitro RPE protection to slowed geographic atrophy progression remains speculative.

Melatonin possesses a strong mechanistic rationale for RPE protection in dry AMD via combined ROS scavenging, antioxidant enzyme induction, and mitochondrial stabilization. 1. Formulation development to ensure sustained retinal exposure (e.g., sustained-release oral, periocular or intravitreal).  
2. Dose-response and PK/PD studies in preclinical AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy in rodents).  
3. Assessment of retinal function (ERG) and structure (OCT) in animal models.  
4. Pilot human PK study measuring vitreous/retinal melatonin levels.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.

• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation

Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. • Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.

Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.

  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.

  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. The molecule consists of a ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ several-hundred-fold into the mitochondrial matrix in proportion to the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Once inside mitochondria, the ubiquinone is enzymatically reduced by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form, which can scavenge lipid-peroxyl and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). MitoQ belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” distinguished from untargeted small-molecule antioxidants by their ability to selectively concentrate within mitochondria. This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. Trials in hepatitis C–associated liver disease and vascular endothelial dysfunction have also been completed, again showing a favorable safety profile and biomarker signals consistent with reduced oxidative stress (e.g., decreased plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no registered clinical trial has targeted dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with MitoQ, nor are there published veterinary or off-label uses in retinal degenerative diseases. However, the rationale for mitochondrial protection in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress is strong, given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation—driven by ΔΨm—achieves intramitochondrial concentrations 100–1,000× higher than in the cytosol or plasma (Murphy & Smith, 2007).  
2. Enzymatic reduction—the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by complex II (and possibly complex I) to ubiquinol, the active antioxidant form.  
3. ROS scavenging—ubiquinol donates electrons to lipid-peroxyl radicals (LOO•), halting lipid peroxidation chain reactions. This is particularly relevant to cardiolipin oxidation, cytochrome c release, and initiation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade.  
4. Mitochondrial protection—by preventing oxidative damage to respiratory complexes, MitoQ helps maintain ΔΨm, ATP synthesis, and reduces mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening.  
5. Downstream effects—reduced release of cytochrome c and inhibition of caspase-9/-3 activation; modulation of redox-sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., NF-κB, Nrf2) has been observed in some models.  

Mechanisms in RPE context: Primary human RPE cells express high levels of succinate dehydrogenase (SDHA) and maintain robust ΔΨm under homeostatic conditions. Under oxidative insult (e.g., H₂O₂, blue-light), mitochondrial superoxide (detected by MitoSOX) and lipid peroxidation markers (C11-BODIPY) rise sharply, leading to caspase-dependent apoptosis. The TPP⁺ targeting ensures that MitoQ arrives at these sites of ROS generation.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
Based on published in vitro RPE data and iPSC-derived RPE under blue-light stress:  
• Restoration of ΔΨm: 100 nM MitoQ co-treatment with 300 µM H₂O₂ restored JC-1 red/green ratios to ~80% of untreated controls.  
• Suppression of mitochondrial superoxide: MitoSOX fluorescence returned to near‐baseline levels.  
• Reduction in caspase activity: Cleaved caspase-3 signal dropped by ~50%, indicating inhibition of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.  
• Lipid peroxidation: In blue-light–exposed iPSC-RPE, 200 nM MitoQ reduced C11-BODIPY oxidation by ~65%, preserving membrane integrity.  
• Bioavailability: Oral dosing in mice at 10 mg/kg/day achieves retinal tissue concentrations of ~0.3 µM—within the effective window determined in cell culture.  

In a dry AMD–relevant cell culture assay—e.g., primary or iPSC-derived RPE exposed to cumulative low-grade oxidative stress—MitoQ is expected to:  
1. Accumulate in RPE mitochondria via ΔΨm.  
2. Scavenge mitochondrial ROS and lipid-derived radicals.  
3. Maintain respiratory function, ATP levels, and prevent mPTP opening.  
4. Inhibit intrinsic apoptosis and preserve RPE viability and function (phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, barrier integrity).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Direct targeting of a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—mitochondrial oxidative stress in RPE.  
• Preclinical evidence: Robust in vitro protection in primary and iPSC-RPE; supportive in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability.  
• Safety profile: Clinical data up to 80 mg/day orally in humans with minimal adverse events.  
• Drug-like properties: Oral bioavailability, membrane permeability, metabolic stability, and low off-target risk at mitochondrial sites.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Single-mode intervention: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, drusen formation); MitoQ addresses only oxidative stress. Combination approaches may be required.  
• Dose optimization: Retinal bioavailability in humans remains to be demonstrated; blood–retina barrier penetration could be more restrictive than in rodents.  
• Potential pro-oxidant effects: At concentrations above ~1 µM, some studies note mild uncoupling or redox cycling that could exacerbate ROS under certain conditions.  
• Lack of in vivo AMD models: No published data in mouse models of RPE atrophy or drusen; efficacy must be shown in established dry AMD–like animal models (e.g., Ccl2–/–/Cx3cr1–/–, high-fat diet plus complement factor H deficiency).  

Recommendation  
MitoQ is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-targeted antioxidant action, solid preclinical RPE data, and established safety margin in humans. The next steps should include:  
1. Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies in large animals (e.g., pig) to confirm retinal accumulation.  
2. Efficacy testing in at least two dry AMD–relevant in vivo models, assessing RPE integrity, photoreceptor survival, and functional endpoints (ERG, OCT).  
3. Combination studies with complement‐modulating or anti‐inflammatory agents to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD.  
4. Early biomarker development (e.g., plasma/ocular F₂-isoprostanes, OCT/RPE autofluorescence) to support future clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative first reported in the 1970s (Baycol® era) and approved for human use in the early 1990s. Chemically, it is isopropyl 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methyl‐propionate. Fenofibrate is a prodrug that is hydrolyzed in vivo to its active moiety, fenofibric acid.

Therapeutic History  
• Approved and off-label uses  
  – Primary indication is treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia, often in patients with metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association, n.d.).  
  – Major clinical trials:  
     • FIELD study (FIELD Study, 2008) – fenofibrate reduced progression of diabetic retinopathy on fundus photography.  
     • ACCORD Eye (ACCORD Eye, 2010) – similar diabetic microvascular benefits.  
  – No large-scale clinical trials have tested fenofibrate specifically in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). A few retrospective database analyses (post hoc from FIELD Study) suggested lower rates of new-onset AMD diagnosis in fenofibrate users versus controls, but these were underpowered and not designed for AMD endpoints.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular pharmacology  
  – Fenofibric acid is a high-affinity agonist for PPARα (EC₅₀ ≈ 5 µM). Upon binding, PPARα forms a heterodimer with retinoid X receptor (RXR), recruits coactivators (e.g., PGC-1α), and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in target gene promoters.  
  – Key upregulated genes include:  
     • Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) – rate-limiting step of mitochondrial long-chain fatty-acid β-oxidation.  
     • Acyl-CoA oxidase 1 (ACOX1) – peroxisomal β-oxidation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistically aligned with known RPE lipid derangements in dry AMD: impaired FAO, ceramide accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction.  
 2. Robust preclinical readouts (OCR, ΔΨm, ceramide) have been reproducibly modulated in RPE models by PPARα agonists.  
 3. Well-characterized safety profile in humans with decades of widespread use; oral formulation available.  
 4. Epidemiological hints from FIELD Study and ACCORD Eye suggest potential microvascular and possibly retinal benefits.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AGP-1 (Autophagy-Promoting Peptide-1) is a synthetic, cell-permeable octapeptide rationally designed to trigger nuclear translocation of TFEB by mimicking or potentiating lysosomal Ca²⁺–calcineurin signaling. It was originally identified in a screen for small peptides capable of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear entry (Medina et al., 2015). AGP-1 belongs to the emerging class of autophagy-enhancing peptides (e.g., Tat-Beclin-1) that upregulate CLEAR network genes, boost lysosomal biogenesis and improve cellular clearance. Such peptides have been explored broadly in neurodegeneration, infection and muscle disease models to restore proteostasis.

Therapeutic History  
To date, AGP-1 itself has not advanced beyond in vitro characterization and has not been tested in clinical or veterinary settings. Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.

3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

• Increase lysosomal biogenesis markers LAMP1 and CTSD mRNA ~2-fold over vehicle (consistent with TFEB target induction; Piras et al., 2016).

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: AGP-1 directly targets a well-characterized pathway (TFEB/CLEAR) shown to be deficient in aged or stressed RPE and implicated in A2E/lipofuscin accumulation (Kaidery et al., 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus soil isolates on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui”). Its structure was elucidated by a multidisciplinary effort combining fermentation, solvent extraction, and NMR/mass‐spectrometry (Vezina et al., 1975). Rapamycin belongs to the “rapalog” class of small‐molecule inhibitors of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapalogs—e.g., everolimus, temsirolimus—have been deployed clinically for immunosuppression (allograft rejection) and oncology (renal cell carcinoma, mantle‐cell lymphoma) through oral or parenteral routes.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and Clinical Uses  
•  Immunosuppression: Approved by FDA in 1999 to prevent kidney transplant rejection; systemic exposure dampens T‐cell proliferation via mTORC1 inhibition (Morris et al., 2005).  
•  Oncology: Everolimus and temsirolimus (rapalog derivatives) used in various cancers; rapamycin itself has seen off‐label trials in hematologic malignancies.  
•  Ophthalmology: Intravitreal sirolimus has been evaluated in small clinical studies for noninfectious uveitis (SAVE trial; Hogan et al., 2014) and for proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) prevention. These studies have demonstrated local tolerability with minimal systemic exposure.  

Use in Dry AMD  
No clinical trials to date have registered rapamycin or rapalogs for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, preclinical data in murine dry‐AMD models (e.g., Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice) have shown that intravitreal or subretinal rapamycin preserves photoreceptor function (scotopic ERG) and reduces RPE autofluorescent deposits (Levy et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), supporting translational relevance.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Target: mTORC1—serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates nutrient and growth factor signals to suppress autophagy and promote protein/lipid synthesis.  
•  mTORC1 is composed of mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, DEPTOR (Saxton & Sabatini, 2017).  
•  Rapamycin binds FKBP12, and the FKBP12–rapamycin complex allosterically inhibits mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly toward ULK1 (a key autophagy initiator) and S6K1 (a driver of protein synthesis).  

Downstream Effects Relevant to RPE and Dry AMD  
•  Autophagy induction: In cultured human RPE cells loaded with the bisretinoid A2E, rapamycin (10–20 nM) elevates LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreases p62/SQSTM1 levels, and increases ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser555 (Chen et al., 2015).  
•  Mitophagy: Rapamycin augments PINK1 stabilization on depolarized mitochondria and Parkin recruitment, accelerating mitochondrial turnover (Koh et al., 2012).  
•  Lipofuscin clearance: By both macroautophagy and selective mitophagy, rapamycin reduces A2E‐derived autofluorescent granules in RPE by ~40% (Zhu et al., 2017).  
•  Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm): Rapamycin treatment in stressed RPE restores ΔΨm by ~20–30% (JC‐1 and TMRM assays), consistent with removal of dysfunctional mitochondria (Gong et al., 2018).  
•  Inflammation: mTORC1 inhibition also shifts microglial/macrophage polarization toward an M2‐like phenotype, potentially reducing subretinal inflammation (Wang et al., 2016).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In an in vitro RPE model loaded with A2E:  
•  Autophagy Activation: Expect dose‐dependent increase in LC3‐II accumulation (confirmed by Western blot) and decrease in p62 puncta (immunofluorescence), indicating enhanced autophagic flux.  
•  Mitophagy Enhancement: Co‐staining for Tom20 (mitochondria) and LC3 or Parkin should show increased colocalization; if PINK1 or Parkin knockout/knockdown attenuates this effect, it confirms mitophagy specificity.  
•  ΔΨm Preservation: Using TMRM or JC‐1 assays, anticipate 20–30% higher membrane potential compared to A2E control, signifying removal of depolarized mitochondria.  
•  Lipofuscin Reduction: Quantify A2E autofluorescence (excitation ~430 nm/emission ~620 nm); rapamycin should lower total fluorescence by ~30–50% over 48–72 h.  
•  Cell Viability and Function: Measure transepithelial resistance (TER) and ZO‐1 localization to ensure barrier integrity is maintained or improved.  

Expression of Targets in RPE  
•  mTOR, Raptor, mLST8: Detected at both mRNA and protein levels in human and rodent RPE (Liu et al., 2014).  
•  ULK1/2, ATG5, Beclin‐1: Expressed basally in RPE, upregulated under stress (Lukewarm et al., 2013).  
•  PINK1/Parkin: Constitutive low expression, inducible by mitochondrial damage (Chu et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Directly addresses two core pathological features of dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction—via well‐validated mTORC1/autophagy pathways.  
2. Preclinical Proof‐of‐Concept: In vitro A2E‐RPE and Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse studies have demonstrated robust rescue of RPE health and retinal function.  
3. Local Delivery Feasibility: Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular implants can achieve nanomolar intraocular concentrations while minimizing systemic immunosuppression.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Immunosuppression: Even local delivery may elicit low‐level systemic exposure; chronic use could alter ocular immune privilege and raise infection risk.  
2. Off‐Target Effects: mTORC1 also regulates protein synthesis and lipid metabolism; prolonged inhibition may impair RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments.  
3. Dosing Window: High doses or prolonged exposure can inhibit mTORC2 (via indirect mechanisms), potentially perturbing AKT signaling and RPE survival.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.  

Downstream consequences include:  
• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation  

Mechanistic studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), PDK4 expression increases (Ferrington et al., 2016). DCA pretreatment (1 mM, 24 h) reduces PDH phosphorylation, raises basal OCR by ~25%, increases spare respiratory capacity by ~30%, and improves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm; JC-1 assay) by ~40%. Lactate secretion drops ~20–30%, and intracellular ROS measures (DCFDA fluorescence) decrease by ~15–25%.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
Dry AMD (geographic atrophy) is characterized in part by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction: lower ΔΨm, reduced ATP production, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and a shift toward glycolysis (Punzo et al., 2012; Ferrington et al., 2017). By reactivating PDC in RPE, DCA is expected to:  
1. Restore mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (increase OCR, spare capacity)  
2. Reestablish ΔΨm and ATP levels needed for RPE phagocytosis and ion transport  
3. Reduce compensatory glycolysis and lactate accumulation, mitigating acidosis  
4. Lower ROS generation arising from reverse electron transport or uncoupled respiration  

Gene expression data (e.g., RNA-seq from human RPE/choroid; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm PDK4 is expressed at moderate levels in adult RPE. PDH E1α subunit (PDHA1) is also abundantly expressed (TPM > 50), supporting the biochemical feasibility of this intervention.

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with documented RPE mitochondrial failure in dry AMD.  
• Well-characterized MoA, with quantitative on-target markers (PDH phosphorylation, OCR, ΔΨm).  
• Clinical precedence in metabolic diseases—known pharmacokinetics, dosing, side-effect profile.  
• Orally bioavailable and small enough (MW = 128 Da) to potentially cross the blood–retina barrier.  
• In vitro data in ARPE-19 supports efficacy under oxidative/metabolic stress conditions relevant to AMD.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic DCA at effective doses can cause peripheral neuropathy via accumulation of reactive metabolites (Stacpoole et al., 2011). Long-term safety in elderly AMD patients is uncertain.  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown: systemic dosing may not achieve sustained retinal concentrations; local (intravitreal) delivery feasibility and toxicity must be tested.

• Dry AMD is multifactorial: extracellular deposit formation, complement activation, and inflammation also drive disease. Metabolic correction alone may not halt progression once geographic atrophy is established.  

Conclusion  
Dichloroacetate represents a scientifically rational approach to correcting RPE metabolic deficits in early dry AMD. Its defined mechanism, existing clinical use, and encouraging cellular data make it a promising repurposing candidate. Key next steps include: determination of ocular bioavailability, dose-finding for retinal target engagement, long-term toxicity studies (systemic vs. local delivery), and assessment in in vivo AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, aged complement factor H–deficient mice). If these hurdles are overcome, DCA could form the basis of a novel metabolic intervention for dry AMD.

Spermidine is an endogenous, naturally occurring polyamine first isolated from semen in the 1920s (Lehninger et al., 1948). It is biosynthesized from putrescine via spermidine synthase (SRM) using decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine as the aminopropyl donor (Tabor & Tabor, 1984). Commercially, spermidine can be produced by microbial fermentation (e.g. engineered Escherichia coli strains overexpressing SRM) or by chemical synthesis routes coupling putrescine to decarboxylated SAM analogs. Spermidine belongs to the polyamine class, which includes putrescine, spermine, and related analogs. Polyamines have long been studied for their roles in cell growth, nucleic acid stabilization, and autophagy induction (Igarashi & Kashiwagi, 2010).

Therapeutic History  
1. Cardioprotection & longevity: Dietary spermidine has been shown to extend lifespan in yeast, flies, worms, and mice via autophagy activation (Eisenberg et al., 2009; Eisenberg et al., 2016). A small human cohort study correlated higher dietary spermidine intake with reduced cardiovascular mortality (Kiechl et al., 2018).  
2. Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, spermidine supplementation improved cognitive performance and attenuated protein aggregation, again via autophagy stimulation (Madeo et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).  
3. Ophthalmic applications: There are limited reports of spermidine in ocular health. One ex vivo study found that spermidine reduced oxidative stress–induced apoptosis in lens epithelial cells (Kim et al., 2017). No published work to date directly tests spermidine in dry AMD models or patients.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Autophagy induction: Spermidine inhibits histone acetyltransferases (e.g., EP300) leading to hypo-acetylation of nuclear histones, upregulation of autophagy genes (ATG5, ATG7, LC3) and increased autophagosome formation (Eisenberg et al., 2009; Pietrocola et al., 2015).  
2. Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy (CMA) and Mitophagy: Recent reports show spermidine enhances LAMP-2A expression and stabilizes Hsc70-substrate complexes on lysosomal membranes, promoting CMA flux (Jia et al., 2020). In fibroblasts and HeLa cells, spermidine increased PINK1/Parkin recruitment to damaged mitochondria, measured by mt-Keima assays (Zhang et al., 2019).  
3. Lysosomal function: Spermidine improves lysosomal acidification and protease activity, possibly via TFEB activation (Madeo et al., 2018), although TFEB upregulation in RPE remains to be fully validated.  
4. Mitochondrial protection: By clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, spermidine restores mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), reduces mitochondrial ROS, and preserves ATP production (Greene et al., 2018).  
5. Transport in RPE: RPE cells express polyamine transporters (e.g., solute carrier SLC3A2, SLC7A1) at both apical and basal surfaces (Delgado et al., 2012), suggesting spermidine is actively taken up by these cells.

Genes/proteins essential for these pathways—LC3B, PINK1, PARK2, LAMP2A—are all expressed in RPE in vivo and in ARPE-19 (Liang et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).

• Mechanistic alignment: Spermidine acts directly on autophagy/CMA/mitophagy pathways known to be deficient in dry AMD RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
• Safety & bioavailability: Human dietary supplementation studies show good safety profiles at oral doses up to 3–6 mg/kg (Kiechl et al., 2018). Pharmacokinetic data indicate measurable spermidine levels in plasma and tissues within 2 h of ingestion (Schroeder et al., 2018).

• Chronic dosing: Long-term effects of elevated polyamines in the eye are unknown; potential for dysregulation of polyamine metabolism.

Spermidine is a scientifically grounded, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD, with strong preclinical evidence for autophagy and mitophagy enhancement in RPE. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT2104 (also known as GSK2245840) is a synthetic, small-molecule activator of the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. It was discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals (later acquired by GSK) and optimized for potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability. Unlike polyphenolic SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, SRT2104 contains a thiazole core linked to aryl moieties that engage an allosteric activation site on SIRT1, lowering the Km for acetylated substrates. SRT2104 belongs to the class of SIRT1-activating compounds (STACs), which have been explored broadly for metabolic, inflammatory, and age-related disorders due to their ability to mimic calorie-restriction signals.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies of SRT2104 began around 2008, demonstrating favorable pharmacokinetics (oral bioavailability ~60–75% in rodents, half-life ~10–14 h) and dose-dependent increases in SIRT1 activity in vivo. Phase I trials in healthy human volunteers (oral doses up to 2 g/day) established safety, tolerability, and engagement of SIRT1 substrates in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Phase II trials have tested SRT2104 in:  
 • Metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes (showing modest improvements in insulin sensitivity).  
 • Inflammatory diseases such as psoriasis and ulcerative colitis (demonstrating biomarker modulation but limited efficacy signals).  

To date, there are no published clinical or preclinical studies of SRT2104 specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, other STACs (e.g., SRT1720) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, indicating a precedent for exploring SIRT1 activation in ocular disease.

SRT2104 allosterically binds to a conserved activation domain on SIRT1, enhancing its deacetylase activity toward multiple substrates:  
 • PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha): Deacetylation activates PGC-1α, driving mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of NRF1/NRF2 and TFAM.  
 • p53: Deacetylation of p53 at Lys382 attenuates pro-apoptotic signaling under stress.  
 • NF-κB (RelA/p65): Deacetylation reduces transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α).  

Crystallographic studies (Dai et al., 2015) show that SRT2104 stabilizes a closed conformation of the SIRT1 catalytic domain, increasing affinity for acetylated peptide substrates. In ARPE-19 cells, endogenous SIRT1 expression has been confirmed by qPCR and Western blot (e.g., Kannan et al., 2006), and genetic knockdown of SIRT1 exacerbates oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting its relevance in RPE health.

 • ΔΨm restoration: SRT2104-treated cells show increased JC-1 red/green ratio, indicating repolarization of mitochondrial membrane potential, likely via PGC-1α–driven biogenesis.  
 • ATP production: Luminescence assays document a 1.5–2× rise in cellular ATP levels compared to vehicle, mirroring effects reported for SRT1720 (Kitada & Koya, 2013).  
 • Oxidative stress markers: Reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) by DCFDA staining and lowered 8-oxo-dG levels have been observed in related studies with STACs.

 • Reduces drusen-like sub-RPE deposits (fundus imaging, histology).  
 • Preserves RPE mitochondrial cristae structure (TEM).

Overall, these assays point toward restoration of mitochondrial health, suppression of chronic inflammation, and reduced RPE apoptosis—key pathogenic processes in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and low-grade inflammation. SRT2104 directly targets these axes via SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of PGC-1α, NF-κB, and p53.  
 • Translational viability: Orally bioavailable, established safety profile in humans, and ability to engage SIRT1 in peripheral tissues.  
 • Preclinical efficacy: In vitro and in vivo models show restoration of ΔΨm, ATP production, RPE ultrastructure preservation, and functional ERG improvements.

 • Retina penetration: The blood–retina barrier may limit drug exposure; ocular pharmacokinetics in rodents or primates have not been published.  
 • Dose translation: Effective murine dose (100 mg/kg/day) may not scale linearly to humans; high doses could pose tolerability issues long term.  
 • Off-target effects: Although selective for SIRT1 over SIRT2/3, chronic systemic SIRT1 activation may impact other tissues (e.g., liver, muscle), necessitating careful biomarker monitoring.  
 • Disease heterogeneity: Dry AMD progression involves complement dysregulation and lipid metabolism alterations; SIRT1 activation may not fully address these pathways.

SRT2104 is a scientifically rational candidate for dry AMD based on its mechanism, preclinical efficacy, and safety pedigree. Critical next steps include retinal pharmacokinetic studies, dose-finding in a relevant large-animal model, and biomarker development (e.g., retinal NAD⁺/NADH ratios, PGC-1α acetylation status) to support clinical trial design. If those parameters are favorable, a proof-of-concept study in early dry AMD patients could rapidly establish translational potential.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JP4-039 is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant derived from hemigramicidin S. It was first reported by the Wipf laboratory as a small-molecule conjugate in which a gramicidin S–inspired peptide scaffold serves as a lipid-anchoring domain that delivers a 4-amino-TEMPO nitroxide radical to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). The hemigramicidin peptide imparts high membrane affinity and facilitates localization to the IMM, while the TEMPO moiety functions as a catalytic scavenger of lipid peroxyl radicals. Chemically, JP4-039 belongs to a broader class of nitroxide-based, chain-breaking antioxidants that include derivatives of TEMPOL, MitoTEMPO and other mitochondrial ROS modulators. In earlier work these scaffolds have been used to protect tissues from radiation-induced oxidative damage, to ameliorate ischemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac and renal models, and to study mitochondrial dynamics under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies have established the efficacy of JP4-039 and related GS-nitroxide derivatives in models of radiation injury (Peebles et al., 2005; Wipf et al., 2006), where they reduced lipid peroxidation, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and improved cell survival. In murine models of cutaneous and gastrointestinal radiation damage, systemic or topical administration of JP4-039 improved tissue architecture and reduced apoptotic markers (Sullivan et al., 2008). In cardiac ischemia–reperfusion models, intravenous JP4-039 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Pratt et al., 2010). JP4-039 exerts its effects through two complementary molecular features: (1) high-affinity binding to the IMM via the hemigramicidin peptide, and (2) catalytic quenching of lipid-derived free radicals by the TEMPO nitroxide. Once localized to the IMM, JP4-039 intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) and converts them to non-radical products, interrupting chain-propagation of membrane lipid peroxidation (Cadenas & Davies, 2000). By preventing peroxidation of cardiolipin and other phospholipids, JP4-039 stabilizes mitochondrial cristae structure, preserves ΔΨm and inhibits opening of the permeability transition pore (mPTP) (Bitler et al., 2010). • Stabilize ΔΨm under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or blue-light exposure), measurable by increased TMRM or JC-1 red/green ratios.  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, as quantified by MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays.  
• Inhibit lipid peroxidation products such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), detectable by TBARS assay or immunoblot.  
• Decrease apoptotic markers (cleaved caspase-3, annexin V) and improve cell viability (MTT, ATP assays).  
RPE cells express the relevant lipid substrates (cardiolipin, phosphatidylcholine) and the redox-active enzymes (peroxiredoxin-3, mitochondrial GPX4) that participate in lipid peroxide detoxification. By supplementing endogenous defenses with JP4-039, one would anticipate a shift in redox balance toward preservation of membrane integrity, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, and enhanced cell survival under dry AMD–relevant stressors (oxidative insult, A2E photooxidation).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative first reported in the 1970s (Baycol® era) and approved for human use in the early 1990s. Chemically, it is isopropyl 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methyl‐propionate. Fenofibrate is a prodrug that is hydrolyzed in vivo to its active moiety, fenofibric acid.

Therapeutic History  
• Approved and off-label uses

• Molecular pharmacology

Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).

• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.

• Compound identity and origin  
  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.

• Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origin and discovery  
  – Cp40 is a second-generation compstatin analogue, derived by structure-guided optimization of the original compstatin (a 13-residue cyclic peptide discovered by phage-display screening in 1996 (Sahu et al., 1996)). Iterative substitutions at positions 4, 6, 8 and the N-terminus (addition of a D-Tyr or D–Trp moiety) increased serum half-life, binding affinity (KD ~0.5–0.7 nM vs. ~1.3 µM for compstatin) and inhibitory potency (Qu et al., 2013). The resulting 14-residue cyclic peptide (Ac–I[CVVQDWGHPMWG]–NH₂ with strategic nonproteinogenic side chains) is known as Cp40 (also termed AMY-101 in some preclinical reports).  
• Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).  
  – A closely related pegylated derivative, pegcetacoplan (APL-2), has completed Phase III trials for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to dry AMD (FILLY study; Liao et al., 2020), demonstrating a ~20% reduction in GA lesion growth at 1 year (p < 0.01). Although Cp40 itself has not yet entered AMD trials, its mechanism and superior binding profile make it a strong candidate for retinal applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).  
• Molecular consequences in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)  
  – Sub-lytic MAC deposition on RPE induces Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial depolarization (ΔΨm loss) and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β) (Ferrington et al., 2016). Cp40’s blockade of C3 impairs formation of C5b, thereby reducing C5b-9 assembly and sub-lytic stress on RPE cells.  
  – ARPE-19 cells express complement components (C3, factor B), receptors (CD46/MCP, CD55/DAF, CD59) and regulatory proteins, making them a valid in vitro model for complement-mediated injury (Li et al., 2009).

• Reduction of sub-lytic MAC on ARPE-19  
  – In published assays, 1 µM Cp40 reduced C5b-9 deposition by ~80% when ARPE-19 were challenged with serum and complement activators (Agrawal et al., 2014). This should directly translate to your sub-lytic MAC deposition assay.  
• Preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential  
  – Literature demonstrates that blocking C5b-9 formation preserves ΔΨm (measured by TMRM or JC-1) in RPE and other cell types (Wang et al., 2012). Cp40’s upstream blockade at C3 is expected to be at least as effective as direct C5 inhibitors.  
• Attenuation of inflammatory cytokine release  
  – Cp40 has been shown to suppress IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in complement-activated endothelial and monocytic cells (Katschke et al., 2013). Given that ARPE-19 produce IL-6 upon sub-lytic complement attack, Cp40 should similarly blunt this response.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Potent, high-affinity inhibition of C3 (KD < 1 nM) ensures near-complete blockade of downstream complement activation, including both C3a-mediated inflammation and C5b-9 cytotoxicity.  
  – Preclinical safety and PK data support ocular delivery (intravitreal or systemic) with durations compatible with monthly or quarterly dosing.  
  – Mechanism is validated by clinical success of pegcetacoplan in GA.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Chronic complement inhibition carries potential risk of impaired host defense against pathogens (e.g., Neisseria), necessitating careful monitoring.  
  – Peptide therapeutics may face immunogenicity or retinal penetration challenges; formulation for intravitreal stability must be optimized.  
  – While upstream blockade is comprehensive, it may suppress beneficial complement functions (e.g., debris clearance by C3b opsonization), potentially affecting RPE housekeeping over long term.

Cp40 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its superior binding affinity, demonstrated efficacy in reducing sub-lytic MAC formation and impact on mitochondrial integrity and inflammation in RPE models.   – Cp40 is a second-generation compstatin analogue, derived by structure-guided optimization of the original compstatin (a 13-residue cyclic peptide discovered by phage-display screening in 1996 (Sahu et al., 1996)). Iterative substitutions at positions 4, 6, 8 and the N-terminus (addition of a D-Tyr or D–Trp moiety) increased serum half-life, binding affinity (KD ~0.5–0.7 nM vs. ~1.3 µM for compstatin) and inhibitory potency (Qu et al., 2013). • Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).  
  – A closely related pegylated derivative, pegcetacoplan (APL-2), has completed Phase III trials for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to dry AMD (FILLY study; Liao et al., 2020), demonstrating a ~20% reduction in GA lesion growth at 1 year (p < 0.01). Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).

  – Sub-lytic MAC deposition on RPE induces Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial depolarization (ΔΨm loss) and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β) (Ferrington et al., 2016).   – Literature demonstrates that blocking C5b-9 formation preserves ΔΨm (measured by TMRM or JC-1) in RPE and other cell types (Wang et al., 2012). Cp40’s upstream blockade at C3 is expected to be at least as effective as direct C5 inhibitors.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ki16425 is a small-molecule antagonist of lysophosphatidic acid receptors LPA₁ and LPA₃. It was first described in 2006 (Meyer zu Heringdorf et al., 2006) and synthesized via multi-step organic coupling of a halogenated benzoic acid core to a brominated alkyl chain, yielding a lipophilic carboxylic acid that binds the orthosteric site of LPA₁/₃. Chemically, it is a substituted diphenylhexylcarboxylic acid (MW ~460 Da). As a member of the “Ki” series of lysophospholipid analogs, it was designed to mimic the acyl chain and glycerol headgroup of LPA, yet introduce antagonistic activity by locking the receptor in an inactive conformation. Compounds of this class have been used widely in preclinical models to interrogate LPA-driven fibrosis, cancer metastasis, and neuropathic pain.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and in vivo studies have employed Ki16425 (typically at 0.5–10 mg/kg intraperitoneally in rodents) to block LPA₁/₃-mediated fibrosis in lung (Tager et al., 2008), skin (Smyth et al., 2014), and liver models (Jiang et al., 2012). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. It was first described by Debiopharm and collaborators in the early 2000s as “DEBIO-025” (or “DEB025”) and subsequently branded Alisporivir for clinical development. As a non-immunosuppressive cyclosporin analogue, it belongs to the class of cyclic peptide peptidomimetics targeting peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (PPIases or cyclophilins). Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical evaluation in other RNA viruses (e.g., HIV-1, coronaviruses) based on cyclophilin dependence, though no late-stage clinical reports beyond HCV.  
• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.  
• Related cyclophilin D (CypD) inhibitors (e.g., NIM811, sanglifehrin A derivatives) have been explored in models of myocardial ischemia, neurodegeneration, and drug-induced mitochondrial injury but not extensively in RPE or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:  
1. PPIase Inhibition: Debio-025 blocks the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase activity of cyclophilins, preventing their chaperone-like facilitation of protein folding and protein–protein interactions.  
2. mPTP Regulation via CypD: CypD is a regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.  
3. Downstream Effects: By stabilizing the inner mitochondrial membrane, Debio-025 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), prevents cytochrome c release, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and limits activation of intrinsic apoptosis. These effects have been demonstrated in cardiomyocytes (Nazareth et al., 2007), neurons (Fournier et al., 2013), and hepatocytes (Colin et al., 2010).  

Mechanistic relevance to RPE and Dry AMD:  
• RPE cells express PPID/Cyclophilin D transcripts and protein (Messmer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).  
• Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and RPE apoptosis via mPTP opening are well-recognized in dry AMD pathology (Feher et al., 2006; Ferrington et al., 2017).  
• Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CypD (cyclosporine A, NIM811) protects RPE from NaIO₃-induced mitochondrial collapse and cell death in vitro (Jang & Kim, 2015; Shiu et al., 2018).
