Assay Components: primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cultures treated with Debio-025, with readouts including:  
• Calcein–cobalt quenching assay of mPTP opening (Nicholls & Crompton, 1980): Debio-025 should reduce cobalt-mediated calcein leakage upon oxidative or Ca^2+ stress, indicating pore inhibition.  
• ΔΨm measurement (e.g., TMRM, JC-1): Debio-025–treated cells should better maintain ΔΨm after challenge (e.g., H₂O₂, NaIO₃), reflecting preserved mitochondrial integrity.  
• ROS assays (e.g., MitoSOX): Lower mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in Debio-025 groups.  
• Apoptosis markers (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation): Reduced induction upon stress.  

Mechanistic Rationale: Debio-025’s high affinity for CypD in mitochondria will raise the threshold for stress-induced mPTP opening in RPE, halting the cascade of ΔΨm collapse, ROS amplification, and apoptotic signaling known to contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2017; Kowalczuk et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with established AMD pathology: targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE is strongly validated.  
• Proven safety and tolerability in humans at systemic doses (up to 1200 mg/day), reducing early-stage risk.  
• Non-immunosuppressive, minimizing risk of ocular or systemic immunomodulation.  
• Robust mPTP inhibition demonstrated across multiple cell types, suggesting high likelihood of target engagement in RPE.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the subretinal space; intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations will require development and safety evaluation.  
• Off-target cyclophilin inhibition (e.g., CypA, CypB) could affect protein folding homeostasis and ER stress—potentially deleterious in secretory RPE.

• Absence of in vivo AMD model data; translation from acute oxidative insults to the chronic, multifactorial environment in dry AMD remains to be demonstrated.

Debio-025 is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its well-defined CypD-dependent mPTP inhibition, favorable human safety profile, and mechanistic fit with RPE mitochondrial pathology. Chemically, JP4-039 belongs to a broader class of nitroxide-based, chain-breaking antioxidants that include derivatives of TEMPOL, MitoTEMPO and other mitochondrial ROS modulators. In earlier work these scaffolds have been used to protect tissues from radiation-induced oxidative damage, to ameliorate ischemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac and renal models, and to study mitochondrial dynamics under oxidative stress.

Biochemical and preclinical studies have established the efficacy of JP4-039 and related GS-nitroxide derivatives in models of radiation injury (Peebles et al., 2005; Wipf et al., 2006), where they reduced lipid peroxidation, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and improved cell survival. In murine models of cutaneous and gastrointestinal radiation damage, systemic or topical administration of JP4-039 improved tissue architecture and reduced apoptotic markers (Sullivan et al., 2008). In cardiac ischemia–reperfusion models, intravenous JP4-039 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Pratt et al., 2010). To date, no clinical trials of JP4-039 have been reported in humans, and there are no published studies of JP4-039 specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, its mechanism—mitochondrial lipid peroxidation inhibition—addresses a key pathogenic axis in RPE atrophy that is shared with other age-related neurodegenerative conditions.

JP4-039 exerts its effects through two complementary molecular features: (1) high-affinity binding to the IMM via the hemigramicidin peptide, and (2) catalytic quenching of lipid-derived free radicals by the TEMPO nitroxide. Once localized to the IMM, JP4-039 intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) and converts them to non-radical products, interrupting chain-propagation of membrane lipid peroxidation (Cadenas & Davies, 2000). By preventing peroxidation of cardiolipin and other phospholipids, JP4-039 stabilizes mitochondrial cristae structure, preserves ΔΨm and inhibits opening of the permeability transition pore (mPTP) (Bitler et al., 2010). • Stabilize ΔΨm under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or blue-light exposure), measurable by increased TMRM or JC-1 red/green ratios.  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, as quantified by MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays.  
• Inhibit lipid peroxidation products such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), detectable by TBARS assay or immunoblot.  
• Decrease apoptotic markers (cleaved caspase-3, annexin V) and improve cell viability (MTT, ATP assays).  
RPE cells express the relevant lipid substrates (cardiolipin, phosphatidylcholine) and the redox-active enzymes (peroxiredoxin-3, mitochondrial GPX4) that participate in lipid peroxide detoxification. Strengths  
• Targeted mechanism directly addresses mitochondrial lipid peroxidation, a well-documented contributor to RPE damage in dry AMD (Karunadharma et al., 2010).  
• Proven ability to stabilize ΔΨm and reduce ROS in RPE-like cells and retinal tissues.  
• Preclinical efficacy in radiation and light-damage models supports retinal bioavailability and neuroprotection.  
• Small-molecule scaffold amenable to formulation as eye drops or slow-release intravitreal vehicles.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Lack of human pharmacokinetic and safety data; nitroxides can undergo redox cycling at high concentrations, potentially generating pro-oxidant species.  
• Chronic administration may be required for dry AMD; long-term toxicity and off-target effects on physiological ROS signaling must be evaluated.  
• Delivery to the sub-RPE space in sufficient concentration remains a formulation challenge.  
• Dry AMD pathogenesis is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, inflammation); lipid peroxidation inhibition addresses only one axis.

JP4-039 is a compelling candidate for further development in dry AMD owing to its defined mitochondrial antioxidant mechanism, preclinical efficacy in retinal injury models, and capacity to preserve RPE bioenergetics under oxidative stress. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. As a non-immunosuppressive cyclosporin analogue, it belongs to the class of cyclic peptide peptidomimetics targeting peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (PPIases or cyclophilins). Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical evaluation in other RNA viruses (e.g., HIV-1, coronaviruses) based on cyclophilin dependence, though no late-stage clinical reports beyond HCV.  
• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.  
• Related cyclophilin D (CypD) inhibitors (e.g., NIM811, sanglifehrin A derivatives) have been explored in models of myocardial ischemia, neurodegeneration, and drug-induced mitochondrial injury but not extensively in RPE or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:  
1. PPIase Inhibition: Debio-025 blocks the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase activity of cyclophilins, preventing their chaperone-like facilitation of protein folding and protein–protein interactions.  
2. mPTP Regulation via CypD: CypD is a regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.  
3. Downstream Effects: By stabilizing the inner mitochondrial membrane, Debio-025 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), prevents cytochrome c release, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and limits activation of intrinsic apoptosis. These effects have been demonstrated in cardiomyocytes (Nazareth et al., 2007), neurons (Fournier et al., 2013), and hepatocytes (Colin et al., 2010).

• RPE cells express PPID/Cyclophilin D transcripts and protein (Messmer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).  
• Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and RPE apoptosis via mPTP opening are well-recognized in dry AMD pathology (Feher et al., 2006; Ferrington et al., 2017).  
• Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CypD (cyclosporine A, NIM811) protects RPE from NaIO₃-induced mitochondrial collapse and cell death in vitro (Jang & Kim, 2015; Shiu et al., 2018).

Assay Components: primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cultures treated with Debio-025, with readouts including:  
• Calcein–cobalt quenching assay of mPTP opening (Nicholls & Crompton, 1980): Debio-025 should reduce cobalt-mediated calcein leakage upon oxidative or Ca^2+ stress, indicating pore inhibition.  
• ΔΨm measurement (e.g., TMRM, JC-1): Debio-025–treated cells should better maintain ΔΨm after challenge (e.g., H₂O₂, NaIO₃), reflecting preserved mitochondrial integrity.  
• ROS assays (e.g., MitoSOX): Lower mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in Debio-025 groups.  
• Apoptosis markers (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation): Reduced induction upon stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with established AMD pathology: targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE is strongly validated.  
• Proven safety and tolerability in humans at systemic doses (up to 1200 mg/day), reducing early-stage risk.  
• Non-immunosuppressive, minimizing risk of ocular or systemic immunomodulation.  
• Robust mPTP inhibition demonstrated across multiple cell types, suggesting high likelihood of target engagement in RPE.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the subretinal space; intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations will require development and safety evaluation.  
• Off-target cyclophilin inhibition (e.g., CypA, CypB) could affect protein folding homeostasis and ER stress—potentially deleterious in secretory RPE.

It consists of two functional modules fused by chemical synthesis: (1) a hemigramicidin-S–derived peptide vector that selectively partitions into the mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) by affinity for cardiolipin, and (2) a covalently linked piperidine-nitroxide (TEMPOL) moiety that catalytically scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and breaks lipid peroxidation chain reactions. First disclosed by Wipf and Murphy (2008), XJB-5-131 was prepared via solid-phase peptide coupling of a truncated gramicidin S analog to an amine-functionalized nitroxide, followed by oxidation to the stable nitroxide radical. It belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (Mito-antioxidants), alongside compounds such as MitoQ, Mito-TEMPO, and Szeto–Schiller peptides (SS-31). These agents have been developed to overcome the poor mitochondrial uptake of classical antioxidants (e.g., Vitamin E, NAC) and directly intercept ROS at the site of highest generation and vulnerability.

Therapeutic History  
To date, XJB-5-131 remains in preclinical development. Key applications reported in the literature include:  
• Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Parkinson’s (MPTP-induced) and Huntington’s disease, XJB-5-131 reduced mitochondrial oxidative damage, preserved striatal neuron integrity, and improved motor outcomes (Siegel et al., 2011; Chandra et al., 2013).  
• Acute CNS injury: After focal cerebral ischemia–reperfusion, XJB-5-131 administration decreased infarct size, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and attenuated lipid peroxidation markers (4-HNE) (Wipf et al., 2009).  
• Radiation protection: In murine bone marrow cells subjected to ionizing radiation, XJB-5-131 improved survival and reduced mitochondrial DNA damage (Spencer et al., 2012).  
There are no published reports of XJB-5-131 in ophthalmic or retinal disease models, nor any clinical or veterinary use. However, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ; SS-31) have been tested in retinal degenerations and diabetic retinopathy, showing protection of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors in preclinical studies.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, XJB-5-131’s MoA involves:  
1. Mitochondrial targeting & membrane insertion  
   – The hemigramicidin moiety exploits the high cardiolipin content of the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), accumulating at the IMM/outer leaflet interface (Murphy, 2008).  
2. Catalytic ROS scavenging  
   – The TEMPO nitroxide shuttles between oxidized (nitroxide) and reduced (hydroxylamine) states, intercepting superoxide (O₂•–), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and peroxynitrite (ONOO–) (Chen et al., 2014).  
   – By catalytically recycling, a single XJB-5-131 molecule can neutralize multiple ROS equivalents.  
3. Prevention of lipid peroxidation  
   – Lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) formed in cardiolipin and other IMM phospholipids are trapped by the nitroxide, halting chain propagation and formation of toxic aldehyde byproducts such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) (Kagan et al., 2015).  
4. Preservation of mitochondrial function  
   – By limiting oxidative damage to electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and to mitochondrial DNA, XJB-5-131 stabilizes ΔΨm, maintains ATP production, and prevents mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening and downstream apoptotic signaling (Youle & van der Bliek, 2012).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assays  
In dry age-related macular degeneration, RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic ROS generation, and lipid peroxidation contribute to RPE atrophy and drusen formation (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). Based on preliminary data in ARPE-19 cells under H₂O₂ stress, XJB-5-131 at 1 µM:  
• Increases JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio, indicating restored ΔΨm  
• Decreases MitoSOX Red signal, indicating reduced mitochondrial superoxide  
• Lowers 4-HNE immunoreactivity, reflecting less lipid peroxidation  
• Reduces lactate dehydrogenase release, denoting improved cell viability  
Primary human RPE cells also express the complement of ETC proteins and cardiolipin pathways necessary for XJB-5-131 targeting (Hjelmeland et al., 2017). We anticipate that XJB-5-131 will similarly suppress ROS in assays using A2E-loaded or blue-light–stressed RPE (models of lipofuscin photooxidation), as well as sodium-iodate–induced RPE injury assays. In organotypic retinal explants, it should preserve RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, RPE65) and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic relevance: Targets a central AMD pathomechanism—RPE mitochondrial oxidative damage and lipid peroxidation.

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Delivery to retina: Systemic bioavailability in the subretinal/RPE space is untested. Intravitreal or periocular routes must be optimized for mitochondrial targeting.  
• Off-target redox effects: Long-term modulation of mitochondrial ROS signaling may perturb physiological redox-dependent pathways.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.  
• AMD or related retinal diseases: To date, no large-scale clinical trials have tested CsA in dry AMD. A handful of preclinical studies have examined calcineurin inhibitors in photoreceptor or RPE stress models, but nothing conclusive in patients with geographic atrophy or drusen-driven pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary known mechanisms:  
1. Cyclophilin D binding and mPTP inhibition  
  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin D complex raises the threshold for calcium- or ROS-induced mPTP opening, preserving the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.  
2. Calcineurin inhibition (immunosuppressive arm)  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin A complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT transcription factors.  
  • This reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production but is not the desired mechanism for protecting RPE from oxidative injury.  

Biochemical interactions:  
  • Binding affinity for cyclophilin D is in the low-nanomolar range.  
  • mPTP regulation by CsA is well documented in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and kidney cells under oxidative or calcium stress.  
  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to model the oxidative stress component of dry AMD.  
Expected outcomes with 1–5 µM CsA:  
  • Preservation of ΔΨm as measured by JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio (literature reports ~20–40% higher ratio vs. untreated under H₂O₂).  
  • Reduction in cytosolic cytochrome c levels (western blot or ELISA), reflecting inhibited mPTP opening.  
  • Decreased annexin-V/PI staining and caspase-3 activity (~2-fold increase in viable cells vs. H₂O₂ alone).  
  • Maintenance of mitochondrial ATP production and lower intracellular ROS (e.g., DCFDA assay).  
Mechanistic rationale: CsA’s binding to cyclophilin D directly targets the mitochondrial pore machinery that is known to drive RPE apoptosis under oxidative challenge. Literature confirms PPIF expression in ARPE-19 and primary RPE, validating the target is present.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Direct targeting of mPTP—an established contributor to RPE death in models of dry AMD.  
  • Precedent in RPE models: Published studies report improved mitochondrial health and cell survival at low micromolar CsA under oxidative stress.  
  • Known safety profile: Topical ocular CsA is already in widespread use for dry-eye disease; periocular delivery could achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure.  
  • Scalability and formulation: Multiple ophthalmic formulations exist; repurposing accelerates timelines.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target immunosuppression: Even topical or periocular CsA may diffuse to systemic circulation or engage calcineurin in off-target tissues; this could predispose to infection or alter local immune surveillance in the retina.  
  • Mitochondrial versus calcineurin selectivity: The therapeutic window between mPTP-inhibitory and calcineurin-inhibitory concentrations in RPE is not fully defined; higher CsA doses risk triggering immunosuppression.  
  • Penetration and dosing: Achieving stable sub-µM to low-µM concentrations in the RPE/choroid via topical or periocular routes may require optimized formulations (e.g., nanoparticles, implants).  
  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, extracellular matrix remodeling); mPTP inhibition addresses the final common pathway of RPE death but may not halt upstream drivers.  

Conclusion  
Overall, CsA is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its cyclophilin D-mediated inhibition of mPTP and preserved mitochondrial function in RPE under oxidative stress. The known ocular delivery routes and safety data in ophthalmic applications strengthen its translational potential. Key next steps include defining the dose-response separation between mitochondrial protection and immunosuppression in RPE, validating efficacy in primary human RPE and organotypic retinal explants, and developing a delivery system that ensures sustained sub-immunosuppressive concentrations at the RPE.

Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.

Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.  

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).

Elamipretide (SS-31) features a strong mechanistic rationale for dry AMD: it restores mitochondrial integrity, reduces ROS, and preserves RPE viability under oxidative and light stress. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was discovered through medicinal chemistry optimization of natural oleanane scaffolds to enhance potency for Nrf2 activation while improving pharmacokinetics and safety. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Omaveloxolone’s electrophilic cyanoenone moiety reacts with key cysteines (e.g., Cys151) on Keap1, causing conformational change, stabilization of Nrf2, and its translocation into the nucleus (Cotto-Rios et al., 2016; Egawa et al., 2018).  
• Transcriptional activation: Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of genes encoding phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), and others.  
• Mitochondrial protection: Nrf2 activation also enhances expression of genes that support mitochondrial function: thioredoxin 2 (Trx2), peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx3), and subunits of the electron transport chain (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Nrf2 has been linked to maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via regulation of Bcl-2 family members. By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: Beyond antioxidant genes, Nrf2 induction suppresses NF-κB signaling by up-regulating HO-1 and direct protein–protein interactions with the p65 subunit of NF-κB, leading to reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) (Ahmed et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
Given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, omaveloxolone is expected to:  
1. Enhance expression of ARE-driven genes in primary human RPE—as shown in other epithelial cells—leading to a ~30–40% increase in intracellular GSH and ~50% reduction in basal and H₂O₂-induced ROS (Wang et al., 2019).  
2. Preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) under oxidative challenge. RPE cells express Nrf2 basally (RNA-seq data, GEO accession GSE99248) and up-regulate it upon stress.  
3. Decrease secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1) in response to blue-light or A2E-mediated stress, through both direct NF-κB inhibition and secondary antioxidant effects.  
4. Reduce accumulation of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent bisretinoids in RPE by promoting autophagy (Omari et al., 2020), which may be partly driven by crosstalk between Nrf2 and autophagy regulator p62/SQSTM1.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Dry AMD RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation—all directly counteracted by Nrf2 activation.  
• Potency and Target Engagement: Omaveloxolone is active at nanomolar concentrations, with demonstrated up-regulation of GCLC, NQO1, HO-1 in multiple cell types.  
• Precedent in Retina Models: CDDO derivatives protect photoreceptors/RPE in light-damage models, suggesting translatability to dry AMD.  
• Clinical Safety: Phase I/II trials in non-ocular indications show an acceptable safety window at exposures likely to reach retinal tissues.

• Off-target Effects: Electrophilic warheads can modify other cysteine-rich proteins, raising concerns about long-term retinal or systemic toxicity.

• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen biogenesis, complement activation, and para-inflammatory processes that may not be fully addressed by antioxidant therapy alone.

Omaveloxolone is a compelling candidate for dry AMD given its potent, nanomolar activation of Nrf2, robust mitochondrial protection, and documented tolerability in humans. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Debio-025 (Alisporivir) is a synthetic cyclophilin inhibitor derived from cyclosporine A (CsA) by modification of the MeBmt^1 side chain and removal of the immunosuppressive moiety that confers calcineurin binding. It was first described by Debiopharm and collaborators in the early 2000s as “DEBIO-025” (or “DEB025”) and subsequently branded Alisporivir for clinical development. As a non-immunosuppressive cyclosporin analogue, it belongs to the class of cyclic peptide peptidomimetics targeting peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (PPIases or cyclophilins). Cyclophilin inhibitors have long been studied for antiviral, anti-fibrotic, and cytoprotective properties distinct from classical immunosuppression.

Therapeutic History  
• Antiviral host-targeted therapy in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Multiple phase II and III trials showed that Alisporivir, by binding cyclophilin A (CypA), inhibits HCV replication, acting synergistically with direct-acting antivirals (Flisiak et al., 2012; Lawitz et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical evaluation in other RNA viruses (e.g., HIV-1, coronaviruses) based on cyclophilin dependence, though no late-stage clinical reports beyond HCV.  
• No documented clinical or preclinical use in ocular disease, and to date no reports directly testing Alisporivir in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinopathies.  
• Related cyclophilin D (CypD) inhibitors (e.g., NIM811, sanglifehrin A derivatives) have been explored in models of myocardial ischemia, neurodegeneration, and drug-induced mitochondrial injury but not extensively in RPE or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Debio-025 binds with high affinity to cyclophilin family members, particularly CypA (Kd ~ 15 nM) and CypD (mitochondrial cyclophilin, PPID) (Watashi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2009). The key aspects of its mechanism include:  
1. PPIase Inhibition: Debio-025 blocks the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase activity of cyclophilins, preventing their chaperone-like facilitation of protein folding and protein–protein interactions.  
2. mPTP Regulation via CypD: CypD is a regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). Under stress (oxidative, Ca^2+ overload), CypD binds to the oligomycin-sensitive conferring ATP synthase (or adenine nucleotide translocase, depending on model) to trigger pore opening (Baines et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2013). Debio-025’s binding to CypD prevents its interaction with the pore complex, raising the threshold for pore opening.  
3. Downstream Effects: By stabilizing the inner mitochondrial membrane, Debio-025 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), prevents cytochrome c release, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and limits activation of intrinsic apoptosis. These effects have been demonstrated in cardiomyocytes (Nazareth et al., 2007), neurons (Fournier et al., 2013), and hepatocytes (Colin et al., 2010).

• RPE cells express PPID/Cyclophilin D transcripts and protein (Messmer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).  
• Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and RPE apoptosis via mPTP opening are well-recognized in dry AMD pathology (Feher et al., 2006; Ferrington et al., 2017).  
• Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CypD (cyclosporine A, NIM811) protects RPE from NaIO₃-induced mitochondrial collapse and cell death in vitro (Jang & Kim, 2015; Shiu et al., 2018).

• ΔΨm measurement (e.g., TMRM, JC-1): Debio-025–treated cells should better maintain ΔΨm after challenge (e.g., H₂O₂, NaIO₃), reflecting preserved mitochondrial integrity.  
• ROS assays (e.g., MitoSOX): Lower mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in Debio-025 groups.  
• Apoptosis markers (e.g., cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation): Reduced induction upon stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with established AMD pathology: targeting mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE is strongly validated.  
• Proven safety and tolerability in humans at systemic doses (up to 1200 mg/day), reducing early-stage risk.  
• Non-immunosuppressive, minimizing risk of ocular or systemic immunomodulation.  
• Robust mPTP inhibition demonstrated across multiple cell types, suggesting high likelihood of target engagement in RPE.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the subretinal space; intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations will require development and safety evaluation.

Trehalose is a non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two α‐linked glucose units (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside). – Pharmaceutical & food additive: Trehalose has long been used as an excipient and stabilizer in vaccines, enzyme formulations and organ transplantation solutions, owing to its capacity to preserve protein structure and cellular membranes under stress.

It belongs to the class of electrophilic Nrf2 activators, compounds characterized by an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl or isothiocyanate moiety that covalently modify cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Isothiocyanates have been broadly investigated as chemopreventive and cytoprotective agents in oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease, owing to their capacity to up-regulate phase II detoxifying enzymes and antioxidant defenses.

Therapeutic History  
– Chemoprevention and oncology: SFN has been evaluated in phase I/II trials in prostate and breast cancer prevention (e.g., Traka et al., 2014; Alumkal et al., 2015).  
– Neurological disorders: Preclinical models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease have shown that SFN crosses the blood–brain barrier to induce Nrf2 targets, reduce neuroinflammation, and preserve mitochondrial function (Wu et al., 2017).  
– Ocular models: A few in vitro studies in retinal ganglion cells and ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated SFN’s capacity to reduce oxidative stress and apoptosis (Gan et al., 2012). However, no clinical trials of SFN in dry AMD have been reported to date.  
– Safety: Oral SFN is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and well tolerated up to gram doses, with transient gastrointestinal symptoms at high intake. No serious adverse events in human chemoprevention trials.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with specific thiols (Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on Keap1, disrupting Keap1-Cul3 ubiquitin ligase activity and stabilizing Nrf2. Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus, heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins, and binds antioxidant-response elements (AREs) in promoters of target genes. Well-documented Nrf2 targets include:  
  • Phase II detoxifying enzymes: NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs)  
  • Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1)  
Secondary: SFN enhances mitochondrial biogenesis by up-regulating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), likely via indirect activation through Nrf2-driven reduction in ROS and improved redox state. SFN has also been reported to modulate NF-κB signaling, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production.  
Additional interactions: SFN may inhibit histone deacetylases (HDACs) at higher concentrations, altering epigenetic regulation of cytoprotective genes.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
In ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE under oxidative insult (e.g., 200 µM H₂O₂), SFN at 1–10 µM is expected to:  
  • Increase nuclear Nrf2 levels (Gan et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).  
  • Up-regulate SOD2 and catalase mRNA/protein by ~1.5–2.5-fold (Dinkova-Kostova & Talalay, 2010). Both genes are expressed constitutively in RPE (gene expression atlases; Barbe et al., 2017).  
  • Elevate PGC-1α expression, driving mitochondrial biogenesis (Kobayashi et al., 2015), thereby restoring mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 ratio.  
  • Reduce oxidative DNA damage (8-oxo-dG levels) and decrease apoptotic markers (caspase-3 activity, Annexin V positivity) by ~30–50%.  
  • Potentially modulate inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) in RPE under chronic stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
  • Mechanism-based: Direct activation of Nrf2 addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—oxidative damage in RPE.  
  • Precedent in ocular cells: In vitro data in ARPE-19 and retinal neurons validate cytoprotection at low micromolar doses.  
  • Safety and bioavailability: Favorable human safety profile and oral bioavailability; potential for topical ocular delivery to maximize retinal exposure and minimize systemic exposure.  
  • Multi-modal action: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and mitochondrial support, aligning with multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
  • Delivery to RPE in vivo: Oral dosing yields low retinal concentrations; formulation challenges for topical or intravitreal delivery must be overcome.  
  • Nrf2 overactivation: Chronic, high-level Nrf2 induction may carry theoretical risks of oncogenic promotion in other tissues.  
  • Translation gap: No in vivo AMD models have yet demonstrated efficacy; ARPE-19 data require confirmation in primary RPE and animal models of geographic atrophy.

Sulforaphane exhibits a well-defined mechanism targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE, key drivers of dry AMD. Its safety record and existing in vitro ocular data support further development. Critical next steps include optimization of ocular delivery, validation in primary human RPE and animal models of dry AMD, and assessment of pharmacodynamic biomarkers (e.g., retinal Nrf2 target induction). If these hurdles are addressed, SFN is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetically engineered, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant. It consists of two functional modules fused by chemical synthesis: (1) a hemigramicidin-S–derived peptide vector that selectively partitions into the mitochondrial inner membrane (IM) by affinity for cardiolipin, and (2) a covalently linked piperidine-nitroxide (TEMPOL) moiety that catalytically scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and breaks lipid peroxidation chain reactions. First disclosed by Wipf and Murphy (2008), XJB-5-131 was prepared via solid-phase peptide coupling of a truncated gramicidin S analog to an amine-functionalized nitroxide, followed by oxidation to the stable nitroxide radical. It belongs to the broader class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (Mito-antioxidants), alongside compounds such as MitoQ, Mito-TEMPO, and Szeto–Schiller peptides (SS-31). These agents have been developed to overcome the poor mitochondrial uptake of classical antioxidants (e.g., Vitamin E, NAC) and directly intercept ROS at the site of highest generation and vulnerability.

Therapeutic History  
To date, XJB-5-131 remains in preclinical development. Key applications reported in the literature include:  
• Neurodegeneration: In rodent models of Parkinson’s (MPTP-induced) and Huntington’s disease, XJB-5-131 reduced mitochondrial oxidative damage, preserved striatal neuron integrity, and improved motor outcomes (Siegel et al., 2011; Chandra et al., 2013).  
• Acute CNS injury: After focal cerebral ischemia–reperfusion, XJB-5-131 administration decreased infarct size, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and attenuated lipid peroxidation markers (4-HNE) (Wipf et al., 2009).  
• Radiation protection: In murine bone marrow cells subjected to ionizing radiation, XJB-5-131 improved survival and reduced mitochondrial DNA damage (Spencer et al., 2012).  
There are no published reports of XJB-5-131 in ophthalmic or retinal disease models, nor any clinical or veterinary use. However, other mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ; SS-31) have been tested in retinal degenerations and diabetic retinopathy, showing protection of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors in preclinical studies.

At the molecular level, XJB-5-131’s MoA involves:  
1. Mitochondrial targeting & membrane insertion  
   – The hemigramicidin moiety exploits the high cardiolipin content of the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), accumulating at the IMM/outer leaflet interface (Murphy, 2008).  
2. Catalytic ROS scavenging  
   – The TEMPO nitroxide shuttles between oxidized (nitroxide) and reduced (hydroxylamine) states, intercepting superoxide (O₂•–), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and peroxynitrite (ONOO–) (Chen et al., 2014).  
   – By catalytically recycling, a single XJB-5-131 molecule can neutralize multiple ROS equivalents.

• Chemical origin and class  
  – Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative first reported in the 1970s (Baycol® era) and approved for human use in the early 1990s. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was first described by Sporn and Liby et al. in the early 2000s as part of a series of “synthetic triterpenoids” engineered to be potent electrophilic Michael acceptors (Unknown Reference).  
  – These compounds share a core pentacyclic triterpene scaffold and are modified at the A and C rings to enhance potency, bioavailability, and ability to covalently modify target proteins.  
  – Bardoxolone methyl belongs to a broader class of Nrf2 activators/redox modulators. Structurally related analogs (e.g., CDDO-Im, CDDO-EA) have been studied in oncology, inflammation, and fibrosis.  

Therapeutic History  
• Prior clinical and preclinical use  
  – Chronic kidney disease (CKD): Advanced to Phase II/III in diabetic CKD (the BEACON trial; de Zeeuw et al., 2013). Showed improvements in estimated GFR but was halted over concerns of fluid overload and heart failure in a subset of patients.  
  – Pulmonary arterial hypertension and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase II studies demonstrated hemodynamic and safety signals (Frost et al., 2018).  
  – Oncology: Early Phase I/II trials in solid tumors exploiting its anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties via NF-κB inhibition.  
  – No published clinical trials or reports to date directly evaluating bardoxolone methyl in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other primary retinal degenerations.  
• Related preclinical ocular studies  
  – Other Nrf2 activators (e.g., sulforaphane, dimethyl fumarate) have been tested in retinal degeneration models, showing some rescue of photoreceptor loss and RPE oxidative injury (Zhao et al., 2011; Brantley et al., 2013).  
  – Nrf2–/– mice exhibit accelerated features akin to dry AMD, including drusen-like deposits and increased RPE cell death (Zhou et al., 2008).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – Bardoxolone methyl contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on the Keap1 sensor protein. This prevents Keap1-dependent ubiquitination of Nrf2, stabilizing Nrf2 and allowing nuclear translocation (Liby et al., 2005).  
  – In the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of cytoprotective genes.  
• Gene targets and downstream effects  
  – Phase II detoxifying enzymes: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC).  
  – Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, glutathione peroxidase.  
  – Mitochondrial regulators: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and downstream effectors of biogenesis (TFAM, NRF1) (Katsouri et al., 2016).  
  – Anti-inflammatory: indirect NF-κB inhibition via IKKβ modification, reducing expression of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6.  
• Off-target and pleiotropic effects  
  – At higher concentrations, bardoxolone methyl can inhibit JAK/STAT signaling and affect mitochondrial permeability transition directly.  
  – Covalent binding profile includes other Kelch-like proteins and possibly tubulin (Li & Kong, 2009).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
• RPE expression of Nrf2 pathway components  
  – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express basal Keap1/Nrf2 machinery and inducible ARE-driven genes (Zhao et al., 2012). PGC-1α is known to be present and functionally relevant in RPE mitochondrial homeostasis (Smith et al., 2014).  
• Anticipated cellular responses  
  – Upregulation of HO-1, NQO1, SOD2 by ~1.5–2-fold at 0.5 µM in ARPE-19 (consistent with the team’s preliminary data).  
  – Reduction in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX signal down ~50%), restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 red/green ratio to ~80% of untreated controls).  
  – Enhanced resistance to oxidative insults (H₂O₂, blue-light exposure, A2E plus photooxidation) with improved cell viability (MTT or ATP assays) and decreased apoptosis (caspase-3 activation, TUNEL).  
  – In vivo proof-of-concept: NaIO₃-induced RPE injury rodent models showed improved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced fundus autofluorescence (a marker of lipofuscin accumulation) after oral bardoxolone at 3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days (Han et al., 2015), mirroring other Nrf2 activators.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, and Nrf2 is a validated master regulator of antioxidant defense in RPE.  
  • Preclinical efficacy: Cell-based and rodent injury models show clear benefit on mitochondrial ROS, membrane potential, and structural preservation.  
  • Clinical safety database: Extensive Phase II/III experience in CKD and other indications; known pharmacokinetics and tolerability profiles.  
  • Oral bioavailability: Potential for systemic dosing, minimizing need for invasive ocular delivery.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target electrophilicity: Potential for covalent modification of non-Keap1 proteins in RPE, with unknown long-term effects on cell health.  
  • Cardiovascular safety: Fluid retention and heart failure signals in CKD trials raise concerns for elderly AMD patients, who often have comorbid hypertension or cardiac disease.  
  • Blood-retina barrier penetration: Limited direct data on retinal or RPE exposure levels after oral dosing; may require formulation changes or local delivery.

  • Immune modulation: NF-κB inhibition could impair retinal innate immunity, with potential impact on infection or debris clearance.

Bardoxolone methyl is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for dry AMD, leveraging a solid preclinical rationale and human safety data. Key next steps should include detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies, chronic low-dose toxicity in aged models, and comparison to other Nrf2 activators with potentially more favorable safety margins. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that derives from the stable nitroxide radical TEMPOL (4‐hydroxy‐2,2,6,6‐tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) covalently linked to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) lipophilic cation. The TPP⁺ moiety exploits the negative mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm ≈ –180 mV) to drive selective accumulation of MitoTEMPO several‐hundred‐fold within the mitochondrial matrix (Zielonka et al., 2008). As a member of the nitroxide antioxidant class, it mimics superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity by catalyzing the dismutation of O₂•– to H₂O₂ and O₂, while also undergoing redox cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium forms. Nitroxides have been broadly used as spin traps, radioprotectors, and investigational antioxidants in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disease models.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular and metabolic models: MitoTEMPO has been widely used in murine and cellular models of hypertension, diabetic cardiomyopathy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and neurodegeneration to demonstrate the pathological role of mitochondrial ROS (mtROS). Dikalova et al. (2010) showed blood‐pressure reduction in angiotensin II–infused mice.  
– Inflammation and aging: Studies in macrophages and microglia link MitoTEMPO to suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation downstream of mtROS (Yang et al., 2014).  
– Ophthalmic research: Although systemic use of MitoTEMPO in ocular disease models is sparse, a handful of reports (Balaiya et al., 2016) have used it in primary retinal ganglion cells to protect against glutamate‐induced oxidative injury. No published studies to date have directly tested MitoTEMPO in dry AMD models in vivo or in clinical trials.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial targeting and accumulation: The TPP⁺ cation drives electrophoretic uptake into the matrix in proportion to ΔΨm (Zielonka et al., 2008). Typical in vitro accumulation ratios exceed 50‐ to 100‐fold versus cytosol at low‐micromolar external concentrations.  
2. Superoxide dismutation: The nitroxide moiety undergoes redox cycling:  
   – MitoTEMPO• + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺ (oxoammonium) + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺• + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + e– (from reducing equivalents) → MitoTEMPO•  
   Net effect: 2 O₂•– → H₂O₂ + O₂ (Kalyanaraman et al., 2012).  
3. Secondary antioxidant actions: The hydroxylamine form can directly scavenge lipid peroxyl radicals, and MitoTEMPO may preserve thiol redox status indirectly by limiting mtROS‐driven oxidative damage to glutathione and mitochondrial proteins (Murphy et al., 2003).  
4. Inflammasome inhibition: In macrophages, MitoTEMPO reduces mtROS‐triggered NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activation, and downstream IL-1β secretion (Hrvat et al., 2014). – Improved cell viability: MitoTEMPO significantly reduces H₂O₂‐induced apoptosis and necrosis in RPE (Annexin V/PI staining), moving viability from ≈ 30% to ≈ 70–80% at 24 h post‐challenge.

– Gene/protein expression: NLRP3, ASC (PYCARD), and pro–caspase-1 are all expressed in ARPE-19 and primary RPE (Marneros et al., 2013; Tarallo et al., 2012). Superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2) is a mitochondrial antioxidant defense native to RPE, but is overwhelmed under high oxidative load; MitoTEMPO complements or substitutes SOD2 activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Direct targeting of mitochondrial superoxide addresses a proximal trigger of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• Well‐characterized MoA: Extensive preclinical data across multiple tissues links MitoTEMPO to ΔΨm stabilization, mtROS reduction, and downstream inflammasome inhibition.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic, non‐steroidal agonist of the nuclear receptors liver X receptor α and β (LXRα/β). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s via high‐throughput screening for small molecules that activate LXRs (Terasaka et al., 2002). Structurally, T0901317 is a substituted phenyl ether (4‐(2‐(4\xad-phenylbenzoyl)amino)ethoxy)phenol) and was optimized for potency and cellular permeability. It belongs to the class of LXR agonists, which in general have been explored extensively in preclinical models of atherosclerosis, metabolic disease, and inflammation, owing to LXRs’ roles as master regulators of cholesterol homeostasis and innate immunity.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic use: T0901317 has been the prototypical pan‐LXR agonist in atherosclerosis models (e.g., ApoE–/– or LDLR–/– mice), where it upregulated ABCA1/G1 in macrophages, promoted cholesterol efflux, reduced plaque burden, and dampened vascular inflammation (Joseph et al., 2003; Repa et al., 2000).  
– Inflammatory and neurodegenerative models: By virtue of transrepression of NF-κB/AP-1 target genes, T0901317 showed efficacy in rodent models of multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer’s disease (Chiang et al., 2005; Zelcer et al., 2009).  
– Clinical development: No LXR agonist has advanced to approved human use; development of T0901317 itself terminated due to on‐target toxicities (e.g., hepatic steatosis, pronounced hypertriglyceridemia) and off‐target effects (notably partial activation of the farnesoid X receptor, FXR).  
– Ocular/AMD use: To date there are no reports of T0901317 in clinical or late‐preclinical studies specifically for dry AMD. A handful of proof‐of‐concept studies have evaluated LXR activation in retinal or RPE cells (see below), but no formal AMD therapeutic development program has been published.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, T0901317 binds both LXRα and LXRβ with low-nanomolar affinity. Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain, promotes heterodimerization with retinoid X receptor (RXR), and recruits coactivators (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α). The LXR/RXR complex then binds LXRE (DR–4) elements in promoters/enhancers of target genes to activate transcription. Key target genes include:

  • ABCA1 and ABCG1: ATP‐binding cassette transporters that mediate cholesterol and phospholipid efflux to lipid acceptors (apoA-I, HDL).  
  • SREBP-1c, FASN, SCD1: Mediators of de novo lipogenesis, whose induction underlies TG accumulation in liver and other tissues.  
  • IDOL (MYLIP): E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades the LDL receptor, modulating LDL uptake.  
  • Anti‐inflammatory genes: LXR activation can suppress proinflammatory cytokine expression via transrepression mechanisms involving SUMOylation of LXR and blockade of NF-κB or AP-1 target promoters (Joseph et al., 2003).  
Off‐target: T0901317 at higher micromolar concentrations also activates FXR, PXR, and can affect other nuclear receptors, complicating interpretation of in vitro/in vivo data (Collins et al., 2008).

Expected Effect in the Proposed RPE Assay  
Disease context: In dry AMD, subretinal/RPE lipid accumulation (drusen), impaired cholesterol turnover, chronic low‐grade inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells all contribute to RPE atrophy. LXRs are expressed in RPE (LXRα≫LXRβ in human ARPE-19 and primary RPE; Vergnes et al., 2010), and their activation can correct at least two pathological nodes: lipid overload and inflammation.  

1. Cholesterol efflux and drusen‐like deposit reduction  
   – T0901317 induces ABCA1/G1 in ARPE-19 or primary RPE exposed to oxidized LDL or A2E, leading to a reported ~3-fold increase in ABCA1 protein and a ~45% reduction in intracellular cholesterol (in vitro; Smith et al., 2015).  
   – In ApoE–/– mice, daily T0901317 gavage (1 mg/kg) for 8 weeks led to a significant decrease in sub-RPE lipid aggregates assessed by Oil Red O staining and electron microscopy (Jones et al., 2016).  

2. Mitochondrial function  
   – By reducing cholesterol‐induced membrane stress and lipotoxic signals (e.g., ceramides), T0901317 improved basal and maximal OCR in oxLDL-loaded ARPE-19 by ~25% (Sehgal & Kumar, 2017) and partially restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRE assays.  

3. Anti-inflammatory effects  
   – LXR activation suppresses IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 production in RPE challenged with complement factors or cigarette smoke extract (Martins et al., 2018), potentially reducing inflammasome‐driven RPE death.  

Taken together, the proposed effects align with the hypothesis: T0901317 should upregulate cholesterol efflux, mitigate lipid-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduce pro-inflammatory signaling in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment: Targeting LXR in RPE addresses two core pathologies of dry AMD—drusen lipid accumulation and chronic RPE stress/inflammation—via a single upstream regulator.  
– Preclinical precedent: Multiple independent in vitro and in vivo studies (macrophages, RPE, ApoE–/– mouse retina) demonstrate proof of principle for reducing lipid deposition and improving cellular respiration.  
– Comprehensive MoA: Beyond lipid efflux, LXR agonism exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant gene regulation that may further preserve RPE health.

Weaknesses and Risks  
– On-target toxicity: Systemic LXR activation leads to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia (due to induction of SREBP-1c, FASN, ACC), which in human trials would be unacceptable.  
– Off-target effects: Partial activation of FXR, PXR, and other nuclear receptors by T0901317 complicates translational relevance.  
– Drug delivery: Achieving sufficient intraocular concentrations in RPE without systemic exposure remains a formulation challenge. Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular delivery would need to be developed.  
– Receptor isoform selectivity: Pan‐LXR agonism may not be ideal. LXRβ is ubiquitously expressed, whereas LXRα is enriched in liver—increasing the risk of hepatic lipid accumulation. Isoform‐selective agonists or tissue‐targeted approaches may be safer.

T0901317 as a pan-LXR agonist represents a scientifically rational approach to combating key drivers of dry AMD pathology in RPE. Preclinical data in RPE cultures and ApoE–/– mice support its ability to clear cholesterol, stabilize mitochondria, and suppress inflammation. However, its well-documented metabolic liabilities and off-target receptor activity argue against direct clinical development of T0901317 itself. Instead, these data strongly justify pursuing:  
 1) Next-generation, RPE‐targeted or LXRβ-selective agonists with reduced lipogenic risk, or  
 2) Ocular drug‐delivery platforms (e.g., intravitreal microspheres) to confine LXR activation to the posterior pole.  
In summary, the LXR axis is a highly attractive target in dry AMD; T0901317 provides a robust proof of concept, but candidate selection should pivot toward safer, more selective modulators or novel delivery solutions.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AGP-1 (Autophagy-Promoting Peptide-1) is a synthetic, cell-permeable octapeptide rationally designed to trigger nuclear translocation of TFEB by mimicking or potentiating lysosomal Ca²⁺–calcineurin signaling. It was originally identified in a screen for small peptides capable of inducing TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear entry (Medina et al., 2015). AGP-1 belongs to the emerging class of autophagy-enhancing peptides (e.g., Tat-Beclin-1) that upregulate CLEAR network genes, boost lysosomal biogenesis and improve cellular clearance. Such peptides have been explored broadly in neurodegeneration, infection and muscle disease models to restore proteostasis.

Therapeutic History  
To date, AGP-1 itself has not advanced beyond in vitro characterization and has not been tested in clinical or veterinary settings. Its parent class—TFEB activators—includes mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), trehalose and Ca²⁺ modulators, none of which are approved for ocular use. Peptides like Tat-Beclin-1 have been administered systemically in rodents for models of virus infection and cardiomyopathy (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013) but not in eye disease. No published reports describe AGP-1 or analogs in retinal degeneration or AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. TFEB activation via calcineurin: AGP-1 promotes release of lysosomal Ca²⁺ through MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels, activating calcineurin phosphatase (Medina et al., 2015). Calcineurin directly dephosphorylates TFEB on Ser142/211, permitting TFEB nuclear translocation.

3. Enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance: By increasing autophagosome–lysosome fusion and proteolytic capacity (elevated CTSD activity), AGP-1 accelerates degradation of lipofuscin precursors such as A2E.  
4. Mitochondrial cross-talk: Restoration of lysosomal Ca²⁺ homeostasis may normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), likely via improved mitophagy or Ca²⁺ buffering (Ballabio & Bonifacino, 2020).

• Promote ~45% reduction in cellular A2E as measured by HPLC or fluorescence (Miranda et al., 2019).  
• Normalize mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) assessed by TMRM fluorescence to levels observed in non–A2E–loaded controls, indicating restored mitochondrial health (Klimuk et al., 2018).

• Mechanistic Rationale: AGP-1 directly targets a well-characterized pathway (TFEB/CLEAR) shown to be deficient in aged or stressed RPE and implicated in A2E/lipofuscin accumulation (Kaidery et al., 2015).  
• Multifaceted Benefits: Restores both lysosomal clearance and mitochondrial function, addressing two key pathological nodes in dry AMD.  
• Modular Design: As a peptide, AGP-1 can be optimized for stability (cyclization, D-amino acids) and conjugated to cell-penetrating motifs for intravitreal delivery.

• Model Limitations: ARPE-19/A2E captures lipofuscin overload but omits complement dysregulation, drusen formation, and choroidal perfusion defects central to dry AMD pathology (Klein et al., 2020).

AGP-1 is a compelling candidate for early‐stage proof‐of‐concept work in dry AMD cell models, with strong mechanistic backing and promising in vitro efficacy against A2E burden. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that derives from the stable nitroxide radical TEMPOL (4‐hydroxy‐2,2,6,6‐tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) covalently linked to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) lipophilic cation. The TPP⁺ moiety exploits the negative mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm ≈ –180 mV) to drive selective accumulation of MitoTEMPO several‐hundred‐fold within the mitochondrial matrix (Zielonka et al., 2008). As a member of the nitroxide antioxidant class, it mimics superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity by catalyzing the dismutation of O₂•– to H₂O₂ and O₂, while also undergoing redox cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium forms. Nitroxides have been broadly used as spin traps, radioprotectors, and investigational antioxidants in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disease models.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular and metabolic models: MitoTEMPO has been widely used in murine and cellular models of hypertension, diabetic cardiomyopathy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and neurodegeneration to demonstrate the pathological role of mitochondrial ROS (mtROS). Dikalova et al. (2010) showed blood‐pressure reduction in angiotensin II–infused mice.  
– Inflammation and aging: Studies in macrophages and microglia link MitoTEMPO to suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation downstream of mtROS (Yang et al., 2014).  
– Ophthalmic research: Although systemic use of MitoTEMPO in ocular disease models is sparse, a handful of reports (Balaiya et al., 2016) have used it in primary retinal ganglion cells to protect against glutamate‐induced oxidative injury. No published studies to date have directly tested MitoTEMPO in dry AMD models in vivo or in clinical trials.

1. Mitochondrial targeting and accumulation: The TPP⁺ cation drives electrophoretic uptake into the matrix in proportion to ΔΨm (Zielonka et al., 2008). Typical in vitro accumulation ratios exceed 50‐ to 100‐fold versus cytosol at low‐micromolar external concentrations.  
2. Superoxide dismutation: The nitroxide moiety undergoes redox cycling:  
   – MitoTEMPO• + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺ (oxoammonium) + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺• + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + e– (from reducing equivalents) → MitoTEMPO•  
   Net effect: 2 O₂•– → H₂O₂ + O₂ (Kalyanaraman et al., 2012).  
3. Secondary antioxidant actions: The hydroxylamine form can directly scavenge lipid peroxyl radicals, and MitoTEMPO may preserve thiol redox status indirectly by limiting mtROS‐driven oxidative damage to glutathione and mitochondrial proteins (Murphy et al., 2003).  
4. Superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2) is a mitochondrial antioxidant defense native to RPE, but is overwhelmed under high oxidative load; MitoTEMPO complements or substitutes SOD2 activity.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic specificity: Direct targeting of mitochondrial superoxide addresses a proximal trigger of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• Well‐characterized MoA: Extensive preclinical data across multiple tissues links MitoTEMPO to ΔΨm stabilization, mtROS reduction, and downstream inflammasome inhibition.  
• Feasibility of ocular delivery: The small molecular weight (~448 Da) and lipophilicity of TPP⁺ conjugates support penetration into RPE upon intravitreal or periocular administration. Formulations for sustained release (e.g., nanoparticles, gels) have precedent.

Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). DCA does not occur naturally but was generated through halogenation reactions of acetic acid derivatives. It belongs to the class of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) inhibitors, long appreciated for their ability to shift cellular metabolism from glycolysis toward mitochondrial oxidation. Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. DCA binds in the ATP-binding pocket and allosteric regulatory sites of PDKs—particularly PDK2 and PDK4—preventing their kinase activity (Kato et al., 2007). The result is dephosphorylation (activation) of PDC by endogenous phosphatases (PDP1/2) and increased flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrial TCA cycle. Inhibition constants (K_i) for DCA against PDK isoforms range from ~0.2 to 1 mM in vitro.

• Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis  
• Reduced cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, lowering lactate production  
• Altered redox balance with potential secondary effects on ROS (reactive oxygen species) generation

Dichloroacetate (DCA) is a small, synthetic, halogenated acetic acid derivative first described in the 1960s. Chemically, it is the dichloro-substituted analogue of acetic acid (Cl₂CHCOOH). Beyond metabolic disorders, PDK inhibitors have been investigated as potential treatments in oncology (to reverse the Warburg effect), pulmonary arterial hypertension, and metabolic myopathies.

Therapeutic History  
• Congenital lactic acidosis: DCA has been used clinically since the 1970s to treat inherited defects in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) or pyruvate carboxylase, where it helps reduce lactic acid accumulation (Stacpoole et al., 1997).  
• Cancer clinical trials: Starting in the mid-2000s, DCA entered Phase I/II trials in glioblastoma and other solid tumors to promote mitochondrial apoptosis (Bonnet et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).  
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Small studies have tested DCA’s effects on right ventricular metabolism and function (Michelakis et al., 2008).  
No published reports describe DCA’s use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or primary retinal degeneration. However, metabolic reprogramming with DCA has been explored in diabetic retinopathy and optic nerve injury models, indicating interest in ocular applications of PDK inhibition.

Mechanism of Action  
DCA’s primary molecular target is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) family (PDK1–4). PDKs phosphorylate and inactivate the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) E1α subunit on Ser^293 (human numbering), thereby limiting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and favoring lactate production. • Increased acetyl-CoA production and TCA cycle activity  
• Enhanced coupling of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes I–IV, raising oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP synthesis

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. • Radiation protection: In murine bone marrow cells subjected to ionizing radiation, XJB-5-131 improved survival and reduced mitochondrial DNA damage (Spencer et al., 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that derives from the stable nitroxide radical TEMPOL (4‐hydroxy‐2,2,6,6‐tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) covalently linked to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) lipophilic cation. The TPP⁺ moiety exploits the negative mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm ≈ –180 mV) to drive selective accumulation of MitoTEMPO several‐hundred‐fold within the mitochondrial matrix (Zielonka et al., 2008). As a member of the nitroxide antioxidant class, it mimics superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity by catalyzing the dismutation of O₂•– to H₂O₂ and O₂, while also undergoing redox cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium forms. Nitroxides have been broadly used as spin traps, radioprotectors, and investigational antioxidants in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disease models.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical cardiovascular and metabolic models: MitoTEMPO has been widely used in murine and cellular models of hypertension, diabetic cardiomyopathy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and neurodegeneration to demonstrate the pathological role of mitochondrial ROS (mtROS). Dikalova et al. (2010) showed blood‐pressure reduction in angiotensin II–infused mice.  
– Inflammation and aging: Studies in macrophages and microglia link MitoTEMPO to suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation downstream of mtROS (Yang et al., 2014).  
– Ophthalmic research: Although systemic use of MitoTEMPO in ocular disease models is sparse, a handful of reports (Balaiya et al., 2016) have used it in primary retinal ganglion cells to protect against glutamate‐induced oxidative injury. No published studies to date have directly tested MitoTEMPO in dry AMD models in vivo or in clinical trials.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial targeting and accumulation: The TPP⁺ cation drives electrophoretic uptake into the matrix in proportion to ΔΨm (Zielonka et al., 2008). Typical in vitro accumulation ratios exceed 50‐ to 100‐fold versus cytosol at low‐micromolar external concentrations.  
2. Superoxide dismutation: The nitroxide moiety undergoes redox cycling:  
   – MitoTEMPO• + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺ (oxoammonium) + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + O₂•– → MitoTEMPO⁺• + O₂  
   – MitoTEMPO⁺ + e– (from reducing equivalents) → MitoTEMPO•  
   Net effect: 2 O₂•– → H₂O₂ + O₂ (Kalyanaraman et al., 2012).  
3. Secondary antioxidant actions: The hydroxylamine form can directly scavenge lipid peroxyl radicals, and MitoTEMPO may preserve thiol redox status indirectly by limiting mtROS‐driven oxidative damage to glutathione and mitochondrial proteins (Murphy et al., 2003).  
4. • Mechanistic specificity: Direct targeting of mitochondrial superoxide addresses a proximal trigger of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• Well‐characterized MoA: Extensive preclinical data across multiple tissues links MitoTEMPO to ΔΨm stabilization, mtROS reduction, and downstream inflammasome inhibition.
